# Filesystem MCP Server

Node.js server implementing Model Context Protocol (MCP) for filesystem operations.

Published on npm as [`@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem).

## Features

- Read/write files
- Create/list/delete directories
- Move files/directories
- Search files
- Get file metadata
- Directory access control from command-line arguments, with [Roots](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/client-concepts#roots) as a deprecated, 2025-era convenience
- Serves both protocol eras on stdio: 2026-07-28 clients (`server/discover`, no handshake) and 2025-era clients (`initialize`)

## Directory Access Control

The server may touch only its **allowed directories**. Pass them on the command line. A 2025-era client that supports [Roots](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/client-concepts#roots) can also replace them at runtime, but Roots is [deprecated as of protocol version 2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/deprecated) and a 2026-07-28 connection cannot use it.

### Method 1: Command-line Arguments (Recommended)
Specify Allowed directories when starting the server:
```bash
mcp-server-filesystem /path/to/dir1 /path/to/dir2
```

This is the only method that works on every protocol version, so it is the one to use.

### Method 2: MCP Roots (Deprecated, 2025-era clients only)
A client that connects with a 2025-era protocol version (the `initialize` handshake) and supports [Roots](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/client-concepts#roots) can dynamically update the Allowed directories.

Roots notified by Client to Server, completely replace any server-side Allowed directories when provided.

A Root reached through a symlink is allowed in both its advertised form and its resolved form, as a command-line directory is: a Root of `file:///tmp/project` on macOS allows `/tmp/project` and `/private/tmp/project`. Every requested path is still resolved and checked against the resolved directories, so a symlink inside a Root that points outside it is refused.

**Important**: If server starts without command-line arguments AND a 2025-era client doesn't support roots protocol, the server fails at initialization: it logs the reason to stderr, closes the connection and exits with status 1. A client that supports roots but provides none (or none that are valid) keeps the connection, with no allowed directories until it sends `roots/list_changed` with valid roots.

The 2026-07-28 protocol has no `initialize` handshake and no server-to-client `roots/list` request, so a 2026-07-28 client's roots are never asked for: the command-line directories are the whole allow-list. A server started with none answers every tool call on such a connection with an error saying so.

### How It Works

The server's directory access control follows this flow:

1. **Server Startup**
   - Server starts with directories from command-line arguments (if provided)
   - If no arguments provided, server starts with empty allowed directories

2. **Client Connection**
   - The client's first message picks the protocol era of the connection
   - A **2026-07-28** client sends `server/discover` (or any request carrying the per-request `_meta` envelope): the server uses the command-line directories, and steps 3 and 4 do not apply
   - A **2025-era** client sends `initialize` with its capabilities, and the server checks whether it supports roots (`capabilities.roots`)
   
3. **Roots Protocol Handling** (2025-era clients that support roots)
   - **On initialization**: Server requests roots from client via `roots/list`
   - Client responds with its configured roots
   - Server replaces ALL allowed directories with client's roots
   - Tool calls that arrive before the initial roots are loaded wait for them, so they are checked against the client's roots
   - **On runtime updates**: Client can send `notifications/roots/list_changed`
   - Server requests updated roots and replaces allowed directories again
   - Tool calls that arrive while an update is being fetched wait for it, so none runs against a root the client has just withdrawn
   - Once the client's roots are in force, an update with no valid roots revokes access: every path is refused ("Access denied - no allowed directories") until the client exposes a root again. Before any root has been in force, such an update keeps the command-line directories

4. **Fallback Behavior** (2025-era clients that don't support roots)
   - Server continues using command-line directories only
   - No dynamic updates possible
   - With no command-line directories either, the server logs an error, closes the connection and exits with status 1

5. **Access Control**
   - All filesystem operations are restricted to allowed directories
   - Use `list_allowed_directories` tool to see current directories
   - Server requires at least ONE allowed directory to operate

**Note**: The server will only allow operations within directories specified either via `args` or, for a 2025-era client, via Roots.

## API

### Tools

- **read_text_file**
  - Read complete contents of a file as text
  - Inputs:
    - `path` (string)
    - `head` (number, optional): First N lines
    - `tail` (number, optional): Last N lines
  - Always treats the file as UTF-8 text regardless of extension
  - Cannot specify both `head` and `tail` simultaneously

- **read_media_file**
  - Read a file and return it as a base64-encoded content block with its MIME type
  - Inputs:
    - `path` (string)
  - Streams the file and returns base64 data with the corresponding MIME type. Image and
    audio files are returned as `image`/`audio` content; any other file type is returned as
    an embedded `resource` (a valid MCP content block for arbitrary binary data)

- **read_multiple_files**
  - Read multiple files simultaneously
  - Input: `paths` (string[])
  - Failed reads won't stop the entire operation

- **write_file**

# mcp-server-git: A git MCP server

## Overview

A Model Context Protocol server for Git repository interaction and automation. This server provides tools to read, search, and manipulate Git repositories via Large Language Models.

Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/git

Requires MCP Python SDK 2.x (`mcp>=2.3,<3`). The server is built on the SDK's high-level `MCPServer`: each tool is a typed Python function, and the SDK derives its input schema from the signature.

Please note that mcp-server-git is currently in early development. The functionality and available tools are subject to change and expansion as we continue to develop and improve the server.

### Tools

1. `git_status`
   - Shows the working tree status
   - Input:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
   - Returns: Current status of working directory as text output

2. `git_diff_unstaged`
   - Shows changes in working directory not yet staged
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `context_lines` (number, optional): Number of context lines to show (default: 3)
   - Returns: Diff output of unstaged changes

3. `git_diff_staged`
   - Shows changes that are staged for commit
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `context_lines` (number, optional): Number of context lines to show (default: 3)
   - Returns: Diff output of staged changes

4. `git_diff`
   - Shows differences between branches or commits
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `target` (string): Target branch or commit to compare with
     - `context_lines` (number, optional): Number of context lines to show (default: 3)
   - Returns: Diff output comparing current state with target

5. `git_commit`
   - Records changes to the repository
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `message` (string): Commit message
   - Returns: Confirmation with new commit hash; an error if nothing is staged (as `git commit` without `--allow-empty`), except while a merge is in progress (`MERGE_HEAD` present), where git also allows an empty commit. While a merge is in progress the commit concludes it: its parents are `HEAD` and every `MERGE_HEAD` commit, and the merge state is cleared

6. `git_add`
   - Adds file contents to the staging area
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `files` (string[]): Non-empty array of file paths to stage; `["."]` stages everything
   - Returns: Confirmation of staged files, or a message saying nothing was staged when the call left the index unchanged

7. `git_reset`
   - Unstages all staged changes
   - Input:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
   - Returns: Confirmation of reset operation

8. `git_log`
   - Shows the commit logs with optional date filtering
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `max_count` (number, optional): Maximum number of commits to show (default: 10)
     - `start_timestamp` (string, optional): Start timestamp for filtering commits. Accepts ISO 8601 format (e.g., '2024-01-15T14:30:25'), relative dates (e.g., '2 weeks ago', 'yesterday'), or absolute dates (e.g., '2024-01-15', 'Jan 15 2024')
     - `end_timestamp` (string, optional): End timestamp for filtering commits. Accepts ISO 8601 format (e.g., '2024-01-15T14:30:25'), relative dates (e.g., '2 weeks ago', 'yesterday'), or absolute dates (e.g., '2024-01-15', 'Jan 15 2024')
   - Returns: Array of commit entries with hash, author, date, and message

9. `git_create_branch`
   - Creates a new branch
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `branch_name` (string): Name of the new branch
     - `base_branch` (string, optional): Branch, tag or commit SHA to create from (defaults to the current branch, or to the current commit when HEAD is detached)
   - Returns: Confirmation of branch creation, naming the base branch, or the short SHA when the base is a commit
10. `git_checkout`
   - Switches branches
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `branch_name` (string): Name of branch to checkout
   - Returns: Confirmation of branch switch, or `HEAD is now detached at <short sha>` when `branch_name` is not a branch (a sha, tag or other revision)
11. `git_show`
   - Shows the contents of a commit, or of a file or directory at a revision
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `revision` (string): The revision (commit hash, branch name, tag) or object spec (`HEAD:path/to/file`) to show
   - Returns: Contents of the specified commit, file content, or directory listing

12. `git_branch`
   - List Git branches
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to the Git repository.
     - `branch_type` (string): Whether to list local branches ('local'), remote branches ('remote') or all branches('all').
     - `contains` (string, optional): The commit sha that branch should contain. Do not pass anything to this param if no commit sha is specified
     - `not_contains` (string, optional): The commit sha that branch should NOT contain. Do not pass anything to this param if no commit sha is specified
   - Returns: List of branches

readme.markdown:
# Fetch MCP Server

A Model Context Protocol server that provides web content fetching capabilities. This server enables LLMs to retrieve and process content from web pages, converting HTML to markdown for easier consumption.

Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/fetch

Requires MCP Python SDK 2.x (`mcp>=2.3,<3`).

> [!CAUTION]
> This server can access local/internal IP addresses and may represent a security risk. Exercise caution when using this MCP server to ensure this does not expose any sensitive data.
>
> By default the server refuses to fetch private, loopback, link-local and other non-public addresses, including cloud metadata endpoints such as `169.254.169.254`, and checks every redirect hop the same way. The `--allow-private-ips` argument turns this guard off; see [Customization - Private addresses](#customization---private-addresses). The guard checks the addresses a hostname resolves to before each request, so it does not protect against DNS rebinding between that check and the connection, and a hostname the server cannot resolve itself (one only a proxy can resolve) is not checked.

The fetch tool will truncate the response, but by using the `start_index` argument, you can specify where to start the content extraction. This lets models read a webpage in chunks, until they find the information they need.

### Available Tools

- `fetch` - Fetches a URL from the internet and extracts its contents as markdown.
    - `url` (string, required): URL to fetch
    - `max_length` (integer, optional): Maximum number of characters to return (default: 5000)
    - `start_index` (integer, optional): Start content from this character index (default: 0)
    - `raw` (boolean, optional): Get raw content without markdown conversion (default: false)
    - Annotations: `readOnlyHint: true`, `destructiveHint: false`, `idempotentHint: true`, `openWorldHint: true` (it only reads, and it reaches arbitrary hosts on the internet)

### Prompts

- **fetch**
  - Fetch a URL and extract its contents as markdown
  - Arguments:
    - `url` (string, required): URL to fetch

### Errors

- A failed fetch (a robots.txt refusal, an unreachable page, an HTTP error status, a refused private address, an unusable proxy setting) and arguments that do not match the tool's schema are returned as a tool result with `isError: true`, whose text starts `Error executing tool fetch:` and says what went wrong, so the model can read it and decide what to do.
- Calling a tool the server does not have is a JSON-RPC protocol error, `-32602` (`Unknown tool: <name>`), as the specification requires. So is getting a prompt it does not have (`Unknown prompt: <name>`), or the `fetch` prompt without its `url` (`URL is required`).
- When the `fetch` prompt's fetch fails, the prompt still returns: its message holds the reason the fetch failed.

The server is built on the MCP Python SDK's high-level `MCPServer`: the tool and the prompt are decorated functions, and their type hints and field descriptions are the input schema and the prompt's arguments.

### Protocol versions

The server speaks both eras of the Model Context Protocol over stdio, with nothing to configure: a **2026-07-28** client (discovered with `server/discover`, no session) and a **2025-11-25** client (the `initialize` handshake). The client's first request decides which. Tools and prompts behave the same in both. Methods the 2026-07-28 specification removes, such as `ping`, are answered only on a 2025-11-25 connection.

## Installation

Optionally: Install node.js, this will cause the fetch server to use a different HTML simplifier that is more robust.
To keep the server from ever starting Node.js, see [Customization - HTML extraction](#customization---html-extraction).

### Using uv (recommended)

When using [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) no specific installation is needed. We will
use [`uvx`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/tools/) to directly run *mcp-server-fetch*.

### Using PIP

Alternatively you can install `mcp-server-fetch` via pip:

```
pip install mcp-server-fetch
```

After installation, you can run it as a script using:

```
python -m mcp_server_fetch
```

## Configuration

### Configure for Claude.app

Add to your Claude settings:

<details>
<summary>Using uvx</summary>

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fetch": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["mcp-server-fetch"]
    }
  }
}
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>Using docker</summary>

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fetch": {
      "command": "docker",
      "args": ["run", "-i", "--rm", "mcp/fetch"]
    }
  }
}
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>Using pip installation</summary>

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fetch": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "mcp_server_fetch"]
    }
  }
}
```
</details>

### Configure for VS Code

For quick installation, use one of the one-click install buttons below...

For manual installation, add the following JSON block to your User Settings (JSON) file in VS Code. You can do this by pressing `Ctrl + Shift + P` and typing `Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)`.

Optionally, you can add it to a file called `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace. This will allow you to share the configuration with others.

> Note that the `mcp` key is needed when using the `mcp.json` file.

<details>
<summary>Using uvx</summary>

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "fetch": {
        "command": "uvx",
        "args": ["mcp-server-fetch"]
      }

}
```

readme.markdown:
# Knowledge Graph Memory Server

A basic implementation of persistent memory using a local knowledge graph. This lets Claude remember information about the user across chats.

Published on npm as [`@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory).

## Core Concepts

### Entities
Entities are the primary nodes in the knowledge graph. Each entity has:
- A unique name (identifier)
- An entity type (e.g., "person", "organization", "event")
- A list of observations

Example:
```json
{
  "name": "John_Smith",
  "entityType": "person",
  "observations": ["Speaks fluent Spanish"]
}
```

### Relations
Relations define directed connections between entities. They are always stored in active voice and describe how entities interact or relate to each other.

Example:
```json
{
  "from": "John_Smith",
  "to": "Anthropic",
  "relationType": "works_at"
}
```
### Observations
Observations are discrete pieces of information about an entity. They are:

- Stored as strings
- Attached to specific entities
- Can be added or removed independently
- Should be atomic (one fact per observation)

Example:
```json
{
  "entityName": "John_Smith",
  "observations": [
    "Speaks fluent Spanish",
    "Graduated in 2019",
    "Prefers morning meetings"
  ]
}
```

## API

### Tools
- **create_entities**
  - Create multiple new entities in the knowledge graph
  - Input: `entities` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `name` (string): Entity identifier
      - `entityType` (string): Type classification
      - `observations` (string[]): Associated observations
  - Ignores entities with existing names (and repeats of a name earlier in the same call); their observations are not added
  - Returns the created entities. When any were skipped, the structured result also lists their names in `skipped`, and a second text item says which were skipped (use `add_observations` to extend an existing entity)

- **create_relations**
  - Create multiple new relations between entities
  - Input: `relations` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `from` (string): Source entity name
      - `to` (string): Target entity name
      - `relationType` (string): Relationship type in active voice
  - Skips duplicate relations
  - Fails if either the source or target entity doesn't exist

- **add_observations**
  - Add new observations to existing entities
  - Input: `observations` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `entityName` (string): Target entity
      - `contents` (string[]): New observations to add
  - Returns added observations per entity
  - Fails if entity doesn't exist

- **delete_entities**
  - Remove entities and their relations
  - Input: `entityNames` (string[])
  - Cascading deletion of associated relations
  - No error if an entity doesn't exist; the response reports which names were not found

- **delete_observations**
  - Remove specific observations from entities
  - Input: `deletions` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `entityName` (string): Target entity
      - `observations` (string[]): Observations to remove
  - No error if an observation doesn't exist; the response reports how many were deleted

- **delete_relations**
  - Remove specific relations from the graph
  - Input: `relations` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `from` (string): Source entity name
      - `to` (string): Target entity name
      - `relationType` (string): Relationship type
  - No error if a relation doesn't exist; the response reports how many were deleted

- **read_graph**
  - Read the entire knowledge graph
  - No input required
  - Returns complete graph structure with all entities and relations

- **search_nodes**
  - Search for nodes based on query
  - Input: `query` (string)
  - Searches across:
    - Entity names
    - Entity types
    - Observation content
  - Returns matching entities and their relations

- **open_nodes**
  - Retrieve specific nodes by name
  - Input: `names` (string[])
  - Returns:
    - Requested entities
    - Relations between requested entities
  - Silently skips non-existent nodes

### Resources

- **knowledge-graph** (`memory://knowledge-graph`)
  - The full knowledge graph as a readable MCP Resource
  - MIME type: `application/json`
  - Returns the same shape as `read_graph` (entities and relations)
  - Mutation tools (`create_entities`, `create_relations`, `add_observations`, `delete_entities`, `delete_observations`, `delete_relations`) emit `notifications/resources/updated` for this URI, so subscribed clients see live changes
  - How a client subscribes depends on its protocol version: a 2026-07-28 client names the URI in the `resourceSubscriptions` of its `subscriptions/listen` request and gets the updates on that stream; a 2025-era client calls `resources/subscribe`

## Protocol versions

The server serves both protocol eras on stdio from the same process. The client's first message picks the era of the connection: a 2026-07-28 client opens with `server/discover` and sends its protocol version, identity and capabilities with each request, and a 2025-era client opens with the `initialize` handshake. The tools and the resource are the same on both.

## Requirements

Node.js 24 or later, when the server runs through `npx` or from source.

}

readme.markdown:
# Sequential Thinking MCP Server

An MCP server implementation that provides a tool for dynamic and reflective problem-solving through a structured thinking process.

Published on npm as [`@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking).

## Features

- Break down complex problems into manageable steps
- Revise and refine thoughts as understanding deepens
- Branch into alternative paths of reasoning
- Adjust the total number of thoughts dynamically
- Generate and verify solution hypotheses
- Serves both protocol eras on stdio: 2026-07-28 clients (`server/discover`, no handshake) and 2025-era clients (`initialize`). The thought history lasts as long as the client's connection, on either era

## Tool

### sequential_thinking

Facilitates a detailed, step-by-step thinking process for problem-solving and analysis.

**Inputs:**
- `thought` (string): The current thinking step
- `nextThoughtNeeded` (boolean): Whether another thought step is needed
- `thoughtNumber` (integer): Current thought number
- `totalThoughts` (integer): Estimated total thoughts needed
- `isRevision` (boolean, optional): Whether this revises previous thinking
- `revisesThought` (integer, optional): Which thought is being reconsidered
- `branchFromThought` (integer, optional): Branching point thought number
- `branchId` (string, optional): Branch identifier
- `needsMoreThoughts` (boolean, optional): If more thoughts are needed

## Usage

The Sequential Thinking tool is designed for:
- Breaking down complex problems into steps
- Planning and design with room for revision
- Analysis that might need course correction
- Problems where the full scope might not be clear initially
- Tasks that need to maintain context over multiple steps
- Situations where irrelevant information needs to be filtered out

In practice, you do not call `sequential_thinking` directly by hand unless your client exposes raw tool calls. Instead, connect the server to an MCP-aware host and ask the model to think through a problem step by step. The host can then decide to call the tool one or more times while it works.

### What it looks like in use

Example prompts that typically benefit from this tool:

- `Plan a database migration from PostgreSQL 14 to 16, list risks, and revise the plan if downtime exceeds 5 minutes.`
- `Debug why this deployment only fails in production and show your reasoning step by step.`
- `Compare three architecture options for a file sync engine and branch if one assumption turns out to be wrong.`

### How to tell it is working

If your host or inspector shows tool activity, you should see repeated calls to `sequential_thinking` with fields such as:

- `thought`
- `thoughtNumber`
- `totalThoughts`
- `nextThoughtNeeded`

When the reasoning changes course, you may also see revision or branching fields like `isRevision`, `revisesThought`, `branchFromThought`, or `branchId`.

### Quick manual verification

After installing the server in your MCP host:

1. Restart or reload the host so it reconnects to the server.
2. Confirm the `sequential_thinking` tool appears in the host's MCP tool list or inspector.
3. Ask the host to solve a non-trivial problem in a step-by-step way.
4. Verify that the host invokes the tool multiple times instead of returning a one-shot answer.

readme.markdown:
# Time MCP Server

A Model Context Protocol server that provides time and timezone conversion capabilities. This server enables LLMs to get current time information and perform timezone conversions using IANA timezone names, with automatic system timezone detection.

Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/time

Requires MCP Python SDK 2.x (`mcp>=2.3,<3`).

### Available Tools

- `get_current_time` - Get current time in a specific timezone or system timezone.
  - Required arguments:
    - `timezone` (string): IANA timezone name (e.g., 'America/New_York', 'Europe/London')

- `convert_time` - Convert time between timezones.
  - Required arguments:
    - `source_timezone` (string): Source IANA timezone name
    - `time` (string): Time in 24-hour format (HH:MM)
    - `target_timezone` (string): Target IANA timezone name

A timezone name, here and in `--local-timezone`, must be an exact IANA key, case included: `Europe/Warsaw` is accepted and `europe/warsaw` is rejected on every platform, including macOS, whose case-insensitive filesystem would otherwise resolve it.

### Protocol versions

The server speaks both eras of the Model Context Protocol over stdio, with nothing to configure: a **2026-07-28** client (discovered with `server/discover`, no session) and a **2025-11-25** client (the `initialize` handshake). The client's first request decides which. Tools behave the same in both. Methods the 2026-07-28 specification removes, such as `ping`, are answered only on a 2025-11-25 connection.

### Results and errors

The server is built on the SDK's high-level `MCPServer`. Each tool declares an `outputSchema` and returns its result twice: as `structuredContent`, and as the same object in indented JSON in a text block, for a client that does not read structured output.

- **A tool failure is an `isError` result** whose text the model can read and act on, prefixed `Error executing tool <name>: `. That covers an unknown or non-exact timezone (`Invalid timezone: ...`), an empty timezone (`Missing required argument: <argument>`), a time not in `HH:MM` 24-hour form, a wall-clock time skipped by a clock change, and an argument missing or of the wrong type (the SDK's validation message).
- **An unknown tool name is a JSON-RPC `-32602` error** (`Unknown tool: <name>`), not an `isError` result, as both protocol versions specify.
- The server registers no prompts or resources. Their list methods answer with empty lists.

## Installation

### Using uv (recommended)

When using [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) no specific installation is needed. We will
use [`uvx`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/tools/) to directly run *mcp-server-time*.

```bash
uvx mcp-server-time
```

### Using PIP

Alternatively you can install `mcp-server-time` via pip:

```bash
pip install mcp-server-time
```

After installation, you can run it as a script using:

```bash
python -m mcp_server_time
```

## Configuration

### Configure for Claude.app

Add to your Claude settings:

<details>
<summary>Using uvx</summary>

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "time": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["mcp-server-time"]
    }
  }
}
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>Using docker</summary>

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "time": {
      "command": "docker",
      "args": ["run", "-i", "--rm", "-e", "LOCAL_TIMEZONE", "mcp/time"]
    }
  }
}
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>Using pip installation</summary>

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "time": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "mcp_server_time"]
    }
  }
}
```
</details>

### Configure for Zed

Add to your Zed settings.json:

<details>
<summary>Using uvx</summary>

```json

    "command": "uvx",

  }
],
```
</details>

<details>

```json

```

### Configure for VS Code

For quick installation, use one of the one-click install buttons below...

For manual installation, add the following JSON block to your User Settings (JSON) file in VS Code. You can do this by pressing `Ctrl + Shift + P` and typing `Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)`.

Optionally, you can add it to a file called `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace. This will allow you to share the configuration with others.

> Note that the `mcp` key is needed when using the `mcp.json` file.

<details>
<summary>Using uvx</summary>

```json

      "time": {
        "command": "uvx",

      }
    }
  }
}
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>Using Docker</summary>

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "time": {
        "command": "docker",
        "args": ["run", "-i", "--rm", "mcp/time"]

    }

}
```
</details>

### Configure for Zencoder

1. Go to the Zencoder menu (...)
2. From the dropdown menu, select `Agent Tools`
3. Click on the `Add Custom MCP`
4. Add the name and server configuration from below, and make sure to hit the `Install` button

<details>
<summary>Using uvx</summary>

```json

    "args": ["mcp-server-time"]
  }
```
</details>

### Customization - System Timezone

By default, the server automatically detects your system's timezone. You can override this by adding the argument `--local-timezone` to the `args` list in the configuration.

Example:
```json
{
  "command": "python",
  "args": ["-m", "mcp_server_time", "--local-timezone=America/New_York"]
}
```

The Docker image cannot see the host's timezone, so it reads the `LOCAL_TIMEZONE` environment variable when the container starts, and uses `UTC` when it is unset or empty. Pass it with `-e`: `"-e", "LOCAL_TIMEZONE"` forwards the client's own value, as in the Docker configuration above, and `"-e", "LOCAL_TIMEZONE=America/New_York"` sets one. A `--local-timezone` given after the i

readme.markdown:
# Everything MCP Server

**[Architecture](docs/architecture.md)
| [Project Structure](docs/structure.md)
| [Startup Process](docs/startup.md)
| [Server Features](docs/features.md)
| [Extension Points](docs/extension.md)
| [How It Works](docs/how-it-works.md)**

This MCP server attempts to exercise all the features of the MCP protocol. It is not intended to be a useful server, but rather a test server for builders of MCP clients. It implements prompts, tools, resources, sampling, and more to showcase MCP capabilities.

## Tools, Resources, Prompts, and Other Features

A complete list of the registered MCP primitives and other protocol features demonstrated can be found in the [Server Features](docs/features.md) document.

The `get-env` tool returns the server's environment variables, but masks the value of any credential-like name (a `KEY`, `TOKEN`, `SECRET`, `PASSWORD`, `PASSWD`, `CREDENTIAL`, `AUTH` or `COOKIE` segment, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`) as `"<redacted>"`. To see every value unmasked while debugging, start the server with `GET_ENV_INCLUDE_SECRETS=1` (or `true`). Leave it unset otherwise: with it set, every credential in the server's environment reaches the model's context.

## Protocol versions

The server serves both protocol eras, over stdio and Streamable HTTP, from one process:

- **2026-07-28** clients connect with `server/discover`, send their protocol version, identity and capabilities with each request, and have no session. The server demonstrates the revision's new features for them: multi-round-trip requests (`input_required`) with `requestState`, `subscriptions/listen` change notifications, per-request log levels, cache hints (`ttlMs` / `cacheScope`), the tasks extension (`io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks`) under the `extensions` capability, and `x-mcp-header` with JSON Schema 2020-12 tool schemas.
- **2025-era** clients connect with the `initialize` handshake, as before. Elicitation, sampling and roots are served to them from the same multi-round-trip handlers through the SDK's legacy shim.

Roots, sampling and logging are deprecated as of 2026-07-28 and stay available, labelled deprecated. [Server Features](docs/features.md) marks which era each feature belongs to.

## Configuring `gzip-file-as-resource`

The `gzip-file-as-resource` tool fetches the URL it is given, so these environment variables limit what it will fetch:

| Variable | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GZIP_MAX_FETCH_SIZE` | 10 MiB | The largest response, in bytes, it reads |
| `GZIP_MAX_FETCH_TIME_MILLIS` | 30000 | How long a fetch may take, redirects included |
| `GZIP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` | empty (any name) | Comma-separated host names; a host must be one of them or a subdomain of one. Checked on the caller's URL and on every redirect hop |
| `GZIP_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS` | off | Set to `1` or `true` to allow loopback, private (RFC 1918), CGNAT, link-local (cloud metadata) and other non-public addresses |

By default the tool refuses a URL whose host resolves to a non-public address, and follows at most five redirects, checking each hop the same way. `GZIP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` filters names, not addresses: a listed name that resolves to a private address is still refused unless `GZIP_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS` is set. The address is checked before the request and resolved again when it is made, so a DNS answer that changes in between (DNS rebinding) is not caught. `data:` URLs are not fetched, so neither check applies to them.

## Requirements

Node.js 24 or later, when the server runs through `npx` or from source.

## Usage with Claude Desktop (uses [stdio Transport](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/transports#stdio))

Add to your `claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "everything": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything"]
    }
  }
}
```

On Windows, use `cmd /c` to launch `npx`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "everything": {
      "command": "cmd",
      "args": ["/c", "npx", "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything"]
    }
  }
}
```

For quick installation, use one of the one-click install buttons below...

For manual installation, you can configure the MCP server using one of these methods:

**Method 1: User Configuration (Recommended)**
Add the configuration to your user-level MCP configuration file. Open the Command Palette (`Ctrl + Shift + P`) and run `MCP: Open User Configuration`. This will open your user `mcp.json` file where you can add the server configuration.

**Method 2: Workspace Configuration**
Alternatively, you can add the configuration to a file called `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace. This will allow you to share the configuration with others.

> For more details about MCP configuration in VS Code, see the [official VS Code MCP documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/mcp-servers).

#### NPX

```json

      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything"]

      "command": "cmd",
      "args": ["/c", "npx", "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything"]

```

```shell
cd src/everything
npm install
npm run start:streamableHttp
```

Both HTTP transports (Streamable HTTP and HTTP+SSE) accept browser requests only from a localhost origin: an `Origin` header whose host is `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`, on any port, such as the MCP Inspector's. A request carrying any other `Origin` is refused with `403 Forbidden`. Clients that send no `Origin` header, which i

# Worklittle Jobs

Swipe to apply for jobs using the Worklittle MCP app, and search over 4 million jobs with filters like visa status, distance, and salary, and connect your Worklittle account to save jobs you love.

Public MCP connector and plugin files for [Worklittle](https://worklittle.com). This repository contains skill instructions, a plugin manifest, and a pointer to the public MCP URL. It does not contain API keys, OAuth secrets, or private product source.

## What users get

- Remote MCP at `https://mcp.worklittle.com/`
- Search with visa, distance, salary, and other filters
- Connect a Worklittle account to save jobs

## Connect

Remote Streamable HTTP (any MCP client):

```
https://mcp.worklittle.com/
```

Add that URL in ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor, Claude, Codex, or another app that supports remote MCP. Docs for each client: https://docs.worklittle.com/mcp

Claude Code (this is the Claude CLI, not the connector name):

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http worklittle https://mcp.worklittle.com/
```

Docs: https://docs.worklittle.com/mcp  
Privacy: https://worklittle.com/privacy  
Support: hello@worklittle.com

## Client manifests

The same remote MCP and skills work in Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Codex, and other clients. Each host just looks for its own files:

- Claude Code / Claude plugin directory: `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`
- Cursor Marketplace: `.cursor-plugin/` plus `mcp.json` (Cursor’s required filename)
- Official MCP Registry: `server.json`
- Skills (`npx skills add`): `skills/`

Cursor’s reviewer script is in this repo so a marketplace submit matches their [plugin template](https://github.com/cursor/plugin-template). It does not make this a Cursor-only project.

```bash
node scripts/validate-template.mjs
```

## Agent skills

Install the public job-search skills into Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, and other agents:

```bash
npx skills add worklittle/jobs-mcp
```

Browse them on [skills.sh](https://skills.sh). Docs also publish skills at `https://docs.worklittle.com`.

## License

MIT

## Directories

Listed in the [Claude Market MCP directory](https://www.claudemarket.ai/mcp).

You need an `XQUIK_API_KEY` for the request below. Public reads need no official X developer account or connected X account. Private reads and X account actions require a connected X account. Never send an X password, cookie, session export, or 2FA code to Xquik or an agent. ## Trust & usage - 53,000+ downloads of Xquik's Twitter API packages on npm, PyPI, RubyGems, NuGet, Packagist & Terraform ([source](https://xquik.com/trust#downloads)) - 9,500+ users of Xquik's Twitter scraper Actors on Apify ([source](https://apify.com/xquik)) - 6,700,000+ runs of Xquik's Twitter scraper Actors on Apify ([source](https://apify.com/xquik)) - 4.66 of 5 for the X Tweet Scraper from 16 Apify reviews ([source](https://apify.com/xquik/x-tweet-scraper/reviews)) - 4,000+ accounts on xquik.com ([source](https://xquik.com/trust#accounts)) - 1,600+ installs of Xquik's Twitter Skills on skills.sh ([source](https://xquik.com/trust#skill-installs)) - $39,000+ in revenue verified by TrustMRR ([source](https://trustmrr.com/startup/xquik)) - 13.2 s p99 REST API server read time over 7 days, failed reads included ([source](https://xquik.com/trust#speed)) - 380+ GitHub stars across Xquik's repos ([source](https://github.com/Xquik-dev)) - 9,900+ downloads of x-developer on npm ([source](https://www.npmjs.com/package/x-developer)) - 1,500+ installs of this repo's Skills on skills.sh ([source](https://skills.sh/xquik-dev/x-twitter-scraper)) - 1,700+ downloads of x-scraper on ClawHub ([source](https://clawhub.ai/xquik/skills/x-scraper)) - This repo meets the OpenSSF Best Practices passing criteria ([source](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/13731)) Checked on 2026-10-25. # GuardBee MCP

**🇬🇧 English** | [🇹🇷 Türkçe](TR.md) | [🇨🇳 中文](ZH.md) | [🇯🇵 日本語](JA.md) | [🇰🇷 한국어](KO.md) | [🇧🇷 Português](PT-BR.md) | [🇪🇸 Español](ES.md) | [🇩🇪 Deutsch](DE.md)

**Security for AI agents and MCP.** GuardBee puts a gateway between your agents and their tools and models that masks personal data and secrets, blocks prompt injection and toxic data flows, asks before risky calls and keeps a tamper-evident audit log, plus scanners that check your code and configs against the OWASP MCP Top 10. Open source (MIT), runs on your machine, no account needed.

The gateway and every server speak MCP **2026-07-28** and **2025-11-25** (MCP TypeScript SDK v2), so they work with clients and servers on either revision.

```bash
# Put your existing MCP servers behind the gateway (backs up your client config first)
npx -y @guardbee/mcp-security-proxy@^1 init --client claude-desktop   # or cursor, claude-code

# Check a codebase against the OWASP MCP Top 10
npx -y @guardbee/mcp-owasp-scan scan . --fail-on=high
```

<sub>Run it yourself: [`examples/demo`](examples/demo) (`npm install && npm start`).</sub>

## Which package should I use?

| You want to… | Install | How |
|---|---|---|
| Protect agents at runtime: mask personal data, block injection and toxic flows, approve risky calls, keep an audit log | [`@guardbee/mcp-security-proxy`](packages/security-proxy) | Put it in front of your MCP servers (`guardbee-proxy init` imports your client config) |
| Check a codebase against the OWASP MCP Top 10 in one pass, in CI | [`@guardbee/mcp-owasp-scan`](packages/owasp-scan) | `npx @guardbee/mcp-owasp-scan scan . --format=sarif --fail-on=high` |
| Give an agent many GuardBee checks from one MCP server | [`@guardbee/security-suite`](packages/security-suite) | `guardbee serve` (recommended set), `--tools=code,network` or `all` |
| Find leaked keys in files, git history or agent transcripts | [`@guardbee/mcp-secret-scanner`](packages/secret-scanner) | `npx @guardbee/mcp-secret-scanner scan . --history` |
| Audit the MCP servers configured on developer machines | [`@guardbee/mcp-config-auditor`](packages/mcp-config-auditor) | `npx @guardbee/mcp-config-auditor discover` |
| Let an agent query a database without seeing raw personal data | [`@guardbee/mcp-db-gateway`](packages/db-gateway) | Point it at your database with a policy |
| Use the detectors in your own code | [`@guardbee/guard-core`](packages/guard-core) | `import { maskPiiInText } from "@guardbee/guard-core"` |

Every other package is a single check (one OWASP risk, one protocol, one file type); each is in `security-suite` too. `npx @guardbee/security-suite list` shows them with what they check.

## Benchmarks

Detection is measured, not claimed: [`packages/pii-bench`](packages/pii-bench) is a reproducible benchmark for Turkish and international personal data, with bootstrap 95% intervals and the datasets in the repo.

| Benchmark | Result |
|---|---|
| Identifiers (TC Kimlik, IBAN, card, phone, e-mail, …), 400 documents + 160 clean | **F1 97.1**, recall 100%, false alarms on clean documents 8.1%, 0.04 ms per document |
| Person names with the optional NER model, same set | **F1 99.5** |
| Hand-written hard cases for names ([tr-names-challenge](packages/pii-bench/README.md#dataset-tr-names-challenge)) | **F1 97.1**, 0 false alarms |
| KVKK Art. 6 special categories with NER ([tr-special-challenge](packages/pii-bench/README.md#dataset-tr-special-challenge)) | **F1 97.5**, 0 false alarms |
| Bypass suite: 5 identifiers × 16 disguises (base64, hex, URL/HTML/`\u` escapes, other scripts' digits, separators) | **80 / 80 masked**, 0 of 16 look-alike strings changed |

The identifier detectors were tuned after reading this set's misses, so the challenge sets are the fairer measure; the [pii-bench README](packages/pii-bench/README.md) lists the limits. Any other detector can be run on the same data through its `System` interface.

## Examples

Ready-to-copy proxy policies (minimal, KVKK, coding agent, LLM gateway), client configs for Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code, and CI templates for GitHub Actions and GitLab: [`examples/`](examples).

## Packages

| Package | npm | Description |
|---|---|---|
| [`packages/ai-code-scanner`](packages/ai-code-scanner) | `@guardbee/mcp-ai-code-scanner` | Scans a codebase for insecure LLM/AI integration patterns (client-exposed keys, unsafe output handling, excessive agency, PII→prompt, prompt injection) |
| [`packages/compliance-checker`](packages/compliance-checker) | `@guardbee/mcp-compliance-checker` | KVKK/GDPR/CCPA compliance checks |
| [`packages/dependency-auditor`](packages/dependency-auditor) | `@guardbee/mcp-dependency-auditor` | CVE scanning for npm/pip/cargo dependencies (OSV) |
| [`packages/dns-intelligence`](packages/dns-intelligence) | `@guardbee/mcp-dns-intelligence` | DNS record enumeration, misconfiguration and dangling-subdomain detection |
| [`packages/db-gateway`](packages/db-gateway) | `@guardbee/mcp-db-gateway` | KVKK/GDPR-compliant gateway between an LLM and a database (PII masking, RBAC, rate limiting, queryable audit log; Prisma/Postgres/MySQL/SQLite/MongoDB adapters; optional insert/update/delete support) |
| [`packages/mcp-server-auditor`](packages/mcp-server-auditor) | `@guardbee/mcp-server-auditor` | Scans other MCP servers' tool definitions for insecure patterns (excessive agency, shell/eval/SQL/SSRF sinks, loose schemas, hardcoded secrets, wildcard CORS) |

# cam [English](README.md) · [中文](README.zh.md) · [日本語](README.ja.md) · [한국어](README.ko.md) · [العربية](README.ar.md) · [🌐 Website](https://hanochzhu.github.io/cam-web/?lang=en) ### A local multi-turn conversational memory system purpose-built for coding agents **Code graph + memory · surgical reads · 100% local · MCP + CLI** **Kernel written in Rust** ## Contents - [Why cam?](#why-cam) - [Get Started](#get-started) - [Key Features](#key-features) - [How It Works](#how-it-works) - [Agent Workflow](#agent-workflow) - [CLI Reference](#cli-reference) - [Memory Rules](#memory-rules) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Benchmarks](#benchmarks) - [Supported Agents](#supported-agents) - [Supported Languages](#supported-languages) - [Supported Platforms](#supported-platforms) - [License](#license) Guides: [Interactive Showcase (Website)](https://hanochzhu.github.io/cam-web/?lang=en) · [Main Agent vs Subagent](docs/agents.md) · [MCP Configs by IDE](docs/mcp.md) · [中文说明](docs/agents.zh.md) --- ## Why cam? When an AI coding agent explores a repository, it usually rediscovers structure the slow way — running `grep`, `glob`, and full-file `Read` one file at a time — and forgets everything in the next session. **`cam` gives the agent two local retrieval planes in a single binary:** | Plane | What it stores | How the agent uses it | | --- | --- | --- | | **Code Graph** | Tree-sitter symbols (functions, types, methods) as a virtual filesystem + 1-hop callers/callees | `ls`, `find`, `read src/file.rs/symbol`, `ref symbol --dir in\|out` — surgical symbol reads instead of whole-file dumps | | **Memory Tree** | Project facts, architecture decisions, debugging write-ups, and user habits | `recall` (Vector + BM25 fused with RRF) and `add` (with branching `--parent` and revision `--supersedes`) | > **One binary, two interfaces:** The **main agent** calls `cam` over **MCP** (`cam mcp`); **subagents** (which rarely inherit MCP tools) call the exact same **CLI** (`cam --json …`). Both share `.cam/cam.db` on disk, 100% local, zero API cost. --- ## Get Started ### Option 1: One-Sentence Agent Install (Recommended) Paste this prompt directly into your coding agent (**Cursor**, **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **Windsurf**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Cline**, etc.) and let it install, index, and wire `cam` for you: ```text Install cam from https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory: require a working Rust toolchain (rustup), run `cargo install --git https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory --locked`, ensure ~/.cargo/bin (or %USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin on Windows) is on PATH, then verify with `cam --help`. In this repo run `cam index`. For the main agent, register MCP stdio: command `cam`, args `["mcp"]` (Cursor: .cursor/mcp.json; Claude Code: .mcp.json). Subagents call `cam --json` in the shell. Do not add extra docs. ```
How each IDE / agent handles this prompt | Environment | What to do | | --- | --- | | **Cursor / Windsurf / Claude Code / Codex** | Paste into Agent / Chat; the agent runs the terminal install, builds `.cam/cam.db`, and writes the MCP config | | **VS Code** (Copilot / Continue / Cline) | Paste into Agent / Chat mode with terminal access enabled | | **JetBrains** (IntelliJ / RustRover / GoLand) | Paste into AI Assistant, or run `cargo install` in the built-in terminal | Note: `cargo install` places `cam` in `~/.cargo/bin` (Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin`). Restart your terminal or IDE if `cam` is not immediately found on `PATH`.
--- ### Option 2: Manual Setup #### 1. Install the CLI Requires a [Rust toolchain](https://rustup.rs/): ```bash cargo install --git https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory --locked cam --help ```
Alternative: Build from local clone or run via Docker **From a local clone:** ```bash git clone https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory.git cd codeagent_memory cargo install --path . --locked ``` **Docker (no Rust toolchain required):** ```bash docker pull ghcr.io/hanochzhu/codeagent-memory:0.1.6 docker run -i --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work ghcr.io/hanochzhu/codeagent-memory:0.1.6 ``` Or build locally: `docker build -t cam https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory.git`
#### 2. Index & query your project ```bash cd your-project cam index # parse repo into .cam/cam.db # Query the code graph cam ls src/ # list files or symbols in a file cam read src/main.rs/main # read a single symbol body cam ref main --dir in # 1-hop callers (in) or callees (out) # Query & write to the memory tree cam recall "how does hybrid recall fuse BM25 and vectors" cam add --summary "..." < notes.md ``` `cam` auto-initializes `.cam/` on first use. Run `cam watch` in the background if you want live incremental graph updates as files change. #### 3. Connect MCP for the main agent Add `cam mcp` to your host's MCP configuration (e.g. `.cursor/mcp.json` or `.mcp.json`): ```json { "mcpServers": { "cam": { "command": "cam", "args": ["mcp"] } } } ``` See [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md) for host-specific config paths and [docs/agents.md](docs/agents.md) for main-agent / subagent prompt rules. The first `recall` or `add` downloads the default embedding model (`potion-multilingual-128M` to `~/.cam/models/`) and falls back to a lexical hash embedder if offline. --- ## Key Features | Feature | Details | | --- | --- | | **SQLite Code Graph** | Tree-sitter parses functions, types, and call edges into `.cam/cam.db` for instant symbol-level navigation | | **Virtual Paths** | `src/main.rs` addresses a file outline; `src/main.rs/main` addresses the symbol body directly | | **Live Incremental Sync** | `cam sync` hashes file contents; `cam watch` keeps the graph updated on save | …

# syllabus to calendar mcp

syllabus to calendar mcp is a free [mcp](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server, published on npm as `syllabus-calendar-mcp`. turn pasted syllabus text into calendar events, build valid .ics files from events and recurring classes, skip holidays and reading weeks, and merge calendars to find conflicts. the math and parsing are done by tested code. it runs on your computer, needs no internet and no login.

parses pasted text from Canvas, Brightspace, Moodle or a PDF export.

free forever. no account.

## comparison

brightspace-mcp-server and @exhabition/brightspace-mcp need a brightspace login before they can read anything. this server needs no account, no api key and no network. it works on syllabus text you paste, so it covers any school's syllabus, not only brightspace courses.

## sample output

paste text like this:

```text
Assignment 1 due Sep 15
Midterm exam October 20 at 10:00
Lab report 2 due Dec 8
```

`extract_schedule_events` with `course` set to BIO 101 and `year` set to 2026 returns:

```text
3 events found.

- Tue, Sep 15, 2026: Assignment 1 (assignment) [BIO 101]
- Tue, Oct 20, 2026 at 10:00: Midterm exam (exam) [BIO 101]
- Tue, Dec 8, 2026: Lab report 2 (lab) [BIO 101]

Next: pass these events to build_ics as events to make an .ics calendar.
```

if a pasted line has no date, it is not dropped. `extract_schedule_events` returns those lines in `undated_lines` and lists them below the events, so you can fix the text and run the tool again.

`build_ics` turns those events into a calendar that starts like this:

```ics
BEGIN:VCALENDAR
VERSION:2.0
PRODID:-//AnonymousOnyx22//syllabus-calendar-mcp//EN
CALSCALE:GREGORIAN
METHOD:PUBLISH
X-WR-CALNAME:BIO 101
```

## install

run it straight from npm with `npx`. you need node.js 20 or newer, see [node version](#node-version) for the details.

```bash
npx -y syllabus-calendar-mcp
```

add it to your ai app's mcp config so the app can start it for you. every app reads its config from its own file, so pick yours:

- [claude desktop](#claude-desktop)
- [cursor](#cursor)
- [vs code copilot](#vs-code-copilot)

### claude desktop

    "syllabus-calendar": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "syllabus-calendar-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

restart claude desktop after you save the file.

### command line

run this in a terminal:

```bash
npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/inspector syllabus-calendar-mcp
```

### cursor

cursor reads `mcp.json` from the project folder at `.cursor/mcp.json`, or from your home folder at `~/.cursor/mcp.json`.

```json
{
  "mcpservers": {
    "syllabus-calendar": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "syllabus-calendar-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

restart cursor after you save the file.

### vs code copilot

put this in `.vscode/mcp.json` in your project folder, or in the `mcp.json` file in your user profile:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "syllabus-calendar": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "syllabus-calendar-mcp"]
    }

vs code also reads a portable `.mcp.json` file in the project root. that file uses the name `mcpservers` instead of `servers`:

    }

restart vs code after you save the file.

## try these four prompts

1. turn syllabus text into events

   > "turn this syllabus into calendar events: assignment 1 due sep 15, midterm exam october 20 at 10:00."

   the model calls `extract_schedule_events` and returns dated events with types and times.

2. add a recurring class

   > "my biology class meets tuesday and thursday from sep 8 to dec 10, 2026 at 10:00. skip the reading week of oct 12 to oct 16."

   the model calls `expand_recurring_classes` and returns meetings plus skipped dates.

3. make an ics calendar

   > "make an .ics file for my course with a reminder one day before each assignment."

   the model calls `build_ics` with events and reminders to produce a valid calendar.

4. check for conflicts

   > "merge my three course calendars and tell me which classes conflict."

   the model calls `merge_calendars`, which merges the calendars, drops duplicate events by uid and lists timed events that overlap.

## tools

four tools. these names are the ones your ai app sees.

readme.markdown:
# Postgres AIops

> **Audit availability:** Real writes require a committed `pending` audit row and stop before contacting the platform if storage is unavailable. Reads and previews may continue with a warning; new audit rows store outcome summaries rather than full responses.

> **Disclaimer**: Community-maintained open-source project. **Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the PostgreSQL Global Development Group or any vendor.** "PostgreSQL" and the elephant logo are trademarks of the PostgreSQL Community Association; all product/trademark names belong to their respective owners. MIT licensed.

Governed AI-ops for **PostgreSQL DBA operations** — connecting to a server with
**psycopg 3** and reading the system catalogs and `pg_stat_*` views — with a
**built-in governance harness**: unified audit log, token/runaway
budget guard, undo-token recording, and descriptive risk-tier labels.
Beyond the mock test suite, the reads, a governed write, and its undo have been
exercised against a live PostgreSQL 16.14 instance — see [`docs/VERIFICATION.md`](docs/VERIFICATION.md).

## What it does

Three flagship signature analyses, plus the guarded reads and writes around them:

- **Slow-query RCA** — take the worst `pg_stat_statements` entry (plus an optional
  `EXPLAIN` plan) and map its numbers — mean time, cache-hit ratio, temp spill,
  call count, plan node types — to a cited cause and a concrete action. Every
  finding carries its measured number, not a black-box verdict.
- **Bloat & vacuum analysis** — combine per-table dead-tuple ratio and autovacuum
  recency into a ranked, cited recommendation (VACUUM / tune autovacuum).
- **Blocking lock-chain RCA** — build the wait-for tree from `pg_blocking_pids`,
  name the **root blocker** (blocks others, waits on none), and give the action;
  a cycle is flagged as a likely deadlock.

## What works

- **CLI** (`postgres-aiops ...`): `init`, `overview`, `server`, `activity`, `query`, `index`, `table`, `repl`, `analyze`, `remediate`, `secret`, `doctor`, `mcp`.
- **MCP server** (`postgres-aiops mcp` or `postgres-aiops-mcp`): **35 tools** (25 read, 10 write), every one wrapped with the bundled `@governed_tool` harness.
- **Encrypted credentials**: the role password lives in an encrypted store `~/.postgres-aiops/secrets.enc` (Fernet + scrypt) — **never plaintext on disk**. Unlock with a master password from `POSTGRES_AIOPS_MASTER_PASSWORD` (MCP/CI) or an interactive prompt (CLI).
- **Reversibility**: mutating writes fetch the **real before-state first** and record a faithful inverse — `create_index`↔`drop_index`; `drop_index` captures `pg_get_indexdef` so undo recreates it exactly; `update_setting` captures the prior value so undo sets it back. Irreversible ops (`terminate_backend`, `cancel_query`, `run_vacuum`, `run_analyze`, `reindex`, `reset_query_stats`) record prior stats for audit but declare no undo.
- **Safety**: every state-changing CLI op supports `--dry-run` and requires double confirmation; every write MCP tool takes a `dry_run` preview. All identifiers that cannot be parameterised (table/index/GUC names) are validated and quoted; all values are bound query parameters.

## Capability matrix (35 MCP tools)

| Domain | Tools | Count | R/W |
|--------|-------|:-----:|:---:|
| **Overview** | `overview` | 1 | read |
| **Server** | `server_version`, `show_settings`, `list_extensions`, `list_databases`, `list_roles` | 5 | read |
| **Activity** | `list_activity`, `long_running_queries`, `list_locks` | 3 | read |
| **Queries** | `top_queries`, `explain_query` | 2 | read |
| **Indexes** | `unused_indexes`, `missing_index_hints`, `index_bloat`, `invalid_indexes` | 4 | read |
| **Tables** | `table_sizes`, `table_bloat`, `autovacuum_status` | 3 | read |
| **Replication** | `replication_status`, `replication_slots`, `wal_status` | 3 | read |
| **Analysis (flagship)** | `slow_query_rca`, `bloat_and_vacuum_analysis`, `blocking_lock_chain_rca` | 3 | read |
| **Writes** | `terminate_backend`, `cancel_query`, `drop_index` | 3 | write (high) |
| | `run_vacuum`, `run_analyze`, `create_index`, `reindex`, `update_setting`, `reset_query_stats` | 6 | write (medium) |
| **Undo** | `undo_list` | 1 | read |
| | `undo_apply` | 1 | write (medium) |

The flagship analyses accept injected records for pure/offline analysis, or pull
live from a configured target. `top_queries`/`slow_query_rca` require the
`pg_stat_statements` extension; the read role should have `pg_monitor`.

## What this tool does, and does not, decide

It delivers PostgreSQL DBA operations — reads and writes — accurately and
efficiently, and records every one of them. It does **not** decide whether a
write is allowed to happen. That is the agent's judgement, or the permission of
the account you connect it with: connect with a PostgreSQL role that has no
write privileges (a read-only role, or one without INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL),
and the writes fail at the server — the place that actually owns the
permission.

So there is no read-only switch, no policy file, no approval gate to configure.
The one thing the tool guarantees is that nothing is silent: **every call, over
MCP and over the CLI alike, lands an audit row** in `~/.postgres-aiops/audit.db`,
and destructive writes still capture their before-state and record an inverse
where one exists.

> Each tool declares a `risk_level`, carried into the audit row as a descriptive
> tier (none/confirm/review) — so a reviewer can see at a glance that a row was
> a high-risk delete. It is a label, not a gate.

Running a smaller / local model? See
[agent-guardrails.md](skills/postgres-aiops/references/agent-guardrails.md) — it lists
the guardrails this tool now enforces for you (so you don't spend prompt budget
restating them) and gives a ready-made system prompt for what's left.

## Quick start

### As a Claude Code plugin

One install gives an agent both the skill and the MCP server:

```
/plugin marketplace add AIops-tools/marketplace
/plugin install postgr

Governed AI-ops for **MySQL 8.x and MariaDB 10.6+ DBA operations** — connecting
to a server with **PyMySQL** and reading `information_schema` /
`performance_schema` — with a **built-in governance harness**: unified audit
log, token/runaway budget guard, undo-token recording, and descriptive
risk-tier labels. The server **flavor** (mysql vs mariadb) is

(`SHOW REPLICA STATUS` vs `SHOW SLAVE STATUS`).

Four flagship signature analyses, plus the guarded reads and writes around them:

  others, waits on none), and parse the **last deadlock** out of

- **Replication lag RCA** — map the replica's IO/SQL thread state,
  `Seconds_Behind_Source` and error fields to a cited cause + action
  (stopped IO thread, failed applier statement, lagging applier, intentional
  `SQL_Delay`).

name: ai-browser
description: Visible Electron browser driven by a semantic accessibility tree: 17 MCP tools, no screenshots.

readme.markdown: AI Browser 中文读者请看这里：README-CN.md（3 分钟速读 + 中文安装指引） A real browser whose only operator is your agent. It reads pages as a semantic tree instead of screenshots, acts through trusted browser input — and because it is a normal, visible Electron window, a human can reach for the mouse at any time. A noisy real-world feed (300+ accessibility nodes) becomes a typed structure — then one ui.act switches the feed and the tree changes with it. Every call is a raw JSON-RPC message over one WebSocket: no SDK, no coordinates. Reproduce: npm start then node examples/feed-tree.mjs Human + agent, same browser, same socket. The agent drives, then simply stops and watches; a person clicks an article in the real window, the agent notices the new tab on its next read, and continues on the page the human chose. No lock, no hand-off API. Try it yourself: npm start then node examples/human-takeover.mjs — click anything when it says YOUR TURN. **What it is.** An Electron app that exposes its tabs over two equivalent interfaces — an MCP server (20 `browse_*` tools) and a raw WebSocket JSON-RPC API (`ws://localhost:9223`, methods `ui.*`). Your agent navigates, reads a structured semantic tree (`role` / `label` / `value` / `states` / `actions`), and clicks or types by `data-ai-id`. There is no screenshot step and no OCR: `src/` contains no capture call at all. **What it is not.** It is not headless. The window really opens, really renders, and stays interactive — see [Letting a human step in](#letting-a-human-step-in). Nor does it "co-drive" with you: the hand-off is a conversation between the agent and the user, not a browser API. > **Security note.** The WebSocket server has no authentication — it listens on localhost and trusts > whoever connects. Do not expose port 9223 beyond loopback, and avoid untrusted networks. --- ## Install **Install the prebuilt package unless you have a reason not to.** Option A is one file you double-click: no Node.js, no dependency tree, no build step. Source install (Option C) pulls a ~276 MB `node_modules` plus a ~100 MB Electron engine download on top — only use it when no package fits your platform, the package misbehaves, or you specifically need to run from source. ### Option A — macOS install package (recommended) Grab `AI-Browser--arm64.dmg` from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Glittering/ai-browser/releases) (~110 MB to download, ~245 MB on disk — most of it is the bundled Chromium engine, which *is* the product). Open the dmg, drag **AI Browser** to `/Applications`, launch it. Done. Two things to know before you download it: - **It is not notarized.** macOS Gatekeeper will refuse to open it on the first try. Right-click the app → **Open**, confirm once, and it runs normally afterwards. (A paid Apple Developer account is what removes this step; until then, this is the honest cost.) - **Only macOS `arm64` is built.** Windows and Linux have no package yet, because neither has been verified on this project — see [Compatibility](#compatibility). Agents still connect through the MCP server (Option B below), and the two channels cooperate: when the packaged app is already running, the MCP server finds it on port 9223 and **reuses it instead of spawning a second copy of Electron** — one browser, one login session, whichever way you start it. So "package for the engine + `npx` for the MCP bridge" is the normal agent setup too. ### Option B — npx (the agent channel) The package is published as [`@glittering0717/ai-browser`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@glittering0717/ai-browser); no clone needed: ```bash npx -y @glittering0717/ai-browser --help ``` To open the visible browser window directly: ```bash npx -y @glittering0717/ai-browser start ``` Requires **Node ≥ 18** and a desktop session (this is a GUI app). If a launch needs its own engine, the first run prepares it (~100 MB, downloaded once). npm ≥ 11 blocks dependency install scripts by default — the launcher detects that and runs Electron's own downloader itself, so nothing extra is needed. If the download from GitHub releases is slow or blocked (common on mainland-China networks), point it at a mirror: ```bash ELECTRON_MIRROR=https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/electron/ npx -y @glittering0717/ai-browser start ``` ### Option C — from source (fallback) Use this when there is no package for your platform, the package gives you trouble, or you need to modify the code. It is the heaviest of the three: `npm install` pulls the full dependency tree (~276 MB), then the Electron engine (~100 MB) on top. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Glittering/ai-browser.git cd ai-browser npm install ``` If the Electron binary download is slow or fails outright, use the mirror: ```bash ELECTRON_MIRROR=https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/electron/ npm install ``` Or make it sticky by creating a `.npmrc` in the project root: ```ini electron_mirror=https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/electron/ ``` Confirm the binary actually landed before blaming anything else — a missing binary still leaves you with an "install that succeeded": ```bash ls node_modules/electron/dist ``` To check the install end to end: ```bash npm start ``` A 1280×800 window opens and the terminal prints `AI Browser WS server listening on ws://localhost:9223`. (The first tab opens on the default start page; ignore it and navigate away.) To build the package yourself: ```bash npm install node scripts/build_dmg.cjs # current arch node scripts/build_dmg.cjs --arch arm64 # or x64 ``` Output lands in `dist/`. The script uses `@electron/packager` plus macOS's built-in `hdiutil` (no external binary downloads); the reasoning — including why `electron-builder` refuses to build this project — is documented in [`docs/DEPENDENCY_AND_DISTRIBUTION_AUDIT.md`](docs/DEPENDENCY_AND_DISTRIBUTION_AUDIT.md). …

tools.name: browse_navigate
tools.description: Load a URL in your tab or the given tab.

tools.name: browse_get_tree
tools.description: Read the page as a semantic tree + page context (modals, messages, stats).

tools.name: browse_act
tools.description: `click` / `type` (append at caret) / `setContent` (replace all) / `clear` / `focus` / `hover` / `scroll_to` / `upload` / `get_value` (read-only) / `drag` / `press` / `wheel` on a `data-ai-id`.

tools.name: browse_diff
tools.description: `snapshot` a baseline, then `diff` to get added / removed / changed paths with before/after values. This is how you prove an action did anything.

tools.name: browse_capabilities
tools.description: Probe what a page affords and which route to take on it (see below).

tools.name: browse_repaint
tools.description: Force the compositor to redraw the tab when the window shows a stale page; returns `repaint_count`.

tools.name: browse_downloads
tools.description: List a tab's downloads with their on-disk paths. Downloads are asynchronous — poll this after clicking an export button.

tools.name: browse_canvas
tools.description: Read `` through captured draw calls: `list` / `read` / `configure` / `capture`. Experimental — see the canvas section below.

tools.name: browse_evaluate
tools.description: Run a JS *expression* in page context (5000-char cap, Node identifiers rejected).

tools.name: browse_scroll
tools.description: Scroll the page, or scroll an element into view.

tools.name: browse_wait
tools.description: Poll until `button_enabled` / `modal_appeared` / `text_contains` / `url_contains`.

tools.name: browse_tabs
tools.description: Tabs: `list` / `new` / `close` / `switch` / `window`. `switch` = default; add `show:true`. `new` never steals the view unless `show:true`.

tools.name: browse_network
tools.description: Chrome-DevTools-style network inspection: `list` (filter by method / URL / status / type), `get` (request + response headers and bodies), `clear`, `configure`.

tools.name: browse_quit
tools.description: Shut the whole browser down and release the process.

tools.name: committed
tools.description: dispatched and acked by the page

tools.description: provably nothing happened (no such target, bad params, CDP down)

tools.name: unknown

name: BrowserAttach
description: Control existing signed-in Chrome and Edge tabs through a locally paired extension.

readme.markdown: # BrowserAttach English · 简体中文 Drive the Chrome / Edge tabs you already have open and already signed in from an MCP client. BrowserAttach connects to the browser through a locally paired extension, keeps your existing sign-in state, and needs neither a remote debugging port nor a separate automation browser. [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@evan_zhong/browser-attach) · [Usage guide](docs/USAGE.md) · [Architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) · [Agent integration](docs/AGENT-INTEGRATION.md) · [Test report](docs/TEST-REPORT.md) · [Issues](https://github.com/EvannZhongg/BrowserAttach/issues) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## What it does - Discover multiple browser profiles, pick one precisely, claim a tab exclusively, and release it when done. - Control existing ordinary `file://` tabs after enabling BrowserAttach's **Allow access to file URLs** setting in the browser's extension details; use the same discovery, claim, observation and input tools. - Read the accessibility tree, query names/values/nearby field context, inspect field values and supported editor models; click, fill and type through refs or strict CSS/XPath, HTML label, placeholder and AX role/name locators. Type can also target the currently focused field explicitly. - Native pointer hover, stepped drags and conditional waits; select HTML options without opening a native popup. - Navigate and go back/forward, open or close tabs, handle JavaScript dialogs, upload local files, and capture the whole page or a single element. - Evaluate JavaScript expressions in the main page; read console, page-error, network and navigation logs captured after claiming, with bounded available stacks and request initiators; opt in to bounded, redacted request/response details when XHR/fetch needs verification. - Read one HTTP(S) URL in a temporary background tab with the profile's sign-in, returning rendered text, current DOM, or complete JSON with the main-document HTTP status when observed. - Standard stdio MCP with 24 tools. The Hub listens on loopback only and pairs with the extension through a random key. ## Requirements - Node.js **22 or newer**, plus npm. - Chrome / Edge **125 or newer** with permission to load unpacked extensions. Latest stable is recommended. - An MCP client that speaks stdio MCP and can find Node/npm on `PATH`. ## Quick start ### 1. Install and pair ```sh npm install --global @evan_zhong/browser-attach browser-attach setup ``` `setup` prints a stable extension directory and starts the local Hub. The directory is usually: - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.browser-attach\extension` - macOS / Linux: `~/.local/share/browser-attach/extension` Open `chrome://extensions` or `edge://extensions`, enable developer mode, choose "Load unpacked" and load that directory. Load it once for every browser profile you want to expose; the extension options page lets you set a recognizable profile name. Or without a global install: ```sh npx --yes --package=@evan_zhong/browser-attach@latest browser-attach setup ``` ### 2. Configure the MCP client Merge the following into your client's MCP configuration, or see [mcp-config.json](mcp-config.json): ```json { "mcpServers": { "browser_attach": { "command": "npx", "args": ["--yes", "--package=@evan_zhong/browser-attach@latest", "browser-attach", "mcp"] } } } ``` On Windows clients that require a full command extension, use `npx.cmd`. With a global install you can also configure `"command": "browser-attach", "args": ["mcp"]`. Restart the MCP client to discover the tools. `@latest` selects the package at launch; upgrading an existing pair is coordinated at startup. The first extension load, and pairs still on an older protocol, need one manual extension reload — see [local data and upgrades](#local-data-and-upgrades). Host entry points are collected in [agent integration](docs/AGENT-INTEGRATION.md), and the connection parameters, JSON/TOML examples and verification steps are in the [setup reference](skills/browser-attach/references/setup.md); other clients use the stdio entry above. The npm package includes an optional [browser-attach skill](skills/browser-attach/SKILL.md) with setup, recovery and cross-site recipes. Copy the whole `skills/browser-attach` directory to your host's skill location if desired; npm installation does not register it with the host. ### 3. Start driving 1. `browser_discover(kind="browsers")` → `browser_discover(kind="tabs")` to confirm the browser, tab title and URL. 2. `browser_claim_tab` with the `tab_id` from `discover(kind="tabs")` (optional `expected_url` / `expected_title` exact guards) to take control and receive this connection's `tab_handle`. 3. `browser_snapshot` to get element `ref`s, then click, fill or run other actions. 4. Observe when the next decision needs new state, and finish with `browser_tab_control(action="release")`. Use `snapshot(diff_since="latest")` or action `observe:{diff_since:"latest"}` for page changes; inspect `mode/reset_reason` and finish pagination. A full-page refresh is not required after every action. When titles change often, omit `expected_title` and check the identity returned by claim instead. Elements may be addressed by `ref` or by a `selector` re-resolved on every call; design trade-offs: [architecture notes](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md#设计取舍). Claiming and ordinary input never activate a tab or window; call `browser_tab_control(action="activate")` explicitly when foreground rendering is needed. When an outcome is unknown, observe again first and avoid duplicate submissions. Full parameters, pagination, uploads and input semantics: [usage guide](docs/USAGE.md). ## Tools | Tool | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `browser_discover` | `kind=browsers/tabs`; discover browser profiles, tab identity and control status | | `browser_claim_tab` | Exclusively claim a discovered tab | | `browser_open_tab` / `browser_tab_control` | Create a tab, optionally claim it with `claim:true`; explicit …
