name: OwnMemory
description: Encrypted memory for Claude, on a server you deploy to your own Cloudflare account.

readme.markdown:
OwnMemory lets Claude remember you across chats and devices, with the memories stored encrypted under a key only you hold, in storage you own.

Claude calls a remote MCP server running in your own Cloudflare account. The server encrypts each memory and stores it in a D1 database in that account (the one-click default) or in an `OwnMemory` folder in your Google Drive. It works in the official Claude apps on the web, iPhone and Android.

**Get started:** create a free Cloudflare account and connect GitHub to it first ([steps](docs/setup.md#one-click-setup)), then click the button above, choose a random owner code of 12+ characters, and open your server's address to follow its four setup steps. About 5 minutes, on a free Cloudflare account. Full guide, including Google Drive storage: [docs/setup.md](docs/setup.md).

**Status:** early (v0.2). Built and tested for Claude: on the web, iPhone and Android, and in Claude Code. Other MCP clients that support remote servers with OAuth should be able to connect, but are untested.

## How your memories stay yours

- **Your passphrase never leaves your browser.** When you connect Claude, the passphrase page turns it into a key that unlocks a random 256-bit memory key. Only the locked copy of that key is stored, in your storage (`keyinfo.json`).
- **Every memory is encrypted** (AES-256-GCM) before it is stored, in a file with a random name. Your storage provider and anyone with the files see only ciphertext.
- **The server keeps no key at rest.** The memory key and your Google token live only inside the OAuth grant, which is encrypted with Claude's access token. The MCP handler is stateless: nothing is written to Durable Objects or logs.
- **Hard rules in code.** Blocked categories, a pause switch, and a filter that refuses passwords, API keys and card numbers, whatever the AI decides.
- **Search by meaning, still private.** Embeddings come from Cloudflare Workers AI in your own account and are stored encrypted like the memories. Set the `SEMANTIC_SEARCH` secret to `off` to keep memory text away from it; search then uses keywords only.
- **See and fix what it remembers.** Your server's `/memories` page lets you browse, search, edit, add and delete memories, decrypted only in your browser.
- **No lock-in.** **Download all** on the memories page gives you every memory as Markdown, and [ownmemory.app/decrypt](https://ownmemory.app/decrypt) decrypts a downloaded copy in your browser, even without your server.

The one unavoidable exposure: the server and Anthropic see a memory's text while a save or search runs, because Claude sends plain text. Running the server yourself is the safeguard.

Who else could get at your memories, person by person, and how to keep them out: [docs/security-model.md](docs/security-model.md).

## Tools Claude gets

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `load_core_memories` | Called at the start of a chat: returns the memory mode, any message for you, and (in OwnMemory-only mode) your profile, preferences and recent work |
| `search_memories` | Search by meaning and keywords, English, Chinese or mixed (finds "What do I like to drink?" without shared words) |
| `list_memories` | Most recent memories, optionally by category |
| `save_memory` | Saves one fact, after the hard rules allow it; points out facts already saved, even when worded differently |
| `import_memories` | Saves up to 50 facts at once, for example everything Claude's built-in memory knows |
| `update_memory` | Changes a fact, keeping the previous wording as dated history |
| `delete_memory` | Deletes a memory; it stays 30 days in D1, or in the Drive trash |
| `review_memories` | Finds memories with the same wording or meaning, to merge |
| `set_memory_mode` | Records how you use OwnMemory alongside Claude's memory: ramp-up, OwnMemory only, or keep both |

## Repository layout

| Path | What's there |
| --- | --- |
| `server/src/` | The Cloudflare Worker: OAuth and sign-in flow (`auth.ts`), passkey and authenticator sign-in on one-click servers (`gate.ts`, `factors.ts`), the memories page's API (`memories.ts`), MCP tools (`tools.ts`), storage backends D1 and Drive (`storage.ts`, `google.ts`), encrypted memory store (`store.ts`), memory format, search and duplicate checks (`format.ts`), memory modes and ramp-up (`settings.ts`), pages (`pages.ts`) |
| `server/public/unlock.js`, `home.js`, `memories.js`, `gate.js` | Scripts for the passphrase page, the setup wizard, the memories page and the passkey / authenticator sign-in step |
| `server/public/keys.js`, `memory-file.js`, `zip.js` | Encryption, the memory file format and the zip builder, shared by the browser, the Worker, the decrypt tool and `site/public/decrypt.html` (copies; `npm run sync-site`), so the format can't drift |
| `site/` | The ownmemory.app landing page and [the decrypt page](https://ownmemory.app/decrypt): static files, no data collected |
| `server/scripts/decrypt.mjs` | Local export to plain Markdown |
| `server/test/` | Unit tests (`npm test`) and a recall evaluation against real embeddings (`npm run eval`) |
| `docs/` | Setup guide, "Who can read your memories" and the key-flow diagram |
| `design/logo/` | Logo sources from the design canvas and PNG/SVG exports |

## Contributing, security and license

- Contributions are welcome; see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Contributors sign a short [contributor license agreement](CLA.md).
- Found a security problem? Please report it privately: [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
- Licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). "OwnMemory" and the OwnMemory logo are trademarks of the project and are not covered by the license; forks need a different name.

readme.markdown:
# codebase-memory-mcp: local code intelligence for AI agents via MCP

**Understand your repository, from source code to the systems around it.** codebase-memory-mcp is an MCP server that connects code, documentation, configuration, and infrastructure in a persistent local knowledge graph. Use it to find an unfamiliar feature, follow a call across services, trace a deployment back to its source, or assess which parts of a project a change could affect.

Give your coding agent structural context through [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) (MCP), or query the graph directly from the CLI. **The MCP server is the core of the project.** Its optional visual companion, **CBM Lens, is in open beta (v0.0.1)**, with a source reader, architecture maps, the Galaxy graph, coverage diagnostics, architecture decisions, and local code chat.

The native C backend exposes **17 MCP tools**, parses [languages and file formats](#language-support) with vendored grammars, and adds [Hybrid LSP](#hybrid-lsp) type resolution for supported languages. The installer supports **45 automatic or conditional client integrations**, including client configuration, skills, agent profiles, and applicable hooks. Indexing and graph queries need no hosted service or API key. Focused graph queries can reduce repeated file reads and token use; see the [measured results](#performance).

[Quick start](#quick-start) · [Capabilities](#features) · [Documentation](#documentation-connected-to-code) · [Infrastructure](#infrastructure-and-deployment) · [Smart CI](#smart-ci-and-test-impact) · [Explore CBM Lens](#cbm-lens-beta-code-visualization-and-source-navigation) · [Agent setup](#agent-setup-skills-profiles-and-hooks) · [MCP tools](#mcp-tools)

> **Local processing:** Source analysis and graph storage run on your machine. CBM Lens can optionally download a model for browser AI after you enable it; inference stays on the device. The installer writes agent configuration for the clients you select. See [Security](#security) for release verification and [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for reporting issues.

**See the graph with CBM Lens (open beta v0.0.1).** Folders become nested platforms, files and symbols become selectable blocks, and arrows show indexed relationships. The recording opens `src/foundation` in the map of this repository, selects `arena.c` and opens its source. Height can show source size; hotspot gravity reflects static fan-in. [Still image](docs/images/lens-architecture.png).

  

**Galaxy.** Explore the code knowledge graph in 3D. The recording follows the outgoing relationships of `cbm_arena_alloc` one layer further, switches to the hierarchy and shows the two-hop call path to `cbm_alloc`. Edge pulses show relationship direction; they do not represent live execution. [Still: two dependency layers around `cbm_max_file_bytes`](docs/images/lens-galaxy.jpg).

  

**Explore.** Browse files in an IDE-style workspace, read syntax-highlighted source in Monaco, and keep the code graph alongside it. File impact shows what depends on the open file, and Code details shows the callers and calls of the symbol under the caret. Select code to [ask the local chat about it](#chat-with-your-codebase-locally).

<details>
<summary>More views: system structure and behavior</summary>

System structure groups symbols into components and lets you inspect their dependencies.

Behavior shows possible calls from a selected operation and the source evidence behind them.

</details>

The high-resolution GIFs show CBM Lens Beta on 20 October 2026; the still images were captured on 12–13 October. All show public source from this repository. See [capture details](docs/images/README.md) for each capture's build, indexed scope and recording setup.

## Why codebase-memory-mcp

- **Find the right code with context**: combine symbol, text, and semantic search with callers, dependencies, source snippets, and file outlines. Targeted queries and compact, paged results can reduce token use and repeated file reads; see [Performance](#performance) for scoped measurements.
- **Connect documentation to implementation**: index document sections, PDF text pages, architecture decisions, and supported references into code. Find the explanation alongside the symbol.
- **Follow the system beyond source files**: trace supported relationships through Docker, Kubernetes, Helm, Kustomize, Terraform/OpenTofu, Terragrunt, Ansible, scripts, Make, and CI configuration.
- **Understand a change before running it**: inspect affected symbols, compare indexed snapshots, and find related tests. [Experimental Smart CI](#smart-ci-and-test-impact) combines static relationships and per-test coverage for supported C/C++ test harnesses, falling back to broader runs when evidence is insufficient.
- **Explore visually with CBM Lens Beta**: read source, follow call paths, inspect architecture and coverage gaps, manage architecture decisions, and ask a local model about selected code.
- **Equip your coding agents**: `install` sets up supported client configuration, durable guidance, skills, Scout/Verify/Auditor profiles, and applicable context hooks. Support varies by client; see the [integration matrix](#multi-agent-support).
- **Keep context local and reusable**: indexes persist between sessions, eligible active MCP sessions can keep them synchronized, and optional graph artifacts let a team share a baseline.
- **Run a native tool on your machine**: standard releases include CBM Lens for macOS, Linux, and Windows. The native runtime needs no Docker or language runtime; parser grammars are included.

## Quick Start

**Install the latest release** (macOS / Linux):
```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp/main/install.sh | bash
```

The standard native release includes CBM Lens. Start it after installation with `codebase-memory-mcp daemon start --open --port=9749`. The [Nix packages](#nix-flake) and [source builds](#build-from-source) a

readme.markdown:
ZenBrain The neuroscience-inspired memory system for AI agents. Memory for agents that lasts across sessions: seven layers, from working memory to long-term facts and procedures, and 20 tested algorithm modules for what memory research describes, such as spaced repetition, Hebbian strengthening, sleep replay and emotional tagging.Pure TypeScript. No third-party dependencies in algorithms and core. 945 tests. Extracted from a production AI platform. ```bash npm install @zensation/algorithms # the library, Node 22 or newer claude mcp add --scope user zenbrain -e ZENBRAIN_DB=~/.zenbrain/memory.db -- npx -y @zensation/mcp # memory for Claude Code ``` The same MCP server runs in Claude Desktop and Cursor (configuration) · Vercel AI SDK middleware: @zensation/ai-sdk Status: pre-1.0, semver — the public API can still change before 1.0. 945 tests green in CI: 933 on each of Node 22, 24 and 26, and 12 more against PostgreSQL with pgvector · the current version of every package published to npm with build provenance · every change recorded in the CHANGELOG · issues and pull requests are answered; replications and counter-results are especially welcome. Self-hosted: the library makes no network calls of its own. Memory lives in SQLite or PostgreSQL that you operate; an embedding model or an LLM is optional and your choice. --- ▶ Try the live playground in your browser — runs this published code, no install required.
📄 Paper & Citation — ZenBrain: A Neuroscience-Inspired 7-Layer Memory Architecture for Autonomous AI Systems - **arXiv preprint** (cs.AI): [arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878) - **Open-access archive** (Zenodo / CERN): [doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19353663](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19353663) - **ORCID**: [0009-0001-1793-012X](https://orcid.org/0009-0001-1793-012X) - **License**: CC BY 4.0 (paper) · Apache-2.0 (code) ```bibtex @misc{bering2026zenbrain, title = {ZenBrain: A Neuroscience-Inspired 7-Layer Memory Architecture for Autonomous AI Systems}, author = {Bering, Alexander}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2604.23878}, archivePrefix = {arXiv}, primaryClass = {cs.AI}, doi = {10.5281/zenodo.19353663}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878} } ``` Feedback, replications, and counter-results are explicitly welcome — please open an issue or reach out via [research@zensation.ai](mailto:research@zensation.ai).
> **Your AI forgets everything after every conversation.** ZenBrain gives it a memory that lasts across sessions, split into layers the way human memory is, and ships the mechanisms memory research describes (spaced repetition, emotional tagging, Hebbian strengthening, forgetting curves, sleep replay) as tested functions. Which of them run on their own and which you call yourself is in [one table](#what-runs-on-its-own-and-what-you-call-yourself). > **Architecture vs. this package.** ZenBrain's architecture is **15 neuroscience-inspired mechanisms — 9 foundational algorithms + 6 Predictive Memory Architecture (PMA) components** ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878)). The six PMA components are proprietary: they ran in the ZenAI production system and are not in these packages, which contain the hooks they plug into. **This open-source package ships the algorithm library: 10 core algorithms + 10 advanced research modules (20 modules), zero-dependency.** --- ## Benchmark: LongMemEval-500 On LongMemEval-500, **three of nine head-to-head comparisons hold** against Letta, Mem0 and A-Mem — all three against A-Mem, the remaining six are ties, none lost. Three competitors x three LLM judges, Bonferroni-corrected (alpha = 0.05/18) and version-matched. The measured ZenBrain arm (per the [correction notice](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22831086) a Python port of a test-harness class, not the seven-layer system) reaches **91.3% of the binary-judge accuracy of a full-context comparison arm (whose answer model reads the whole history) with 1/109.6 of its input tokens in the answer step** (47.7% vs. 52.2%); building the memory is not counted. Works out of the box without an embedding provider — lexical ranking, nothing extra to install. `nomic-embed-text` can be added as the embedding provider; it was the embedder of the measured run. The figures above were not measured with this package: per the correction notice, the measured arm is a Python port of a test-harness class, not an import of the packages. The paper prints where ZenBrain loses as well: on LoCoMo, substring-based aggregate F1 favours lexical retrieval (BM25) by metric design, and we do not contest that. The advantage is most pronounced in the judge-graded comparisons and on cross-session reasoning. **The mechanism comparison further down re-runs from this repository in under a minute** — `bash scripts/compare-mechanisms.sh`, no API keys; it needs git, Node and network access to clone the three compared repositories at the pinned commits. It prints a positive and a negative control before the result, so the instrument can be checked before its output is trusted. **The mechanism ablation behind paper Tables 7–9 also runs from here:** `cd backend && npm run experiments`, and CI compares every point estimate with the published ones. The method and the effect sizes behind the LongMemEval numbers above are in the paper; this repository ships no runner for those. The archived packages below run the significance tests and effect sizes in full, and the mechanism ablation behind paper Tables 7–9. - Method, effect sizes and ablations: [arXiv:2604.23878](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878) - Open-access archive: [10.5281/zenodo.19353663](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19353663) --- ## Reproduction packages The …

# MCP Memory — Memoria local para agentes IA vía MCP

> **Lleva la memoria de tu agente IA a cualquier máquina.**
> Servidor MCP open source que da memoria persistente con búsqueda léxica (BM25) a Claude Desktop, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor, Continue y cualquier cliente compatible con [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). SQLite + FTS5, **cero infra externa, 100% en tu hardware**.

**Tags:** `mcp-server` · `ai-agents` · `sqlite` · `fts5` · `bm25` · `claude-code` · `cursor` · `opencode` · `lexical-search` · `agent-memory` · `local-first` · `self-hosted`

  

<sub>El agente guarda algo en una sesión y lo recuerda en otra — mismo archivo SQLite, proceso nuevo. Sin nube, sin vectores, sin servicios extra.</sub>

---

## 💡 Por qué existe

Los agentes IA olvidan todo entre conversaciones. Las soluciones existentes son cloud-only, multi-tenant pesado, o están atadas a un único cliente. **MCP Memory** resuelve esto con tres ideas simples:

1. **Tu memoria, tu máquina.** Un solo archivo SQLite local. Cero datos en la nube, cero servicios externos que levantar.
2. **Conectas una vez, funciona en todos lados.** Es un servidor MCP estándar — cualquier cliente que hable MCP lo usa sin custom code.
3. **Cero overhead.** `pip install` y tienes 9 tools listas para tu agente en segundos — sin Docker, sin modelos que descargar.

---

## ⚡ Quickstart

Hay dos formas de correrlo. Elige una:

| Modo | Cuándo | Cómo arranca |
|------|--------|--------------|
| **stdio** | Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor… (lo más simple) | El cliente lanza el proceso él solo. No hay server de fondo ni puerto. |
| **HTTP** | Varios clientes contra un mismo server, Docker, clientes web | Lo arrancas tú y queda escuchando en `http://localhost:8765/mcp`. |

### Opción A — stdio (sin dejar nada corriendo)

Con [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) **0.13.4 o superior** instalado no hace falta clonar (las versiones anteriores confían en una CA comprometida, ver [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md#cadena-de-suministro-incidente-emudhra)): el cliente descarga y lanza el server en cada sesión. Para Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add -s user mcp-memory -- uvx --from "git+https://github.com/GermaniU/mcp-memory#subdirectory=server" mcp-memory --stdio
```

Para Claude Desktop, Cursor y el resto, la config JSON está en [`docs/CLIENTS.md`](docs/CLIENTS.md#modo-stdio-recomendado). Todos los procesos comparten el mismo archivo SQLite (`DB_PATH`), así que la memoria es la misma en todos tus clientes.

### Opción B — HTTP (server de fondo)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/GermaniU/mcp-memory.git
cd mcp-memory/server
pip install -e .
mcp-memory
```

> Alternativa sin instalar en tu entorno global: `uvx --from . mcp-memory` (corriendo dentro de `server/`).

No hay pre-requisitos: nada que levantar, nada que descargar. Al arrancar, el server crea el archivo SQLite (`DB_PATH`, default `~/.agent-memory/memory.db`) y su schema (tabla `memories` + índice FTS5) si no existen.

Endpoint MCP: `http://localhost:8765/mcp`. Pégalo en la config de tu cliente (ver [`docs/CLIENTS.md`](docs/CLIENTS.md) — Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor, Continue).

> `mcp-memory --stdio` (o `MCP_TRANSPORT=stdio`) arranca el modo stdio con la instalación local.

### 🔍 Diagnóstico y Chequeo de Salud

Verifica que tu Python tiene FTS5 compilado y que `DB_PATH` es accesible al instante:

```bash
mcp-memory check
```

`mcp-memory --help` lista los comandos y variables de entorno; `mcp-memory --version` imprime la versión instalada.

---

## 🛠 Tools MCP expuestas

| Tool             | Tipo | Para qué |
|------------------|------|----------|
| `memory_save`    | ✏️ escritura | Guardar texto + tags + metadata. |
| `memory_search`  | 👁 lectura | Búsqueda léxica (BM25 vía SQLite FTS5) con filtro por namespace. |
| `memory_update`  | ⚠️ destructiva | Cambiar contenido/tags/metadata por id. Re-sincroniza el índice FTS5 si cambia el contenido. Rechaza `content` vacío. |
| `memory_delete`  | ⚠️ destructiva | Borrar por id. |
| `memory_list`    | 👁 lectura | Paginado por namespace. |
| `memory_recent`  | 👁 lectura | Las últimas N por `updated_at`. |
| `memory_stats`   | 👁 lectura | Conteo, namespaces, oldest/newest. |
| `memory_export`  | 👁 lectura | Exporta todas las memorias (o las de un namespace) como JSONL. Devuelve `count` y el string `jsonl`. |
| `memory_import`  | ✏️ escritura | Importa un string JSONL producido por `memory_export`. Salta colisiones de id silenciosamente. Acepta `namespace_override` opcional. |

El **Tipo** se publica como [anotaciones MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools#tool-annotations) (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`): los clientes que las soportan pueden auto-aprobar las lecturas y pedir confirmación antes de modificar o borrar. Al conectarse, el server también envía `instructions` al agente (cuándo buscar, cuándo guardar, cómo formular queries léxicas).

Schemas + ejemplos de invocación en [`docs/CLIENTS.md`](docs/CLIENTS.md).

---

## 🎯 Alcance actual

MCP Memory es deliberadamente pequeño. Hace **una cosa bien: memoria léxica de texto plano**. No es un sistema de RAG completo, no es un knowledge base, no es un grafo.

### Lo que SÍ hace
- ✅ Almacena y recupera **texto puro** en SQLite.
- ✅ Búsqueda léxica (BM25/FTS5) con filtro por `namespace`.
- ✅ Tags + metadata libres en cada entrada.
- ✅ 9 tools MCP estándar para cualquier agente compatible.
- ✅ Persistencia en disco (un único archivo `.db`), backup = copiar el archivo.

### Lo que NO hace (todavía)
- ❌ **No hace búsqueda semántica.** Es léxica (BM25): coincide términos, no significado — sinónimos o paráfrasis sin overlap de vocabulario no matchean.
- ❌ **No soporta imágenes ni gráficas.** Solo texto.
- ❌ **No soporta PDFs ni archivos binarios** — extrae el texto antes de guardarlo.
- ❌ **No es multi-tenant.** Una persona, una máquina, una memoria (con namespaces para separar contextos).
- ❌ **No ti

readme.markdown:
# MemoryComb

**One memory. Every AI. Your whole team.**

MemoryComb is a memory library that lives on your computer. Claude, ChatGPT and your other AIs all read and write the same memory, so you stop re-explaining yourself every time you switch AIs. Every read has a receipt, and an AI Scorecard shows which AI's facts turned out wrong.

**Built to be trusted:** every memory is checked for hidden instructions before any AI reads it, your AIs can fact-check each other (you settle any disagreement), and your memory stays on your computer with encrypted backups to your own iCloud Drive or OneDrive.

This page has the downloads only. MemoryComb is in early testing on **Mac and Windows** (Windows is newer: tell us what breaks).

## Install (pick one)

By installing MemoryComb you agree to the [License](LICENSE.md). Please also read the [Privacy Policy](PRIVACY.md).

### If you use the Claude app (easiest)
1. Download **memorycomb-*.mcpb** from the [latest release](../../releases/latest).
2. Double-click it. Claude opens its install screen; click **Install**.
   Claude shows a red "not verified" warning for every extension that isn't in its directory yet. What MemoryComb touches: only its own memory folder on your computer (`~/.memorycomb`) and an encrypted daily backup in your iCloud Drive (Mac) or OneDrive (Windows).
3. Start a new chat and ask: **"What's in my MemoryComb?"**

### Mac: Terminal (Claude Code, ChatGPT and everything else)
```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/BryceBlackRoot/memorycomb/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

### Windows: PowerShell (early test)
```powershell
irm https://github.com/BryceBlackRoot/memorycomb/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
```
It installs MemoryComb for your user only (no admin password), starts it at login, and opens the dashboard's **Get started** page.

## After installing
Your dashboard is at **http://127.0.0.1:8765** (it only opens on your own computer). From there:
- **Get started**: tap the AI you're connecting.
- **Import**: bring in what ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Grok already know about you.
- **Team**: share one memory with the people you work with (test version: runs while your computer is on).

## Privacy
Your memory never leaves your computer unless you switch on sharing (for ChatGPT or teammates). MemoryComb goes online only to check for a newer version once a day (it asks for the version number, nothing else) and for sharing you switch on.

## Free
MemoryComb is free. Everything is included: unlimited memories, every AI, every trust feature, and team sharing. No trial, nothing to buy, and nothing is ever deleted. Team sharing runs from the computer of whoever starts the shared project, so teammates can reach it while that computer is on.

## Uninstall
```bash
~/.local/bin/memorycomb uninstall
```
On Windows: `memorycomb uninstall` in PowerShell.
This removes the app and its login item but **keeps your memory** in `~/.memorycomb`. In the Claude app, remove the extension under Settings › Extensions.

## Feedback
Found a problem or have an idea? Open an issue on this page.

## Legal
[License](LICENSE.md) · [Privacy Policy](PRIVACY.md) · [Third-party notices](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md)

MemoryComb is early test software provided as is. Memories and AI answers can be wrong: check anything important yourself. Nothing in MemoryComb is professional advice.

readme.markdown:
# GitHub Organization Signal Scanner MCP Server

An MCP server that resolves a company domain to its GitHub organization with repo, language and activity signals. It wraps the Mamba Labs GitHub Organization Signal Scanner actor on Apify and returns a Clay-ready flat JSON row to any MCP client.

## What's Inside

- [What it does](#what-it-does)
- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
- [Example prompts](#example-prompts)
- [Inputs](#inputs)
- [Output](#output)
- [Example output](#example-output)
- [Features](#features)
- [Full actor documentation](#full-actor-documentation)
- [Mamba Labs GTM Suite](#mamba-labs-gtm-suite)
- [License](#license)

## What it does

Give it a company domain and it finds that company's GitHub organization and returns repository count, followers, creation date, top languages, total stars, the most recent push, how many repositories are actively worked on, and whether the company ships a public SDK. One flat row per company, read through GitHub's own documented REST API.

Forks and archived repositories are excluded from the language and star derivations, and the exclusion is counted on the row. A rate limited request reports `not_extractable` and never a zero, because a zero is a number a buyer would filter on. A login that resolves to a personal user account rather than an organization is reported as `identity_mismatch`. It reads organization and repository metadata only: it does not clone repositories, read source, scan for secrets or assess code quality.

All of the scanning runs on Apify. This package is a thin client that calls the actor and hands back the result unchanged.

## Quick start

You need Node.js 18 or newer and an Apify account with an API token.

Add this to your Claude Desktop config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mamba-github-organization-signal-scanner": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@mambalabsdev/mcp-github-organization-signal-scanner"],
      "env": {
        "APIFY_TOKEN": "your-apify-token"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Get your token at https://console.apify.com/account/integrations, paste it in, and restart Claude Desktop. The `scan_github_organization_signals` tool will be available.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 18 or newer
- An Apify account with an API token
- Optional: your own GitHub personal access token, free to create at github.com/settings/tokens with no scopes at all for public data, if you want to scan more than a handful of companies

## Example prompts

- "Find the GitHub organization for stripe.com and summarize its activity."
- "Scan the GitHub org `vercel` and tell me its top languages and total stars."
- "Does figma.com ship a public SDK? Check its GitHub organization."
- "Scan notion.so's GitHub org, counting a repo as active if it was pushed in the last 30 days."

## Inputs

- `company_domain` (optional): bare company domain, for example `stripe.com`. This is the lookup key and the join key for every other actor in the fleet.
- `company_name` (optional but strongly recommended): what the identity gate checks a discovered record against, so supplying it is the cheapest way to reduce wrong matches.
- `github_org` (optional): if you already know the organization login, for example `stripe`, put it here and the tool skips discovery entirely and goes straight to the API, which is faster and spends fewer rate limited requests.
- `includeRepoDetail` (optional): when true (the default) the organization repositories are read and the language, star, activity and SDK signals are derived from them. Set false to return the organization record only, which is one request instead of several and is friendlier to the unauthenticated rate limit.
- `includeContributorEstimate` (optional): when true one extra request reads the contributor count of the organization's most starred repository, as a floor on the size of its public engineering surface. False by default, because one extra request per company is real money against a 60 per hour unauthenticated budget.
- `activeWindowDays` (optional): how recently a repository must have been pushed to count as active. One of `30`, `90`, `180` or `365`, with 90 the default. This changes what active means on the row.
- `repoPageBudget` (optional): how many pages of 100 repositories to read for a large organization. One of `1`, `2`, `3` or `5`. This is a cost and completeness dial, not a change of answer: the row always reports how many repositories were sampled and whether the sample is complete.
- `githubToken` (optional): your own GitHub personal access token, free to create with no scopes at all for public data. Without it the tool runs at GitHub's 60 requests per hour, which is enough for a handful of companies and not enough for a list. With it the limit is 5,000 per hour.
- `skipCache` (optional): when false (the default) a successful lookup is cached for seven days and reused. Set true to force a fresh fetch.
- `max_charge_usd` (optional): a cost cap in USD for this run. The actor stops before an item that could take its charges past this amount. Omit it to rely on the maximum cost per run set in Apify.

## Output

The tool returns the actor's flat JSON row for the company, with 32 snake_case fields and no nested objects. `github_discovery` says how the organization was found, `github_rejected_candidate` records a candidate the identity gate turned away, `repos_sampled` and `repos_complete` say how much of the organization was read, and `repos_excluded` counts the forks and archived repositories left out. See the Apify Store page for the full output schema.

## Example output

```json
{
  "degraded": false,
  "degradation_reason": null,
  "company_domain": "stripe.com",
  "company_name": "Stripe",
  "github_org": "stripe",
  "github_url": "https://github.com/stripe",
  "github_discovery": "homepage_link",
  "github_rejected_candidate": null,
  "github_account_type": "Organization",
  "public_repos": 98,
  "followers": 3469,
  "org_created_at": "2011-0

…

readme.markdown:
# Korely Memory

Memory for AI agents that knows what is still true.

Korely stores what your agent learns as **typed facts with a validity window**. When something changes, the old fact is superseded instead of overwritten. Your agent reads the current truth, and you can still ask what was true on any past date.

```python
import time
from korely_memory import Korely

korely = Korely()  # reads KORELY_API_KEY from the environment

korely.add("Maria is on the Pro plan, billed yearly.", user_id="maria")
korely.add("Maria downgraded to Free.", user_id="maria")

time.sleep(10)  # facts are extracted server-side; see "Writes settle asynchronously"

ctx = korely.get_context(query="what plan is Maria on?", user_id="maria")
print(ctx.context)
# ## Known facts
# - Maria downgraded_to Free (since 2026-09-08)
# - Maria billing_frequency yearly (since 2026-09-08)
#
# Pro is gone from the current facts. It was superseded, not deleted.
```

The exact predicate is chosen by the extractor, so `downgraded_to` here might be
`subscribes_to` or `plan` on your run. What is guaranteed is the behaviour: the
old value leaves the current set, and stays retrievable with its `invalid_at`.

Nothing was deleted. The Pro fact is still there, carrying `invalid_at` and a pointer to what replaced it:

```python
korely.get_facts(user_id="maria", include_invalidated=True)
# Maria downgraded_to Free    valid_from=... invalid_at=None
# Maria plan Pro              valid_from=... invalid_at=2026-09-08T08:31:09Z
```

## Time travel over real dates

Pass `timestamp` when the event happened in the past, and facts inherit it as
`valid_from`. Then `as_of` answers over the world's timeline, not your ingestion
order:

```python
korely.add("Franco signed up on the Pro plan.", user_id="franco", timestamp="2026-01-15")
korely.add("Franco downgraded to Free.",        user_id="franco", timestamp="2026-06-20")

korely.get_facts(user_id="franco", as_of="2026-03-01")   # subscribes_to -> Pro plan
korely.get_facts(user_id="franco", as_of="2026-08-01")   # subscribes_to -> Free
korely.get_facts(user_id="franco")                       # subscribes_to -> Free
```

Without `timestamp` every fact starts being true the moment you write it, so
`as_of` on an earlier date returns nothing. That is correct, and usually not
what you want when you are importing history.

`as_of` answers what was true on a date, as the store knows it today.
`known_as_of` (Korely Agent 0.1.26) answers the other question: what the store
knew on that date. They differ when a change is told late. An agent learns on
5 October that a customer moved on 1 September:

```python
korely.get_facts(user_id="maria", as_of="2026-09-20")        # lives_in -> Turin
korely.get_facts(user_id="maria", known_as_of="2026-09-20")  # lives_in -> Milan
```

On 20 September the move had happened, and the store did not know it yet.
`known_as_of` is on `get_facts`, `get_profile` and `get_context`, which rebuilds
the block as the store could have built it then: what an agent could have
known when it decided. Each fact carries `closed_known_at`, when the store
learned it had ended.

## Writes settle asynchronously

`add()` returns as soon as the memory is stored, then extraction runs server-side. That means:

| Call | Available |
|---|---|
| `search()` over raw memories | immediately |
| `get_facts()` and `get_context()` typed facts | after a few seconds |

The `time.sleep(10)` above exists only so the snippet works when you paste it. **You do not need it in production**: an agent writes at the end of one turn and reads at the start of the next, and by then the facts are there.

If you do need to know exactly when, ask instead of guessing. Every memory carries a `status` of `processing`, `ready`, or `error`, and `events()` reports what is still in flight:

```python
page = korely.events()
page.processing  # 0
page.events[0]   # MemoryEvent(memory_id='mem_...', status='ready', ...)
```

`processing == 0` means none of your project's writes (in the `user_id` scope, if you pass one) is still being extracted, however many there are, so a script can wait on that one number instead of walking every id. After a `batch()` import, wait for `batch_status()` to finish first: memories the job has not stored yet are not counted.

Polling is the only signal: no webhook fires when extraction finishes. The webhook events are `memory.created`, `fact.invalidated` and `quota.warning`.

## Install

```bash
pip install korely-memory      # Python, plus the `korely` CLI
npm install korely-memory      # Node / TypeScript
```

Both clients have **zero runtime dependencies**.

For LangGraph, the optional `pip install 'korely-memory[langgraph]'` adds a store, memory tools and a context helper: see [python/README.md](python/README.md#langgraph).

## Get a key

The hobby tier is free and needs no signup form:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.korely.ai/v1/agents/init \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"agent_caller": "your-name-here"}'
```

The response carries a `kor_live_` key. Set it as `KORELY_API_KEY` and the SDK, the CLI, and the REST API all authenticate with it. From code, `Korely.init_agent()` (Python) and `Korely.initAgent()` (JS) make the same call.

The account behind that key has no login: the key is the account. Keep it, because it is also the only way to delete the account (`korely delete-account --yes`, or `delete_account(confirm=True)` in the SDK).

Or let the CLI do it for you. `korely init` saves the key to `~/.korely/config.json`, and the SDK reads it from there when `KORELY_API_KEY` is not set, so this is enough to get going:

```bash
pip install korely-memory
korely init --agent --agent-caller your-name
python -c "from korely_memory import Korely; print(Korely().get_context(query='hi').tokens)"
```

## TypeScript

```ts
import { Korely } from "korely-memory";

const korely = new Korely();

await korely.add("Maria downgraded to Free.", { user_id: "maria" });
const ctx = await korely.getContext

…

readme.markdown:
# FIDE Laws of Chess on Arxo

**Explore a chess arbiter's decision through a pinned model, explicit facts and an inspectable answer.** Ten retained fictional cases cover illegal moves, flag fall, rapid/blitz exceptions, recording and arbiter judgment.

**Node.js 20+ · ESM · canon package 0.1.0 · model 0.1.1 · FIDE edition effective 1 January 2023**

[Start in Node.js](#start-in-nodejs) · [Cases](#choose-a-case) · [Evidence](#inspect-the-evidence) · [Depth](#formalization-depth) · [Submit a case](https://github.com/arxohq/arxo-fide-chess/issues/new) · [Source repository](https://github.com/arxohq/arxo-fide-chess)

This is an independent open-source teaching and research demonstration. For an actual chess ruling, use the authentic FIDE Laws and the competent arbiter. Source text and model scope are pinned; the package does not claim general chess-engine capability or complete formalization.

## Start in Node.js

Requirements: **Node.js 20+**. The example uses ES modules; keep the `.mjs`
extension. This recipe was checked on macOS arm64 with Node.js 20.20.2 on
14 October 2026. No global CLI, Git clone or MCP client is needed for this route.

Create a fresh directory, open a terminal there, then run:

```sh
npm init -y
npm install --ignore-scripts @arxo/canon-fide-chess@0.1.0 @arxo/law@0.4.3
```

Save this as `example.mjs`, then run `node example.mjs`:

```js
import { open } from '@arxo/law';
import { loadModel } from '@arxo/canon-fide-chess/chess';
import { game, white, getCaseInput } from '@arxo/canon-fide-chess/examples/arbiter';

const model = await loadModel();
const chess = await open(model.spec, {
  offline: true,
  local: { packages: { [model.spec]: model.package } },
});

const input = getCaseInput('SecondIllegal');
const loss = await chess.truth('game_lost_by', [game, white], input);
const draw = await chess.truth('game_drawn', [game], input);
console.log(loss.evaluationStatus, loss.truthStatus); // COMPUTED, TRUE_ONLY
console.log(draw.evaluationStatus, draw.truthStatus); // COMPUTED, NEITHER
```

The two output lines are **loss**, then **draw**:

```text
COMPUTED TRUE_ONLY
COMPUTED NEITHER
```

`COMPUTED` means the query was evaluated. `TRUE_ONLY` means it has positive
support and no negative support. `NEITHER` means neither polarity is supported;
it does not establish that the proposition is false.

Now replace only `getCaseInput('SecondIllegal')` with
`getCaseInput('SecondIllegalNoMate')` and run `node example.mjs` again:

```text
REQUIRES_JUDGMENT NEITHER
COMPUTED TRUE_ONLY
```

The second line now establishes a draw. This case supplies the fact that the
opponent cannot checkmate by any legal series. The separate loss query still
requests an arbiter's assessment because other reachable loss grounds remain
unresolved. Read both status fields; `REQUIRES_JUDGMENT` identifies an assessment
the model does not decide on its own.

To try another retained episode, choose a name from [the case table](#choose-a-case).
To propose your own episode, [open an issue](https://github.com/arxohq/arxo-fide-chess/issues/new)

fictional or anonymized case.

The SDK executes the rules through `@arxo/law-engine@0.5.3`. Installation alone does not register this distribution in the SDK's automatic canon resolver: keep the explicit `local.packages` handoff above. The loader implements no chess decisions or formulas.

## Use as an MCP server

The separate native MCP wrapper runs the same pinned model over stdio:

```sh
npx -y @arxo/mcp-fide-chess@0.1.0
```

Node.js 20+, Linux x64 or macOS arm64. |---|---|---|
| `TouchIntentUnknown` | A movable own piece; intentional touch not adjudicated | `must_move_first_touched_piece`: `REQUIRES_JUDGMENT / NEITHER` |
| `FirstIllegal` | One completed illegal move | Loss: `REQUIRES_JUDGMENT / NEITHER`; draw: `COMPUTED / NEITHER` |
| `SecondIllegal` | Two illegal moves under the model's specified closure | Loss: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |
| `SecondIllegalNoMate` | Two illegal moves; inability to checkmate established | Draw: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |
| `FlagFall` | Flag observed, time control not completed, mate possible | Loss: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |
| `FlagFallNoMate` | The same flag; inability to checkmate established | Draw: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |

| `BlitzFirstIllegalCompetitive` | Blitz 3+2 under competitive rules B.2 | Opponent receives 120 seconds; 60-second query is `NEITHER` |
| `ShortOfTimeRecording` | Standard chess, no increment, 240 seconds left | `must_record_moves`: `COMPUTED / FALSE_ONLY` |
| `DeviceWarning` | Electronic device evident; arbiter gave a warning | Loss and differing-penalty queries: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |

All 18 original case/query expectations are retained and checked. The fixture export provides `caseNames`, `game`, `white`, `black`, `king`, `CaseName` and `getCaseInput(name)`. Each call returns an independent copy; an unknown name throws `RangeError`.

`getCaseInput` preserves the CLI's canonical assertions, constants, context and options. The loader supplies neither absent facts nor adjudications. The model's explicitly declared closures are part of its rules; they are not a general assumption that a missing fact is false.

readme.markdown:
# jira-easy-mcp

Another Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Jira, without Auth token. Provides tools for complete Jira automation including issues, projects, boards, sprints, comments, worklogs, and more.

> **Tested on:** Jira Server / Data Center 7.13, 8.20, 9.12 and 10.3 (every tool, automated, see [Development & Testing](#development--testing))

---

## 🔑 Why This MCP?

**Works with Basic Authentication (username + password)** — no API tokens required!

Most Jira MCP servers require OAuth or API tokens, which many organizations restrict or don't allow. This MCP uses **HTTP Basic Authentication**, so you can connect using just your Jira username and password. Perfect for:

- 🏢 **Enterprise environments** where admins don't allow API token creation
- 🔒 **Self-hosted Jira Server** instances without OAuth configured
- ⚡ **Quick setup** without going through IT approval processes

---

## Quick Start

### VS Code (Workspace Configuration)

Create `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace root:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "jira": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "jira-easy-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "JIRA_BASE_URL": "https://your-jira-instance.com",
        "JIRA_USERNAME": "your-username",
        "JIRA_PASSWORD": "your-password",
        "JIRA_PROJECTS_FILTER": "ABC,DEF,XYZ",
        "JIRA_RESPONSE_FORMAT": "JSON"
      }
    }
  }
}
```
Add to your VS Code settings for accessing in all workspaces.

> **Note:** `JIRA_PROJECTS_FILTER` and `JIRA_RESPONSE_FORMAT` are optional. Projects filter limits access to specified projects. Response format can be `JSON` (default) or `TOON` (text-oriented notation).

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add jira \
  -e JIRA_BASE_URL=https://your-jira-instance.com \
  -e JIRA_USERNAME=your-username \
  -e JIRA_PASSWORD=your-password \
  -- npx -y jira-easy-mcp
```

### Codex CLI

Add to `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.jira]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "jira-easy-mcp"]
env = { JIRA_BASE_URL = "https://your-jira-instance.com", JIRA_USERNAME = "your-username", JIRA_PASSWORD = "your-password" }
```

### Other clients

**Cursor:** `~/.cursor/mcp.json` or `.cursor/mcp.json` (use `"mcpServers": { ... }` wrapper)  
**Windsurf:** Add to your Windsurf MCP settings (use `"mcpServers": { ... }` wrapper)  
**Claude Desktop:** Edit `claude_desktop_config.json` (macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/`, Windows: `%APPDATA%\Claude\`; use `"mcpServers": { ... }` wrapper)  
**Gemini CLI:** `~/.gemini/settings.json` (use `"mcpServers": { ... }` wrapper)

All use the same `command`, `args`, and `env` configuration as VS Code above.

> **Windows:** if the client cannot start `npx`, use `"command": "cmd"` with `"args": ["/c", "npx", "-y", "jira-easy-mcp"]`.
>
> **Tool limits:** some clients (notably Cursor) cap how many tools they send to the model, historically around 40 across all servers. This server has 41; turn off the ones you don't need in the client's MCP settings.

### Credentials from the OS keychain (optional)

To keep your password out of config files, omit `JIRA_USERNAME`/`JIRA_PASSWORD` and store a credential under the service name `JiraMCP`:

- **macOS:** `security add-generic-password -s JiraMCP -a your-username -w` (prompts for the password; on first start macOS asks to allow `node` to read it)
- **Windows:** `cmdkey /generic:JiraMCP /user:your-username /pass` (use `/generic`, not `/add`)

If several accounts are stored, set `JIRA_USERNAME` to choose one. When both `JIRA_USERNAME` and `JIRA_PASSWORD` are set, they are used and the keychain is not read. Keychain support uses the optional `keytar` package; if it can't be installed on your machine, use the environment variables.

---

## Common Use Cases

| Task | Tool | Example Prompt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Search issues** | `jira_search` | "Search for all open bugs assigned to me in project ABC" |
| **Get issue details** | `jira_get_issue` | "Show me the details of issue ABC-123" |
| **View issue images** | `jira_get_issue_images` | "Show me the screenshots attached to ABC-123" |
| **Upload attachment** | `jira_upload_attachment` | "Attach /Users/me/Desktop/error.png to ABC-123" |
| **Create issue** | `jira_create_issue` | "Create a new bug in project ABC with title 'Login button not working'" |
| **Update issue** | `jira_update_issue` | "Change the priority of ABC-123 to High and assign it to john.doe" |
| **Edit custom fields** | `jira_update_issue` + `jira_get_edit_meta` | "Set Severity on ABC-123 to Critical" (unique name or `customfield_` id) |
| **Add comment** | `jira_add_comment` | "Add a comment to ABC-123 saying 'Fix deployed to staging'" |
| **Change status** | `jira_transition_issue` | "Move ABC-123 to Done" |
| **Log time** | `jira_add_worklog` | "Log 2 hours of work on ABC-123 for yesterday" |
| **List projects** | `jira_get_projects` | "Show me all projects I have access to" |
| **View sprints** | `jira_get_sprints` | "What's in the current sprint for project ABC?" |
| **Link issues** | `jira_create_link` | "Link ABC-123 as blocking ABC-124" |
| **Generate filter URL** | `jira_generate_filter_url` | "Create a shareable link for all open bugs updated in the last 7 days" |

---

## Testing with MCP Inspector

The MCP Inspector provides a web UI to test all tools interactively:

```bash
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector npx jira-easy-mcp
```

This opens a browser at `http://localhost:6274` where you can:

- View all available tools
- Test each tool with custom parameters
- See the raw JSON responses

> **Note:** Put these values inside inspector UI before connecting: `JIRA_BASE_URL`, `JIRA_USERNAME`, `JIRA_PASSWORD`.

---

## Custom fields

Jira REST API v2 identifies custom fields by id (`customfield_10006`). Values are the raw REST payload for that field type. Display names work only when they are unique (exact, case-sensitive) on the relevant screen.

### Read (`jira_get_issue`)

Default response: system fields plus custom fi

# MCP Browser

Claude, Cursor and other MCP clients cannot open Reddit, X, LinkedIn or Facebook. Those sites block AI fetchers, so you end up reading the threads yourself and pasting them in. MCP Browser is a Mac app that lets your AI read those sites through your own Chrome login, so it sees exactly what you see and answers with links. It also reads your Search Console, Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity data. No API keys, no OAuth setup.

Website: [webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser)

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| ![Claude fails to fetch a Reddit thread](docs/before.png) | ![Claude reads the same thread through MCP Browser](docs/after.png) |

## Install

Mac with Apple Silicon. Download, open, sign in, press Connect.

1. Download the app from the [latest release](https://github.com/Bishwas-py/mcpbrowser/releases/latest) or from [webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser). Drag it into Applications and open it. The app is signed and notarized.

# KEPTA — the memory for AI systems

## Your AI forgets everything. Every chat starts from zero.

**KEPTA is the fix: one local, encrypted memory that every AI reads and writes — Claude, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Cline, any MCP client, and scripts over HTTP. No cloud. No account. One file you own.**

Everything an AI system learns goes into an encrypted knowledge base on your own computer — and every AI recalls it in milliseconds, however long the context grows. Documents, decisions, client knowledge, whole chat histories: remembered, linked, contradicted, superseded — never lost.

This repository is the **source-available core** (BUSL-1.1 — every line public, converts to AGPL-3.0-or-later four years after each release): the memory engine, the MCP server, the HTTP API — and the Python client, which is MIT so any Python project can embed it. **Everything that makes the memory smart lives in this free engine. There are no tiers inside the memory — nothing is held back to sell anything.**

Questions, security feedback or benchmark critique? → **[Discussions](https://github.com/DamianTodorovic/kepta/discussions)**

readme.markdown:
Brain Memory

  
  
  

A hierarchical, file-system-based memory plugin for AI coding agents. Inspired by human neuroscience — memories are organized into deep nested life-domain categories, connected via associative networks, strengthened through spaced recall, and naturally decay over time.

One hosted **MCP connector** reaches every major agent and chat app — **Claude Code**, **OpenAI Codex CLI**, **OpenCode**, **GitHub Copilot CLI**, **Kilo**, the **Claude.ai** apps, **ChatGPT**, **Google Antigravity** (Gemini CLI's successor), **OpenClaw** / **NVIDIA NemoClaw**, **Hermes Agent**, and **Goose**. Prefer a free, local-first install? The native plugin runs entirely from `~/.brain/` on Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, and Antigravity — and dedicated [native integrations](integrations/) plug the same brain into OpenClaw and Hermes as their memory engine.

```
~/.brain/
├── professional/
│   └── companies/
│       └── acme-corp/
│           └── projects/
│               └── alpha-launch.md        ⚡ 0.88
├── personal/
│   └── education/
│       └── typescript-generics.md         ⚡ 0.72
├── social/
│   └── communities/
│       └── open-source-contrib.md         ⚡ 0.65
└── family/
    └── events/
        └── annual-reunion-planning.md     ⚡ 0.55
```

## Why Brain Memory?

Existing AI memory solutions use flat databases with tag-based retrieval. Brain Memory is different:

- **The directory tree IS the semantic structure** — `professional/companies/acme/projects/` tells the agent everything about context without vector search
- **Human-inspectable** — Browse your "brain" in any file explorer
- **Git-friendly** — Full version history of how memories evolve
- **Strength + decay** — Recalled memories get stronger, forgotten ones fade. Just like your brain
- **Recall receipts** — Memory that visibly fires: every answer shaped by a memory ends with a one-line attributable receipt (`◉ memory: "<title>" (<type>, <age>)`), minted by the engine so it can't be hallucinated
- **Provenance-bounded trust** — Every memory records where it came from (`user`, `agent-inferred`, `tool-output`, `external`), and recall weighs it: a fact planted by a web page or tool output is down-ranked, flagged `low_trust`, marked `⚠` on its receipt, and can never outrank what you said directly — no matter how many copies of it get written. And because memories are plain files, Brain records a **SHA-256 baseline** of each one at write time — so `brain audit` also catches a memory edited *outside* any write path, the one poisoning route every write-path defense is blind to
- **Bitemporal — it knows *when* a fact was true** — Every memory separates record time (when the brain learned it) from valid time (`valid_from` / `valid_until`, when it was actually true). So "we deploy to Fly.io" and "we deploy to Render" aren't a contradiction to guess between — they're one fact with a boundary. `brain recall "deploy target" --as-of 2026-03-01` answers what was true in March; `--as-known-of` answers what the brain knew then. Facts that stopped being true are demoted and marked `⌛ expired`, never silently served as current
- **Deterministic recall — every agent ranks identically** — Scoring is arithmetic over files, not a model call: TF-IDF/BM25 relevance, decayed strength, spreading activation, context match, salience. Claude, Codex, and Gemini asking the same question of the same brain get the *same* ranking, in the same order, offline. No embedding-model version can silently reshuffle what your agent remembers
- **Associative network** — Memories link to each other with weighted connections. Recalling one activates related ones automatically
- **Context-dependent recall** — Memories encoded in a similar context to the current session are scored higher
- **Spaced reinforcement** — Memories recalled after longer intervals get bigger boosts, cramming produces diminishing returns
- **Cognitive types** — Episodic, semantic, and procedural memories each decay differently, just like in the brain
- **Always-present knowledge** — Pin critical conventions and preferences so they load every session, bypassing recall and never decaying — the facts your agent must never miss
- **Procedural skills** — Reusable how-to workflows with progressive disclosure, learned automatically from repeated experience and exportable to your agent's native skills
- **On-demand depth** — Subcategories are created as needed, not pre-defined
- **Consolidation** — Weak related memories merge into stronger combined knowledge
- **Zero dependencies — and measured, not assumed** — Pure file I/O: no database, no server, no embedding model. That is a deliberate result, not a shortcut. On our hardest retrieval scenario (1,021 memories, 1,000 plausible distractors) a real embedding model ranked the target memories *worse* than BM25 — see the [retrieval-only pilot](benchmark/README.md#retrieval-only-pilot-no-agent-no-llm-spend)

## Install

There are two ways to give an agent its brain. They are complementary — most people end up with both:

| Path | Reaches | Storage | Cost | Best for |
|------|---------|---------|------|----------|
| **Hosted MCP connector** | Every MCP-capable host (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, Claude.ai apps, ChatGPT, Antigravity, OpenClaw, Hermes, Goose) | Brain Cloud (hosted) | account | One connector, everywhere — including web & mobile chat |
| **Local-first native plugin** | The current CLIs (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, Antigravity) | `~/.brain/` on your machine | free | Zero-config ambient memory, no account, files you own |
| **[Assistant integrations](integrations/)** | OpenClaw / NVIDIA NemoClaw (memory-slot plugin), Hermes Agent (memory provider) | `~/.brain/` on your machine | free | Your always-on personal assistant sharing one brain with your coding agents |

readme.markdown:
# yab-mcp

The MCP server of Yab, Yet Another Browser, for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any MCP client.

Yab, Yet Another Browser, is a free WebKit browser for the Mac. With this server, any agent gets one real browser on your Mac: the one you're signed in to. Your agent opens tabs of its own beside yours, reads pages as text, clicks, types and fills forms with your sign-ins, your cookies and your IP. There is no cloud browser, no debug port and no Chrome to set up, and it's free. A press on Send, Pay, Delete and the like waits for your yes on a card in Yab, unless you chose Bypass in Yab's settings: the browser holds that yes, not the model. Saved passwords are filled by Yab and never shown to the agent. Agent tabs live in a window off screen and come in front of you only when you ask. With Yab closed, the first call opens it hidden, with no window and no Dock tile, and it quits after half an hour with nothing to do. `yab serve` keeps it running that way.

[Download Yab](https://yetanotherbrowser.com/dl?ref=github) · [For developers](https://yetanotherbrowser.com/developers) · [Manual](https://yetanotherbrowser.com/manual)

## Remote assistants (0.2.0 preview)

On the assistant's own computer, run `npx yab-mcp login --client dots`.
When Yab's Connect flow supplies a nonce, add `--nonce` with that value.
It prints the code and returns immediately; a background process saves the
connection after the person allows it in Yab.
Yab on the Mac shows the eight-character code under Settings > AI > Assistants.
After the person allows it there, choose who does the work:

- **Direct browser control:** configure your assistant's MCP server with command
  `npx` and args `["-y", "yab-mcp", "--remote"]`. The assistant calls `open`,
  `snapshot`, `click`, `type`, etc. itself, using its own model/account.
  `--remote` bridges JSON-RPC over stdio; it does not accept a natural-language
  prompt or start a Yab model run. Calling the `task` MCP tool still delegates.
- **Delegation:** `npx yab-mcp task "Find a table for Friday"` starts a separate
  agent using the model selected for Tasks in Yab on the Mac. ChatGPT (via Codex)
  consumes the user's ChatGPT limits; Claude uses their Claude plan instead.
  Choose this when you intend to use that plan, including from a shell-only bot.
  It prints its session ID and returns; run `npx yab-mcp status SESSION` for the
  next update, or `npx yab-mcp status` for the newest task after a Mac reconnects.
  Repeat until it says done.

Both modes keep the assistant's existing account access and approval settings.
The connection token stays in `~/.config/yab-mcp/auth.json` (mode 0600), or the
path in `YAB_MCP_AUTH_FILE`. When the home folder is read-only, as on some bots'
computers, it goes to the first writable of `/workspace/shared/.yab-mcp/`,
`/workspace/.yab-mcp/` and `.yab-mcp/` in the current folder. If the computer
ends the background process that waits for the person's Allow, the next
`task`, `status` or `--remote` finishes connecting.
`YAB_MCP_URL` selects a test server; production uses `https://yab-sync.21st.workers.dev`.
Plain `npx yab-mcp` starts the local app's MCP server.

## Requirements

- A Mac with macOS 15.4 or later.
- Yab, free: [download](https://yetanotherbrowser.com/dl?ref=github). It updates itself.
- Agents allowed in Yab: Settings › AI › Agents › Let agents use Yab. Until then, every call says so.
- Node.js 18 or later, for `npx`. A client can also run Yab directly, without Node: see [Without Node](#without-node).

Chrome is your main browser? Yab can still be the one your agents use, usually closed. `yab import chrome` brings Chrome's sign-ins into Yab after you say yes in Yab, so your agent hits fewer sign-in pages.

Already use Yab? Settings › Developers adds it to Claude Code and Codex with one click, and Copy Config gives the JSON for any other client. You don't need this package for that.

## Install

### Claude Code

The plugin brings the tools and Yab's skill:

```
/plugin marketplace add yetanotherbrowser/yab-mcp
/plugin install yab@yab-mcp
```

From a shell: `claude plugin marketplace add yetanotherbrowser/yab-mcp`, then `claude plugin install yab@yab-mcp`.

Only the tools:

```sh
claude mcp add --scope user yab-browser -- npx -y yab-mcp
```

If Yab's Settings › Developers already added Yab to Claude Code, skip this: you'd have the same tools twice.

### Codex

The plugin, tools and skill:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add yetanotherbrowser/yab-mcp
codex plugin add yab@yab-mcp
```

Or only the tools, in `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.yab-browser]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "yab-mcp"]
tool_timeout_sec = 900
default_tools_approval_mode = "approve"
```

`tool_timeout_sec` lets a call wait up to 15 minutes while Yab asks you something; the plugin keeps Codex's default of 5. `default_tools_approval_mode` stops Codex asking before every Yab tool; Yab still asks you before Send, Pay and Delete. Leave it out if you want Codex to ask too.

### Cursor

Or add it to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "yab-browser": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "yab-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code

```sh
code --add-mcp '{"name":"yab-browser","command":"npx","args":["-y","yab-mcp"]}'
```

Or in `.vscode/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "yab-browser": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "yab-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Windsurf (Devin Desktop)

In `~/.config/devin/mcp_config.json` (older Windsurf builds: `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {

      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "yab-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Download `yab-mcp-<version>.mcpb` from [Releases](https://github.com/yetanotherbrowser/yab-mcp/releases) and open it: Claude Desktop installs it as an extension. Or add this to `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

# Small Business MCP Starter Kit by Modern Mustard Seed

Ship a remote MCP connector for Claude that is built to pass Anthropic's directory review on the first try.

This kit is the set of patterns Modern Mustard Seed uses for the connectors it runs in production, pulled out into a clean Next.js project you can fork:

- **A route template** on Next.js App Router and [`mcp-handler`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-handler), serving Streamable HTTP at one URL per connector, with no redirect.
- **Tool conventions enforced at load time**: a title, `readOnlyHint` or `destructiveHint` on every tool, snake_case names of 64 characters or fewer, and descriptions that describe instead of steer. Break a rule and `pnpm test` fails, long before a reviewer sees it.
- **Specific error messages** instead of "Bad Request", and **output size caps** under Claude's limits.
- **Rate limiting built for Claude's shared egress range.** Every claude.ai user arrives from `160.79.104.0/21`, so nothing is keyed by IP and nothing returns HTTP 429.
- **An SSRF-safe fetch** for any tool that reads a URL a user supplied, with tests that prove a listening loopback server receives zero requests.
- **An eval harness** that runs real prompts against your live URL, with no model and no API key.
- **Docs, privacy, terms and support page templates** plus `/.well-known/security.txt`, all driven by one config file.
- **A submission checklist** mapped to the directory form's 10 steps and its seven policy acknowledgments, with every rule linked to Anthropic's documentation.
- **A worked example**: a U.S. federal holiday and business-day calendar with five read-only tools that passes all 35 of its own evals.

MIT licensed. Built by [Modern Mustard Seed](https://modernmustardseed.com).

## Working demo

The example connector runs live, deployed from this repository with no changes:

- Connector URL: `https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/holidays` (add it in Claude under **Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector**)
- Docs page reviewers read: https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/docs/holidays
- Privacy, terms and support: https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/privacy, [/terms](https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/terms), [/support](https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/support)
- Official MCP Registry entry: `com.modernmustardseed/holiday-calendar`

Run the evals against it yourself: `node eval/holidays.eval.mjs https://starter.modernmustardseed.com`

## Quickstart: 10 minutes

You need Node 22.6 or later, pnpm, and a Vercel account (any host that runs Next.js works).

**1. Make your copy.** (1 minute)

```sh
gh repo create my-connector --template ModernMustardSeed/small-business-mcp-starter --public --clone
cd my-connector
pnpm install
```

Or select **Use this template** on GitHub.

**2. Run it and prove it works.** (2 minutes)

```sh
pnpm dev
```

In a second terminal:

```sh
pnpm test
pnpm evals http://localhost:3000
```

You should see `32 pass` from the unit tests and `35 of 35 passed` from the evals. Open http://localhost:3000/docs/holidays to see the docs page reviewers read.

**3. Make it yours.** (2 minutes)

Edit `lib/site.ts`: company name, location, website, support inbox, security inbox, and the policy date. Every public page and `security.txt` read from it. Replace `app/icon.svg` and `app/apple-icon.png` with your own mark; the directory listing asks for an icon.

**4. Deploy.** (3 minutes)

Import the repository at [vercel.com/new](https://vercel.com/new), or from the terminal:

```sh
vercel deploy --prod
```

Vercel sets `VERCEL_PROJECT_PRODUCTION_URL`, which the pages use for their links. Leave Attack Challenge Mode and any bot-protection rule off for your MCP paths: they answer Claude with a challenge page.

**5. Check the deployment.** (1 minute)

```sh
pnpm preflight https://your-project.vercel.app
pnpm evals https://your-project.vercel.app
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays --transport http --method tools/list
```

Preflight checks HTTPS, no redirect, no 403 or 429, every public page returning 200, the MCP handshake and the annotation rules.

**6. Try it in Claude.** (1 minute)

In Claude, open **Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector** and paste `https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays`. Ask: "An invoice dated 2026-11-20 is due in 10 business days. What date is that?" In Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add --transport http holidays https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays
```

## Build your own connector

1. Copy `lib/holidays/tools.ts` to `lib/<yours>/tools.ts`. Declare each tool as a `ToolSpec`: name, title, description, zod input schema, annotations, a per-minute limit, optional global limits, the fields that are safe to log, and a `run` function that returns `ok(data)` or `fail(code, sentence)`.
2. Copy `app/holidays/route.ts` to `app/<yours>/route.ts` and point it at your tools.
3. Copy `app/docs/holidays/page.tsx` to `app/docs/<yours>/page.tsx`. Keep the "For reviewers" section: you paste it into the form.
4. Rewrite `app/privacy/page.tsx` so every sentence is true of your tools: what they receive, what they read, what you keep and for how long, who else touches it.
5. Copy `eval/holidays.eval.mjs`. Write 20 to 50 cases from prompts real users type, with expected values from an authority outside your code. Include the error cases.
6. If a tool fetches a URL a user gave you, use `safeFetch` from `lib/mcp/safe-fetch.ts`. Never `fetch` a user-supplied URL directly.
7. Deploy, run `pnpm preflight` and `pnpm evals` against production, test every tool in Claude, then work through [docs/SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md](docs/SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md).

Why each pattern exists, with the rule it answers: [docs/PATTERNS.md](docs/PATTERNS.md).

## What is in the box

|---|---|
| `app/holidays/route.ts` | The connector endpoint. One file per connector. |
| `lib/mcp/tool.ts` | `ToolSpec`, `registerTools`, `runTool`: conventions, limits, e

# iCloud Calendar MCP Server

A [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server that gives MCP clients access to iCloud Calendar
over CalDAV: list calendars, read, create, update, move and delete events. It works on Linux, macOS and Windows,
since it talks to iCloud directly instead of going through the macOS Calendar app.

This is a maintained fork of [zwrong/iCalendar](https://github.com/zwrong/iCalendar), itself derived from the macOS
`mcp-ical` server. See [Changes in this fork](#changes-in-this-fork).

## Tools

| Tool | Description |
|---|---|
| `list_calendars` | Names of the available calendars |
| `list_events` | Events in a date range, optionally for one calendar, sorted by start time |
| `create_event` | New event: title, times, all-day, location, notes, URL, alarms, recurrence |
| `update_event` | Change any of those fields, or move the event to another calendar |
| `delete_event` | Delete an event by identifier |
| `debug_calendar_connection` | Connection check: calendars and event counts over the last 7 days |

The `calendars://list` resource also lists the calendars. With `MCP_ICAL_READ_ONLY=true`, the three write tools are
not registered at all.

## Requirements

- Python 3.12 or later and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)
- An Apple ID with iCloud Calendar enabled
- An **app-specific password** for that Apple ID

### App-specific password

1. Sign in to [appleid.apple.com](https://appleid.apple.com/), open **Sign-In and Security**, then
   **App-Specific Passwords**.
2. Generate a password, for example named `mcp-icloud-caldav`.

The username is your Apple ID address, which is not necessarily an `@icloud.com` address.
An app-specific password gives access to iCloud CalDAV, CardDAV and IMAP: keep it out of version control and revoke
it if it leaks.

## Installation

The package is published on PyPI as `mcp-icloud-caldav`. With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), MCP clients can
start it directly, without a separate install step:

```bash
uvx mcp-icloud-caldav
```

`uvx` downloads the package into a cached, isolated environment on first use. To install it permanently instead:
`uv tool install mcp-icloud-caldav` (or `pipx install mcp-icloud-caldav`).

From source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Glob0x17/mcp-icloud-caldav.git mcp-icloud-caldav
cd mcp-icloud-caldav
uv sync --no-dev
uv run mcp-icloud-caldav
```

## Configuration

Credentials are read in this order:

1. **Environment variables** (recommended)

   | Variable | Required | Default |
   |---|---|---|
   | `ICLOUD_USERNAME` | yes | |
   | `ICLOUD_PASSWORD` | yes | |
   | `CALDAV_SERVER_URL` | no | `https://caldav.icloud.com/` |

2. **`MCP_ICAL_CONFIG`**: path to a JSON file shaped like [`config.json.example`](config.json.example)
3. **`config_private.json`**, then **`config.json`**, at the repository root (kept for compatibility)

Other settings:

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `MCP_ICAL_READ_ONLY` | `false` | `true` leaves out `create_event`, `update_event` and `delete_event` |
| `MCP_ICAL_LOG_LEVEL` | `INFO` | `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING` or `ERROR`. Logs go to stderr |

The server speaks MCP over stdio and is started by the client. To check it by hand:

```bash
ICLOUD_USERNAME=you@example.com ICLOUD_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx uvx mcp-icloud-caldav
```

It waits on stdin and prints nothing on stdout.

## Client setup

Use the absolute path of `uvx` (`which uvx`) if the client cannot find it: clients often start servers without your
shell `PATH`, which shows up as `spawn uvx ENOENT`. Usual locations:

| Installed with | Path |
|---|---|
| The uv installer (Linux, macOS) | `~/.local/bin/uvx` |
| Homebrew on Apple silicon | `/opt/homebrew/bin/uvx` |
| Homebrew on Intel Macs | `/usr/local/bin/uvx` |

The command and its argument are separate fields: the command is `uvx` (or its path) and `mcp-icloud-caldav` is an
argument. A config where the command is the single string `"uvx mcp-icloud-caldav"` fails with `ENOENT`, because
the client looks for a program with that exact name, space included.

### Keeping the password out of the client config

Most clients store `env` values in clear text in their config file. A small wrapper that reads an env file avoids
that:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav && chmod 700 ~/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav
cat > ~/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav/env <<'EOF'
ICLOUD_USERNAME=you@example.com
ICLOUD_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx
MCP_ICAL_READ_ONLY=true
EOF
chmod 600 ~/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav/env

cat > ~/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
set -a; source "$HOME/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav/env"; set +a
exec /absolute/path/to/uvx mcp-icloud-caldav
EOF
chmod +x ~/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run
```

Then point the client at `~/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run`. Starting read-only and switching to `false` once reading works
is a sensible first step.

### Claude Desktop

In `claude_desktop_config.json` (Settings, Developer, Edit Config). On macOS it is
`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "icloud-calendar": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["mcp-icloud-caldav"],
      "env": {
        "ICLOUD_USERNAME": "you@example.com",
        "ICLOUD_PASSWORD": "xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

or, with the wrapper, `"command": "/home/you/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run"` and no `env`. Quit Claude Desktop
completely and start it again after editing. On macOS, server logs are in
`~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp-server-icloud-calendar.log`.

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user icloud-calendar \
  -e ICLOUD_USERNAME=you@example.com -e ICLOUD_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx \
  -- uvx mcp-icloud-caldav
```

or, with the wrapper, `claude mcp add --scope user icloud-calendar -- ~/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run`.

Do not quote what follows `--`: `-- uvx mcp-icloud-caldav` registers `uvx` as the command and `mcp-icloud-caldav` as
it
