# upGrowth Growth Toolkit (MCP server)

A free, public, read-only [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server with 29 growth marketing tools. Connect it to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini CLI or any MCP client and ask growth maths, SEO and AI-visibility questions in plain language.

- **Endpoint:** `https://upgrowth.in/connected-app/mcp` (Streamable HTTP). Alias: `https://mcp.upgrowth.in/mcp`
- **Auth:** none. No sign-up, no API key.
- **Data:** your inputs and the answers are never stored. We keep anonymous usage counts (event, tool name, host and a broad client type such as ChatGPT or Claude) in Cloudflare Workers Analytics Engine; no IP addresses. 28 of the 29 tools make no outside calls; `ai_crawler_access_check` fetches only the public `robots.txt` and `llms.txt` of the domain you name.
- **Official MCP Registry:** `in.upgrowth/growth-toolkit`
- **Docs and setup guide:** https://upgrowth.in/growth-toolkit-mcp/
- **Terms:** https://upgrowth.in/growth-toolkit-terms/
- **Version:** 1.4.2

Built and maintained by [upGrowth Digital](https://upgrowth.in/), a growth marketing consultancy in Pune, India.

## Connect it

**Claude (all plans):** Customize > Connectors > "+ Add" > "Add custom connector". Name it upGrowth, paste the endpoint URL, choose "No sign in" under Authentication and click Add. On Team and Enterprise plans an owner adds it first under Organization settings > Connectors.

name: Draugr
description: Security scanning for AI agents: SAST, SCA, secrets, IaC, DAST, ranked by real risk.

readme.markdown:
# Draugr

> Runs every security scanner you trust, then decides which findings matter. SAST, SCA, secrets, IaC and containers, every finding ranked by exposure, criticality, exploitability and reachability.

**Describe your app. Draugr figures out the rest.**

Every application carries problems nobody put there on purpose: a library that turned out to have a
hole in it, a password committed by accident, a server setting that leaves a door open. Draugr finds
them, works out which ones actually matter for *your* app, and answers the question you are really
asking before a release. **is this safe to ship?**

It runs the established open-source scanners for you, Trivy, Semgrep, Gitleaks and others, so there
is nothing to choose between, wire up, or read five of. You describe what you built, once, in one
file: where the repositories are, what images it builds, what it exposes, what infrastructure it
runs on. Draugr picks the checks that apply, runs the right tool for each, and produces evidence you
can hand to somebody else. Bring the scanners you already pay for, or use the open-source defaults.

Findings are **ranked**, not listed. A scanner's "critical" describes a flaw in the abstract. How
bad it could be at its worst, anywhere. The same flaw is act-now in the service strangers can reach
and backlog in the internal tool three people use, and no scanner can tell those apart because the
difference is in the file you wrote, not in the code. And [`draugr diff`](docs/guides/pr-diff.md)
gates a pull request on **new** findings only, so inheriting two hundred existing ones does not
block every change.

**[Quickstart](#quickstart)** · [See it in action](#see-it-in-action) ·
[What it checks](#what-it-checks) · [In your pipeline](#in-your-pipeline) ·
[Documentation](#documentation) · [What Draugr doesn't promise](#what-draugr-doesnt-promise) ·
[Security](#security--supply-chain)

## See it in action

**Priority (P1–P4) is not severity.** Severity says how bad a flaw is at its worst, anywhere.
Priority weighs that against how exposed and how important the part of your app it sits in is, which
no scanner can work out, because it is not in the code.

**[draugr-dev/draugr-demo](https://github.com/draugr-dev/draugr-demo)** is a deliberately
vulnerable app wired to Draugr: every control lights up, findings land in the repo's
**Security → Code scanning** tab, and its example pull requests show the new-vs-fixed diff.

## Quickstart

```bash
curl -fsSL https://draugr.dev/install.sh | sh
```

Installs to `~/.local/bin`, no `sudo`. It verifies before it installs and says which checks ran, the
archive's SHA-256 against the release `checksums.txt`, plus the cosign signature on that file when
[cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/) is on your `PATH`, and installs nothing if a check
fails. The script is [readable in the repo](install.sh); a download by hand, the GitHub CLI and `go
install` are in the [install guide](docs/getting-started/install.md).

```bash
draugr init            # describe this project in a draugr.saga.yaml
draugr tools install   # fetch the scanners it needs, pinned and verified
draugr scan            # scan what the descriptor describes
```

`tools install` takes its answer from the descriptor beside it, so a small service gets three
scanners rather than every one Draugr can provision. `--all` when you are preparing a machine for
several projects.

Then describe what you actually ship:

```yaml
project: my-app
release:
  version: "1.0"
config:
  controls:
    images:
      enabled: true
components:
  - name: web
    images:
      - image: alpine:3.19
```

```bash
draugr scan draugr.saga.yaml            # console summary; exits non-zero on fail
draugr scan draugr.saga.yaml -o out/    # also writes report.json + results.sarif
draugr scan draugr.saga.yaml --format markdown   # or html, junit, json, sarif
```

**Your editor already knows this file.** Draugr's
[JSON Schema](https://draugr.dev/schema/draugr.saga.schema.json) is registered with
[SchemaStore](https://www.schemastore.org/), so any `*.saga.yaml` gets completion, hover docs and
typo warnings on open with nothing to configure.

Or let discovery write the descriptor for you:

```bash
draugr survey github repos --org my-org -o draugr.saga.yaml
draugr survey k8s images --namespace prod -o draugr.saga.yaml
```

Full walkthrough: [quickstart](docs/getting-started/quickstart.md).

**Setting it up on a real repository?** Reply to [the pinned discussion](https://github.com/draugr-dev/draugr/discussions/1370) with what the repository is and which scanners you run, and we'll write the descriptor with you, including the exposure and criticality that take judgment.

## What it checks

Each control is backed by a tool Draugr executes rather than bundles, so every scanner stays under
its own license, and you can swap it.

| Control | Looks for | By default |
|---|---|---|
| `sca` | known flaws in the libraries you depend on | Trivy, Grype and Mend opt-in |
| `secrets` | passwords and keys committed by accident, history included | Gitleaks |
| `sast` | patterns in the code you wrote that let somebody in | Semgrep, gosec opt-in for Go |
| `iac` | settings that leave a door open, in Terraform, Kubernetes and Dockerfiles | Trivy |
| `images` | what is baked into your container images | Trivy, Grype opt-in |
| `licenses` | terms attached to code you did not write | Trivy |
| `dast` | problems only visible from outside a running app | Nuclei, authenticated, and from an OpenAPI spec |
| `headers` | how your site answers a browser | native |
| `tls` | certificates and encryption | native |
| `kubernetes` | your Kubernetes cluster, against the CIS benchmarks | native, kube-bench opt-in |
| `cloud` | your cloud account as it is, against the CIS benchmarks | Prowler |
| `threats` | whether anything you talk to is on a public blocklist | abuse.ch URLhaus |
| `provenance` | whether an image is signed by the builder you expect | Sigstore cosign |

Every scanner

readme.markdown:
# agent-tollgate-engine

Live at **https://skinwinking.com**. Machine-readable: [`/llms.txt`](https://skinwinking.com/llms.txt), [`/openapi.json`](https://skinwinking.com/openapi.json), MCP at `https://skinwinking.com/mcp`.

Pay-per-call trading intelligence and fee-bearing swap routing for autonomous agents, on Cloudflare Workers.

Revenue paths:
1. x402 micropayments in USDC (Polygon or Solana) for `orderbook-imbalance` (0.02 USDC) and `token-audit` (0.20 USDC).
2. 30 bps platform fee on swaps built by `quote-and-build` (Jupiter on Solana, LI.FI cross-chain/EVM).

All payments go straight to the merchant addresses in `wrangler.toml`. The server holds no keys and no funds.

## Layout

| Package | Role |
|---|---|
| `packages/core` | config, route catalog, on-chain payment verification (EVM, Solana, x402 facilitator), replay protection interface |
| `packages/api-worker` | Hono Worker, `x402PaymentGate` middleware, Durable Object nonce store, route handlers |
| `packages/omni-router` | Jupiter (Solana) and LI.FI (cross-chain) quote builders with fee embedding |
| `packages/discovery` | `/llms.txt`, `/openapi.json`, MCP server (HTTP at `/mcp`, stdio via `npm run mcp`) |
| `packages/simulation-agent` | end-to-end simulated agent |

## Local run

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .dev.vars        # then set SOLANA_RPC_URL and EVM_RPC_URL to private endpoints
npm run dev                      # http://127.0.0.1:8787, simulation receipts enabled
```

`npm run dev` sets `SIM_SECRET`, which enables HMAC simulation receipts (`Bearer sim_...`). Never set `SIM_SECRET` in production.

If port 8787 is busy: `npx wrangler dev --port 8799 --var SIM_SECRET:dev-simulation-secret` and `BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8799`.

## Simulation

With `npm run dev` running in another terminal:

```bash
npm run simulate
```

Steps: unpaid call returns 402, simulated payment succeeds, replay is rejected, a Solana swap quote proves the fee account is inside the built transaction, a Polygon to Base quote proves the LI.FI integrator fee.

## Production prerequisites

1. **RPC**: public endpoints are rate-limited or blocked. Use private ones.
   ```bash
   npx wrangler secret put SOLANA_RPC_URL
   npx wrangler secret put EVM_RPC_URL
   ```
2. **LI.FI integrator**: register `LIFI_INTEGRATOR` at https://portal.li.fi, set the fee wallet to the EVM payout address, and set the fee to 0.3%. Without it LI.FI rejects quotes that carry `fee`.
3. **Solana fee token accounts**: the Jupiter fee is paid in the output token to the merchant's associated token account for that mint. The route returns `FEE_ACCOUNT_MISSING` until that account exists. Receiving a small amount of the token (or creating the ATA in Phantom) creates it. USDC and wSOL cover the main pairs.
4. Optional `X402_FACILITATOR_URL` enables `X-402-Signature` settlement through an x402 facilitator.

## Deploy

```bash
npx wrangler deploy
```

Attach the domain under Workers & Routes in the Cloudflare dashboard (custom domain on the worker).

## Payment proofs

| Header | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Authorization: Bearer 0x<64 hex>` | Polygon USDC transfer to the merchant, at least the route price, at least `EVM_MIN_CONFIRMATIONS` deep, younger than `PAYMENT_MAX_AGE_SEC` |
| `Authorization: Bearer <base58 signature>` | Solana USDC transfer, `confirmed` commitment |
| `X-402-Signature: <base64 payload>` | x402 payload verified and settled via the facilitator |

Each proof is accepted once (Durable Object, 7 day TTL).

# XCP-ng AIops

> **Audit availability:** Real writes require a committed `pending` audit row and stop before contacting the platform if storage is unavailable. Reads and previews may continue with a warning; new audit rows store outcome summaries rather than full responses.

> **Disclaimer**: Community-maintained open-source project. **Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Vates, the XCP-ng project, or the Xen Orchestra project.** "XCP-ng", "Xen Orchestra", and "Xen" are trademarks of their owners. MIT licensed.

AI-powered **XCP-ng** operations **via Xen Orchestra's REST API** with a
**built-in governance harness** — unified audit log, policy engine,
token/runaway budget guard, undo-token recording, and descriptive risk
tiers. Built for homelabs and small/self-hosted XCP-ng fleets that want an AI
agent to triage VM health, storage pressure, backup failures, and patch
posture — with every write audited, previewable, and (where honest)
reversible. Self-contained: no dependencies beyond `httpx` and the MCP SDK.

> **Requires a Xen Orchestra instance** (XO from sources or the Xen Orchestra
> Appliance, 5.x with `/rest/v0`). XO is the management plane this tool talks
> to — **direct per-host XAPI access is out of scope for v0.1**. Do NOT use
> for Proxmox VE — use proxmox-aiops.

## What works

- **CLI** (`xcpng-aiops ...`): `init`, `overview`, `vm list/get/stats/health-rca/start/stop/reboot/migrate`, `host list/get/missing-patches`, `pool list/get/posture`, `sr list/get/vdis/usage-rca/rescan`, `snapshot list/create/delete/revert`, `backup jobs/logs/failure-rca`, `task list`, `secret set/list/rm/migrate/rotate-password`, `doctor`, `mcp`.
- **MCP server** (`xcpng-aiops mcp` or `xcpng-aiops-mcp`): **29 tools** (19 read, 8 write, 2 undo), every one wrapped with the bundled `@governed_tool` harness.
- **Four flagship RCA analyses** (cause + action structured output): VM health, SR usage, backup-job failures, pool patch & HA posture.
- **Encrypted credentials**: the XO authentication token lives in an encrypted store `~/.xcpng-aiops/secrets.enc` (Fernet + scrypt) — **never plaintext on disk**. Unlock with a master password from `XCPNG_AIOPS_MASTER_PASSWORD` (MCP/CI) or an interactive prompt (CLI).
- **Reversibility**: `vm_start` ↔ `vm_stop` record each other as inverses; `vm_migrate` captures the REAL source host before moving and records "migrate back"; `snapshot_create` captures the created snapshot's REAL id from the XO response and records "delete THAT snapshot". Irreversible ops (`snapshot_delete`, `snapshot_revert`, `vm_reboot`) capture prior state for the audit record and honestly declare **no undo**.
- **Safety**: destructive CLI ops require double confirmation and support `--dry-run`; every write MCP tool takes a `dry_run` preview (no write call, no undo recorded).
- **Self-lockout guard (partial — read this)**: Xen Orchestra is commonly a VM on a pool it manages, and stopping that VM kills the API this tool talks to — `vm_start` can then no longer be sent, so recovery needs hypervisor console access (`xe vm-start`). Set `xo_self_vm_uuid` on the target (`xcpng-aiops init` asks) and `vm_stop` refuses exactly that uuid — on `--dry-run` as well, since a preview that green-lights a call the tool will then refuse is reporting the wrong outcome. **If you do not set it there is no protection at all**: XO's REST API exposes no self endpoint and its token carries no claims, so the tool cannot discover which VM it runs on, and it fails open rather than guess. The `dry_run` preview adds a weaker `selfVmHint` when a VM's reported IP matches the configured XO host — that is a coincidence worth checking, not a finding, and it never blocks (it sees nothing without the guest agent and fires on every VM behind a shared proxy).

## Capability matrix (29 MCP tools)

| Domain | Tools | Count | R/W |
|--------|-------|:-----:|:---:|
| **Overview** | `overview` | 1 | read |
| **VMs** | `vm_list`, `vm_get`, `vm_stats`, `vm_health_rca` | 4 | read |
| | `vm_start`, `vm_stop`, `vm_reboot`, `vm_migrate` | 4 | write (medium) |
| **Hosts** | `host_list`, `host_get` | 2 | read |
| **Pools** | `pool_list`, `pool_get`, `pool_patch_ha_posture` | 3 | read |
| **SRs / VDIs** | `sr_list`, `sr_get`, `vdi_list`, `sr_usage_rca` | 4 | read |
| | `sr_rescan` | 1 | write (medium) |
| **Snapshots** | `snapshot_list` | 1 | read |
| | `snapshot_create` (medium), `snapshot_delete` (high), `snapshot_revert` (high) | 3 | write |
| **Backups** | `backup_job_list`, `backup_log_list`, `backup_failure_rca` | 3 | read |
| **Tasks** | `task_list` | 1 | read |
| **Undo** | `undo_list`, `undo_apply` | 2 | read + replay |

### Flagship RCAs

1. **`vm_health_rca`** — VMs halted unexpectedly (auto-poweron / HA restart priority set), paused/suspended VMs, running VMs without guest tools, CPU/memory pressure from RRD stats → cause + action per finding.
2. **`sr_usage_rca`** — SRs ranked by physical fullness (near-full ≥ 85%, critical ≥ 95%), thin-provision overcommit (virtual allocation > capacity), orphaned VDIs (attached to no VM) with reclaimable bytes per SR.
3. **`backup_failure_rca`** — failed/skipped/interrupted XO backup runs classified: **vdi-chain** (coalesce not finished), **quiesce** (guest VSS), **transport** (remote unreachable), **storage-full**, unknown — with per-job counts and sample messages.
4. **`pool_patch_ha_posture`** — hosts missing patches, hosts pending reboot, **version skew** across a pool's hosts (breaks live migration / rolling updates), multi-host pools without HA.

## What this tool does, and does not, decide

It delivers XCP-ng operations — reads and writes — accurately and efficiently,
and records every one of them. It does **not** decide whether a write is allowed
to happen. That is the agent's judgement, or the permission of the Xen Orchestra
account whose token you connect it with: give that XO user a read-only ACL, or
scope its token down, and the writes fail at Xen Orchestra — the place that

readme.markdown:
# Wever Labs Agent Products

Public publication metadata for the hosted Wever Labs MCP server.

Wever Labs exposes **83 production tools** at **https://weverlabs.com/mcp** using Streamable HTTP. Tools cover bounded agent work, delegated authority, commerce, receipts and verification, handoffs, and operations. Atlas tools include `wever_atlas-asset-passport`, `wever_atlas-asset-search`, `wever_atlas-compare` and `wever_atlas-rights-gap`. Documentation: **https://weverlabs.com**.

Standard paid calls cost **0.10 USDC per call on Base mainnet via x402**. The wallet free allowance is **10 free calls per wallet per rolling 30 days**, shared across paid endpoints, not a separate allowance for each tool. Check the [live product catalog](https://weverlabs.com/api/agent-operating-products) and each tool's contract for operation-specific prices and payment requirements. Tool access does not grant payment authority or credentials; preparation and read-only operations retain their stated bounds.

The free `edge-alert` tool is included on the main endpoint. Call it with `{}` for current pregame sports winner prediction-market alerts at an estimated edge of 3 percentage points or more. Each call reads public Polymarket, Kalshi and Novig data, returns market, side, market price, estimated fair price, estimated edge and timestamp, and explicitly returns `no_alerts` when no eligible market clears the threshold. Every price names its source and uses a common $1 payout basis. Each response names checked sports, leagues, sources and coverage limits. It requires no wallet, account or x402 payment. Human page: **https://weverlabs.com/edge-alerts/**.

The free `fair-value` tool on **https://weverlabs.com/mcp** takes one prediction-market name, Kalshi or Polymarket ticker, or URL. Game names support team aliases and reversed order. It returns `needs_match` with dated outcome choices when selection is needed, or `no_match` when no open full-game winner market is returned for the teams. An exact selection returns the existing thesis model's estimated YES fair price, its original comparison and timestamps. Matched Kalshi, Polymarket and Novig quotes appear separately when available, labelled by source and observation time. Access is anonymous, with no wallet or payment. Human lookup: [weverlabs.com/fair-value/](https://weverlabs.com/fair-value/).

The separate free tier at **https://weverlabs.com/mcp-free** exposes **16 tools with no authentication, wallet, or payment required**.

The free `boutique-coupon` tool on **https://weverlabs.com/mcp** returns one shareable code for **10 percent off** at Stripe checkout across all five Rebecca Belle Boutique stores. Agents may share it freely with any human. Calling the tool needs no wallet or payment. Get the current code and redemption steps at [weverlabs.com/coupon/](https://weverlabs.com/coupon/).

`cheapest-ticket` reads public Gametime prices and compares exact NFL and NBA games with TickPick. It returns the event, lowest listed price among the working sources, check time and buy link. SeatGeek needs a server Client ID for its API; Ticketmaster Discovery needs a Consumer Key for event matches and buy links. Humans complete purchases through the returned link.

readme.markdown:
Agent Guild

  
  
  
  

**Run Claude Code, Codex CLI, Antigravity CLI, Grok Build, Docker Agent and
your own shells side by side in real terminals. Pick the same live sessions up
from your phone, VS Code or any browser. Free, on Windows, macOS and Linux.**

Agent Guild is a small manager that runs on your computer and serves one
local web page. Close the page whenever you like; the sessions keep running.

  
  

**[Try the demo](https://oddessentials.github.io/agent-guild/?view=yard&skin=guild&theme=dark)**:
walk the Yard in your browser. Simulated, free, no account and nothing installed.

## Quick start

With Node.js 22 or newer:

```sh
npm install -g @oddessentials/agent-guild
agent-guild
```

The page opens in your browser. Press **New** on a tool's card to start a
session. Sign in to each tool inside its first session, as you would in any
terminal. To look around first, [try the demo](https://oddessentials.github.io/agent-guild/?view=yard&skin=guild&theme=dark)
(simulated, nothing installed) or [watch the trailer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_vQuW0v-uMY).

**Or ask your agent.** Point it at
[the setup skill](https://github.com/oddessentials/agent-guild/blob/main/plugins/agent-guild/skills/setup-agent-guild/SKILL.md),
or run `claude plugin marketplace add oddessentials/agent-guild --sparse .claude-plugin plugins`
and `claude plugin install agent-guild@agent-guild`. It installs and checks Agent Guild,
then connects over [MCP](docs/mcp.md) to see and steer your sessions.

## Why Agent Guild

  
  

* **The real CLIs, unchanged.** Each session is the tool itself in a real
  terminal, not a chat copy of it. Whatever sign-in the tool uses works: a
  subscription, an API key, Amazon Bedrock or your own gateway.
* **Every agent in one place.** Claude Code, Codex CLI, Antigravity CLI, Grok
  Build, Docker Agent, any shell, and tmux or herdr sessions, each card
  showing its helper agents and model, with usage meters for Claude Code and
  Codex CLI.
* **The same session on every screen.** Any browser, a phone over
  [Tailscale](#remote-access-with-tailscale) with touch keys, VS Code, and
  apps for [Apple Vision Pro](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/agent-guild-remote/id6825451331),
  iPhone and iPad (beta) and
  [Android](https://github.com/oddessentials/agent-guild-android/releases/latest).
  Apple Watch and Meta Ray-Ban Display list your sessions and read a
  session's last answer aloud.
* **Native on Windows.** No WSL. Also macOS, Linux, and headless Linux
  servers over SSH.
* **Nothing in between.** No account and no relay server: the manager
  listens on `127.0.0.1`, and other devices reach it through your own
  Tailscale network or reverse proxy. See [Privacy](#privacy).

### How it compares

| | Agent Guild | tmux over SSH | Claude Code Remote Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agents | Any CLI, side by side | Any CLI | Claude Code |
| On a phone | The real terminal in a web page or app, with touch keys | An SSH app | A chat view in the Claude app |
| Sign-in | Whatever the tool uses | Whatever the tool uses | Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise; [not API keys, Bedrock or a gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control) |
| Windows without WSL | Yes | No | Yes |

**Not yet:** push notifications. Phones and the Apple apps reconnect when you
open them again; the sessions keep running on the computer in the meantime.

**License:** open source under the [GNU AGPL 3.0](LICENSE). Free for
personal and commercial use.

## Requirements

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Node.js | 22 or newer |
| Windows | 10 version 1809 or later, x64 or arm64. No WSL needed. |
| macOS | 11 or later, Intel or Apple silicon |
| Linux | x64 or arm64 with glibc 2.28 or later (for example Debian 10, Ubuntu 20.04 or RHEL 8), with a desktop or over SSH |

No compiler is needed, except on Linux without glibc, such as Alpine:
`agent-guild` prints the commands that build its terminal library there. A
missing tool shows **Install** on its card; Antigravity CLI, which is not on
npm, shows its install command instead. For Docker Agent, see
[Docker Agent](#docker-agent).

**[Agent Guild for VS Code](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=OddEssentials.agent-guild)**
opens the same page in an editor tab. Editors that install from Open VSX get it
[there](https://open-vsx.org/extension/OddEssentials/agent-guild).

## Setup

### Access token

You do not create one. The first run generates it, and `agent-guild` opens
the page with it. If a browser asks for it, open the link that
`agent-guild url` prints. Anyone with that link can use your terminals.

To replace it, stop the manager (this ends running sessions), delete
`auth-token` from the [data folder](docs/configuration.md#data-folder), and
start again.

### Docker Agent

Docker Agent is the `docker agent` plugin; Docker Desktop 4.63 and later ship
it, and its card's **Install** downloads the latest release into
`~/.docker/cli-plugins` when no copy runs. The card's installation box lists
every copy the Docker CLI finds and which one runs; the card updates and
removes only the downloaded one, and leaves Docker Desktop's to Desktop.

On Linux, Docker Engine does not include the plugin; the card's **Install**
adds it. The card needs Docker's own `docker` command: Podman's
`docker` and the Ubuntu snap of Docker do not load the plugin. If you
installed Docker Agent on its own as `docker-agent` (Homebrew or a release
download), add this to [`providers.json`](docs/configuration.md#providersjson),
then run `agent-guild restart`:

```json
{ "providers": [{ "id": "docker", "command": "docker-agent", "args": ["run"], "versionArgs": ["version"] }] }
```

### Headless Linux server

1. On the server:

   ```sh
   npm install -g @oddessentials/agent-guild
   agent-guild --no-browser
   ```

   It prints `Open: http://127.0.0.1:47821/#token=…`.

2. On your computer, open a tunnel and leave it open:

   ```sh
   ssh -L 47821:127.0.0.1:47821 you@server
   ```

readme.markdown:
# Goldsky Docs MCP server

A remote MCP server that lets AI assistants search and read the [Goldsky documentation](https://docs.goldsky.com). Goldsky provides onchain data for apps and finance teams: Feeds (REST APIs for wallet balances and transfers, token prices, Polymarket prediction-market data, and block data, payable per request with x402), prebuilt onchain datasets, Turbo pipelines, Subgraphs, Mirror, and Edge RPC across 150+ chains.

- Endpoint: `https://docs.goldsky.com/mcp`
- Transport: Streamable HTTP
- Authentication: none. No API key or account is needed.
- MCP Registry name: `com.goldsky/docs`

The server reads public documentation only. It does not access your Goldsky account, wallets, or data. To use the products the docs describe, create a Goldsky account and API key at [app.goldsky.com](https://app.goldsky.com).

This repository holds the listing README only. The server is hosted by Goldsky.

## Tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `search_goldsky` | Searches the Goldsky docs and returns matching pages with titles and links. |
| `query_docs_filesystem_goldsky` | Reads full doc pages, including code samples and API references. |
| `submit_feedback` | Reports a problem with a docs page (missing, wrong, or out of date). |

## Configure

### VS Code and GitHub Copilot

Add to `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace, or run **MCP: Add Server** from the command palette:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "goldsky-docs": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://docs.goldsky.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http goldsky-docs https://docs.goldsky.com/mcp
```

### Cursor

Add to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "goldsky-docs": {
      "url": "https://docs.goldsky.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

### Other clients

Any client that supports remote MCP servers over Streamable HTTP can connect to `https://docs.goldsky.com/mcp` with no authentication. See [docs.goldsky.com/mcp-server](https://docs.goldsky.com/mcp-server) for more clients.

## Use

Ask your assistant a Goldsky question. It calls the docs tools and answers with links to the pages it used. Examples:

- "How do I get a wallet's token balances with Goldsky Feeds?"
- "How do I get a wallet's Polymarket positions with Goldsky Feeds?"
- "How do I send a Turbo pipeline's output to a Postgres database?"
- "How do I migrate my subgraph from The Graph to Goldsky?"
- "How much does Goldsky Edge RPC cost?"

## Related

- [goldsky-agent](https://github.com/goldsky-io/goldsky-agent): the Goldsky plugin for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Gemini CLI. It adds skills for building pipelines, subgraphs, and RPC setups, and includes this docs server.
- [Goldsky docs](https://docs.goldsky.com)
- Support: [docs.goldsky.com/getting-support](https://docs.goldsky.com/getting-support)

readme.markdown: > **Part of the [Ataraxy Labs](https://ataraxy-labs.com) stack**: agent-native infrastructure for software development. See also: [weave](https://ataraxy-labs.com/weave) (entity-level git merge driver) · [inspect](https://github.com/Ataraxy-Labs/inspect) (semantic code review) · [opensessions](https://github.com/Ataraxy-Labs/opensessions) (tmux sidebar for coding agents). > > Read the manifesto: https://ataraxy-labs.com/#thesis · Essays: https://ataraxy-labs.com/blogs · LLMs: https://ataraxy-labs.com/llms.txt Semantic version control built on Git. Instead of lines changed, sem tells you what entities changed: functions, methods, classes. Why sem? · Using sem with agents · Install · Commands · Agents (MCP) · Cloud consent · Releases sem is a semantic version control tool that works on top of Git. It parses your code with tree-sitter, extracts every function, class, and method as an entity, and diffs at the entity level instead of lines. This means you see "function `blahh` was modified" instead of "lines x-y changed." It works in any Git repo with no setup. Cloud-backed queries are opt-in per repo: logging in does not upload a repo or send a query. See the [cloud consent flow](docs/cloud-consent.html) for the public/private repo states, preview screen, local audit log, and forget controls. ## Using sem with agents Four questions, four verbs. Every verb takes `--json`. | Question | Verb | |---|---| | Where is it? | `sem find`, `sem grep` | | What does my change touch? | `sem impact` | | Is it correct? | `sem check` | | What should a human review? | `sem certify` | **Where is it?** Find a function, class or method by name: ```bash sem find parse_config ``` ``` function parse_config src/config.py:1 ``` Who calls it (`--callers`), what it uses (`--refs`), or its code with its callers and callees (`--context`): ```bash sem find parse_config --callers ``` ``` function parse_config src/config.py:1 function load src/config.py:6 function test_parse_config tests/test_config.py:4 ``` Search text, like `rg`: ```bash sem grep splitlines ``` ``` src/config.py:2: pairs = [line.split("=", 1) for line in text.splitlines() if line] ``` **What does my change touch?** Everything that depends on an entity, and the tests to run: ```bash sem impact parse_config --tests ``` ``` ⚡ 1 tests affected: tests/test_config.py function test_parse_config (L4–5) ``` `sem impact --diff HEAD --tests` answers the same for your whole uncommitted change. **Is it correct?** Run the project's own compiler, type checker, linter and tests, rechecking only what the change can affect when that gives the same answer. Exit 0 means pass, 1 fail, 2 could not decide: ```bash sem check ``` ``` cmd FAIL full sh (0 rechecked, 279 ms) `python3 -m pytest -q tests` exited 1: E AssertionError: assert {'a': '1'} == {'a': '2'} ``` **What should a human review?** A review certificate for a commit range: what changed, which callers the change leaves behind, which tests reach it: ```bash sem certify main..HEAD ``` ``` # sem certificate 94f4bd74e26e..d73d4d092b43 1 files, 2 entities changed (1 added, 1 modified, 0 deleted, 0 renamed, 0 moved). - modified `parse_config` (src/config.py:1): 2 static caller(s) in 2 file(s) that this change does not modify ``` For agents that speak MCP, `sem mcp` serves the same verbs as tools (see [Use with AI agents](#use-with-ai-agents-mcp)). ## Install ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ataraxy-Labs/sem/main/install.sh | sh ``` Or via Homebrew: ```bash brew install sem-cli ``` Or via winget on Windows: ```powershell winget install AtaraxyLabs.sem ``` Or via Scoop on Windows: ```powershell scoop install sem ``` Or install the npm wrapper into `node_modules`: ```bash npm install --save-dev @ataraxy-labs/sem ``` With Bun, trust the package so its `postinstall` script can download the binary: ```bash bun add -d @ataraxy-labs/sem bun pm trust @ataraxy-labs/sem ``` Once installed, update to the latest release any time: ```bash sem config update ``` Or via cargo, from [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/sem-cli): ```bash cargo install sem-cli ``` Or build the latest `main` from source (requires Rust): ```bash cargo install --git https://github.com/Ataraxy-Labs/sem sem-cli ``` Or grab a binary from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Ataraxy-Labs/sem/releases). Or run via Docker: ```bash docker build -t sem . docker run --rm -it -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$(pwd):/repo" sem diff ``` ## Name conflict with GNU Parallel GNU Parallel ships a `sem` binary (`/usr/bin/sem`) as a symlink to `parallel`. If you have both installed, they'll collide. Run `sem --version` to check which one you're using. ([#77](https://github.com/Ataraxy-Labs/sem/issues/77)) **Quick fixes:** ```bash # Option 1: alias in your shell profile (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc) alias sem="$HOME/.cargo/bin/sem" # Option 2: make sure cargo bin comes first in PATH export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" # Option 3: if installed via Homebrew export PATH="$(brew --prefix)/bin:$PATH" ``` If you installed via npm/bun, the binary lives in `node_modules/.bin/sem` and is invoked through `npx sem` or `bunx sem`, which avoids the conflict entirely. ## Commands Works in any Git repo. No setup required. Also works outside Git for arbitrary file comparison. | Verb | The question it answers | |---|---| | `sem find` | Where is it defined? Who calls it, what does it use, what is around it? | | `sem grep` | Where does this text appear? | | `sem impact` | What does changing this entity, or this diff, touch? | | `sem check` | Is my change correct? | | `sem certify` | What should a human review in this commit range? | | `sem diff` | Which functions and classes changed? | | `sem graph` | How is the code connected? | | `sem history` | How did this entity change over time? Who last changed it? | | `sem cloud` | Account, cloud re …

# DirectIQ MCP Server

Connect Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, and any other [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) client to your **DirectIQ** account. Manage contacts, lists, and tags, see how your campaigns performed, and send transactional email in plain language.

DirectIQ is an email marketing and transactional email platform for small businesses, with fast human support and pay-as-you-go pricing. → [directiq.com](https://www.directiq.com)

- **Endpoint:** `https://mcp.directiq.com/mcp`
- **Transport:** Streamable HTTP (remote, hosted by DirectIQ, nothing to install)
- **Auth:** DirectIQ API key in the `x-api-key` header, or `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (OAuth coming soon)
- **Server card:** `https://mcp.directiq.com/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json`
- **Registry name:** `com.directiq.mcp/directiq`

> This repository holds the public documentation, registry metadata, and client configuration for the hosted DirectIQ MCP server at `mcp.directiq.com`, operated by DirectIQ. There is nothing to install or build.

## Quick start

1. **Get an API key:** log in to the [DirectIQ dashboard](https://app.directiq.com), then go to **Settings → API Keys** and copy or generate a key. No account yet? [Sign up free](https://app.directiq.com/identity/signup/start).
2. **Add the server to your client:** see the snippets below.
3. **Try a prompt:** *"Give me an overview of my DirectIQ account."*

## Client setup

### Cursor
[Add to Cursor](https://www.directiq.com/mcp/cursor/). This link opens Cursor with the config filled in. Replace `YOUR_DIRECTIQ_API_KEY` with your key.

Or add it manually to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "directiq": {
      "url": "https://mcp.directiq.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "x-api-key": "YOUR_DIRECTIQ_API_KEY" }
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code (GitHub Copilot)
Add to `.vscode/mcp.json`. VS Code prompts for the key and stores it securely:
```json
{
  "inputs": [
    { "type": "promptString", "id": "directiq_api_key", "description": "DirectIQ API key", "password": true }
  ],
  "servers": {
    "directiq": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.directiq.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "x-api-key": "${input:directiq_api_key}" }
    }
  }
}
```

### Claude Code
```bash
claude mcp add --transport http directiq https://mcp.directiq.com/mcp --header "x-api-key: YOUR_DIRECTIQ_API_KEY"
```

### Claude Desktop
Until OAuth ships, use the `mcp-remote` bridge in `claude_desktop_config.json`:
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "directiq": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.directiq.com/mcp", "--header", "x-api-key:${DIRECTIQ_API_KEY}"],
      "env": { "DIRECTIQ_API_KEY": "YOUR_DIRECTIQ_API_KEY" }
    }
  }
}
```

### Windsurf
`~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json`:
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "directiq": {
      "serverUrl": "https://mcp.directiq.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "x-api-key": "YOUR_DIRECTIQ_API_KEY" }
    }
  }
}
```

### OpenAI Codex
`~/.codex/config.toml`, after setting `export DIRECTIQ_API_KEY=...`:
```toml
[mcp_servers.directiq]
url = "https://mcp.directiq.com/mcp"
env_http_headers = { "x-api-key" = "DIRECTIQ_API_KEY" }
```

### Any other MCP client

readme.markdown:
# TempoRevenue MCP server

Turn a client conversation into a priced proposal draft without leaving Claude, Cursor, Gemini CLI or any MCP client. The draft lands in your [TempoRevenue](https://temporevenue.com) account with a link to review it, then send it for online acceptance.

## Try it without an account

```bash
npx -y @temporevenue/mcp --demo
```

```bash
npx -y @temporevenue/mcp --demo "We need a Shopify redesign, Stripe checkout and QuickBooks sync"
```

Demo mode runs locally. It exposes the same four tools as the live server and answers `create_proposal` with a rule-based estimate: deliverables, hours, a scope risk buffer and a fixed price. Nothing is created and nothing leaves your machine. There is also a [browser version](https://temporevenue.com/resources/chat-to-sow-generator/).

## Tools

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `calculate_sow_pricing` | Itemized estimate from a client message: deliverables, hours, a 15/20/25% buffer and a fixed price, plus a link that opens it in the web calculator. Runs locally in this package, read-only, no account needed. |
| `create_proposal` | Creates a draft proposal from a short description of the client's request. A price stated in the request is used as the total; otherwise it is your rate times the estimated hours, calculated in code. Returns a link to review and send. |
| `get_proposal_status` | Draft, viewed or accepted, with the dates the client opened and accepted it. |
| `list_proposals` | Your most recent proposals, optionally filtered by status. |
| `get_credit_balance` | How many proposals you can still create. |

Nothing is sent to a client until you send it yourself.

## Install

1. Create a free account at [app.temporevenue.com](https://app.temporevenue.com/en/login?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme) (3 proposals a month, no card).
2. Create an API key on the [Integrations page](https://app.temporevenue.com/en/integrations).
3. Add the server to your client.

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add temporevenue -e TEMPOREVENUE_API_KEY=your_api_key -- npx -y @temporevenue/mcp
```

### Claude Code plugin

Adds the server plus a `/quote` command and a skill that turns the conversation into a proposal brief:

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add TempoRevenue/mcp
claude plugin install temporevenue@temporevenue
```

Set `TEMPOREVENUE_API_KEY` in your environment first; without it the plugin runs in demo mode.

### VS Code

One click. VS Code asks for your API key in a password field (leave it empty to try demo mode):

- [Install in VS Code](https://insiders.vscode.dev/redirect/mcp/install?name=temporevenue&inputs=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22promptString%22%2C%22id%22%3A%22temporevenue_api_key%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22TempoRevenue+API+key+%28leave+empty+to+try+demo+mode%29%22%2C%22password%22%3Atrue%7D%5D&config=%7B%22type%22%3A%22stdio%22%2C%22command%22%3A%22npx%22%2C%22args%22%3A%5B%22-y%22%2C%22%40temporevenue%2Fmcp%22%5D%2C%22env%22%3A%7B%22TEMPOREVENUE_API_KEY%22%3A%22%24%7Binput%3Atemporevenue_api_key%7D%22%7D%7D)
- [Install in VS Code Insiders](https://insiders.vscode.dev/redirect/mcp/install?name=temporevenue&inputs=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22promptString%22%2C%22id%22%3A%22temporevenue_api_key%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22TempoRevenue+API+key+%28leave+empty+to+try+demo+mode%29%22%2C%22password%22%3Atrue%7D%5D&config=%7B%22type%22%3A%22stdio%22%2C%22command%22%3A%22npx%22%2C%22args%22%3A%5B%22-y%22%2C%22%40temporevenue%2Fmcp%22%5D%2C%22env%22%3A%7B%22TEMPOREVENUE_API_KEY%22%3A%22%24%7Binput%3Atemporevenue_api_key%7D%22%7D%7D&quality=insiders)

### Cline

Ask Cline to install the server from this repository. It follows [llms-install.md](llms-install.md).

### Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf

Add to `.cursor/mcp.json`, `claude_desktop_config.json` or your client's MCP config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "temporevenue": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@temporevenue/mcp"],
      "env": { "TEMPOREVENUE_API_KEY": "your_api_key" }
    }
  }
}
```

### Gemini CLI

```bash
gemini mcp add temporevenue -e TEMPOREVENUE_API_KEY=your_api_key npx -y @temporevenue/mcp
```

### Remote (no Node.js needed)

Clients with Streamable HTTP support can skip this package and connect to the server directly:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http temporevenue https://app.temporevenue.com/api/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer your_api_key"
```

On claude.ai and ChatGPT, add TempoRevenue as a connector and sign in with OAuth instead of an API key.

## Prompts and resources

Besides the tools, the package serves MCP prompts and resources locally (in demo and live mode, no account):

- `quote-client-message`: turns a client message into a brief and creates the draft after you confirm.
- `check-pending-proposals`: lists proposals the client opened but has not accepted, so you know who to follow up.
- `scope-repo-to-proposal`: reads the current project, lists the remaining deliverables, prices them with `calculate_sow_pricing` and drafts the proposal after you confirm.
- Resource `temporevenue://reference/estimator-defaults` (JSON): base hours per deliverable and the pricing formula.
- Resource `temporevenue://templates/sow-clauses` (Markdown): scope, change request, revision, payment and ownership clauses.

## Templates and rules

- [benchmarks/](benchmarks/): hours by deliverable as CSV and Markdown (TempoRevenue defaults, not market averages), each row linked to the calculator.
- [templates/](templates/): five free statement of work templates (web app MVP, website redesign, API integration, e-commerce build, monthly retainer).
- [.cursor/rules/client-scoping.mdc](.cursor/rules/client-scoping.mdc): a Cursor rule that turns a pasted client request into a brief and calls `create_proposal`.

## How it works


readme.markdown:
# FronyBoard

An MCP server that gives AI agents (Claude Code and friends) a first-class project
tracker.

Where Jira is an issue tracker for humans behind a web UI, FronyBoard replaces each
part with something an agent can use natively:

| Jira | FronyBoard |
|---|---|
| Database | One SQLite file in a dedicated data directory |
| Records | JSON documents (roadmap, period) + Markdown |
| API | MCP tools |
| Workflow engine | Schema + rule validation, run as a gate before every write |
| State transition | An MCP tool call (`transition_task`) |

The schema and operating rules were extracted from a real product's management system
(31 tasks shipped through it), then generalized.

## Install

Requires [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). One line registers FronyBoard in Claude Code;
`uvx` fetches the package from PyPI on first use and caches it:

```powershell
claude mcp add FronyBoard -- uvx fronyboard
```

Any MCP client that can launch a stdio command works the same way — the command is
`uvx fronyboard`. It is also listed in the
[MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) as `io.github.Cafelatte1/fronyboard`.
From a clone, point at the checkout instead (this needs `git`):

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/Cafelatte1/fronyboard
claude mcp add FronyBoard -- uv run --directory <path-to-clone>\backend fronyboard
```

This is the local (stdio) mode: the client starts the server as a child process and
talks to it over a pipe. No HTTP, no network, no credentials — `web.py` and
`fauth.py` are never called. Data is written to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Frony\FronyBoard\data`
(`~/.Frony/FronyBoard/data` where `LOCALAPPDATA` is unset); set `AIRA_DATA_DIR` to
relocate it. Logs (JSON Lines, one line per MCP tool call plus server events) go to
the sibling `logs` folder — `FRONYBOARD_LOG_DIR` overrides.

To share one FronyBoard between several machines, or to use it from the Claude and
ChatGPT apps, run it as an HTTP server instead — see
[docs/self-hosting.md](docs/self-hosting.md).

## Project setup

Connecting the MCP server gives every session the tools and the general workflow
(delivered as server instructions). What it cannot know is **which FronyBoard project
a codebase belongs to** — declare that in the codebase itself by adding this section
to its `CLAUDE.md` (create the file if the project has none):

```markdown
## FronyBoard

This project is tracked by FronyBoard (project key: DLY).
Manage tasks through the FronyBoard MCP tools, following the FronyBoard server instructions.
```

Replace `DLY` with the project's key (register one first with `create_project`).
The section is also the opt-in signal: a codebase without it is treated as not
FronyBoard-managed.

## Model

```
fronyboard.db
├── projects   one row per project (key e.g. DLY): the roadmap record —
│              yearly overview (goal / now / target / checklist) + quarterly milestones
└── periods    one row per opened period (e.g. 2026Q3): tasks ({KEY}-001, ...)
               + `result` (retrospective, written when the period closes)
```

A project is two kinds of records — the roadmap, and one record per period. Both are
JSON documents; the schema and the rules that guard it are in
`backend/src/fronyboard/validation.py`.

- **Task ids are a project-global sequence** (`DLY-042`) — they keep counting across
  periods and are never reused. They are the only link between FronyBoard and a codebase:
  use them in branch names (`feat/DLY-042/short-desc`) and record the branch on the task.
- **A task is a title** (v0.33.0, AIR-086) plus status, tags, `depends_on`, branch and two
  one-line notes of at most 300 characters each. Agents read titles and status; the 25-line
  body nobody read, and the month/week slots that only existed to schedule it, are gone.
  Time is `meta.completed_at`.
- **The two notes answer different questions at different moments** (v0.38.0, AIR-090).
  `content` is written at create time and says **why** the task exists — the pressure behind
  it, or the scope deliberately left out. The approach chosen is not part of it (AIR-092):
  agents wrote it here and again in the commit, so it lives in the commit only. `check` is required by
  `transition_task(status="done")` and says **what proves it done** — the command and its
  output, or an observable a reader can go and see. One free note asked before the work can
  only restate the plan: in a 12-session benchmark every task an agent wrote paraphrased its
  own title, because the note was fixed at create time and `update_task` was never called.
  Reopening a task drops its `check`; nothing is proven any more.
- **Reference chain**: `period → roadmap milestone` (the quarter). That is the only one,
  and the milestone is optional (v0.40.0, AIR-095): a period without one is valid, and its
  tasks are checked like any other's.
- **Statuses** — milestones: `planned | active | done`;
  tasks: `todo | in_progress | done | blocked | cancelled`.
- **`cancelled` is the soft delete** — there is no hard delete. Cancelling requires a
  reason, keeps the record (and its id) forever, and hides the task from queries by
  default (`list_tasks` takes `include_cancelled`). `blocked` = may resume,
  `cancelled` = will not happen; transitioning a cancelled task restores it.
- **Carry-over**: a task that outlives its period is not moved — recreate it in the next
  period under a new id and note the mapping in the closing retrospective.
- **`get_status` is the whole resume** — the overview, each period's open tasks, and
  `recent_done`: the ten most recently finished tasks with their `content`, their `check`
  and when they completed. What is already built is what a cold session needs most, and
  nobody makes a second call to find it (AIR-090). It is still a record of claims: the
  board says what an agent reported, the code is the evidence.
- **`depends_on`** on a task lists the earlier tasks it builds on (other projects allowed).
  It points backwards only — there is no forward index

readme.markdown:
# PetaSats MCP

Buy BSV with USDC on Base from your AI app through a local, non-custodial MCP server.

## What it does

PetaSats supports USDC on Base to BSV only. Keys are made and kept on your machine.

1. You lock USDC in the swap contract on Base.
2. The market maker locks BSV.
3. The kit verifies the lock against a merkle proof and block headers, then claims BSV and reveals the secret.
4. The market maker uses that secret to claim USDC.

Swaps are about $5 to $100. Each buyer may make three swaps and $200 per day; a shared daily total also applies. They usually take 15 to 25 minutes.

## Install and connect

Use Node.js 22 or newer. Pinning `petasats-mcp@0.2.2` is recommended.

```sh
claude mcp add petasats -- npx -y petasats-mcp
```

Claude Desktop (`claude_desktop_config.json`), Cursor (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`):

```json
{"mcpServers":{"petasats":{"command":"npx","args":["-y","petasats-mcp"]}}}
```

VS Code (`.vscode/mcp.json`):

```json
{"servers":{"petasats":{"type":"stdio","command":"npx","args":["-y","petasats-mcp"]}}}
```

Codex (CLI, IDE extension, or app):

```sh
codex mcp add petasats -- npx -y petasats-mcp
```

Any client that starts local stdio servers can use command `npx` and args `-y petasats-mcp`. First start creates keys in `~/.petasats`; `PETASATS_HOME` changes that location. Back up `keys.json`: it is the only copy.

## Fund the kit

`wallet_info` shows the Base address. Send it USDC on Base and a little ETH for gas; 0.0002 ETH covers many swaps.

## Use it

Ask: “Buy $20 of BSV and send it to 1...”

| Tool | Moves funds |
| --- | --- |
| get_quote | No |
| swap_asset_to_bsv | Yes |
| wait_for_swap | No |
| swap_status | No |
| wallet_info | No |
| withdraw_bsv | Yes |
| withdraw_base | Yes |
| fund_wallet | Yes |
| list_liquidity | No |

## Progress and reporting

The server gives the AI an operating guide. With a person watching, it reports one line per stage and a final summary with transaction IDs. For a program it returns only the result. Reporting never holds up a swap, and nothing asks for confirmation after a swap starts.

## Safety model

Funds can go only to the swap contract on Base, the kit’s own addresses, or an address you provide. The kit verifies before reveal. The market maker’s BSV can return about four hours (24 blocks) after lock; your USDC refunds after about 16 hours if the swap does not finish. Recovery resumes after restart. Run one swap at a time and keep the server running during a swap.

## Costs

`get_quote` shows the rate and comparison with market mid. You pay Base gas in ETH, the BSV claim fee, and a small extra BSV fee with `deliver_to`. See `get_quote` for protocol fees.

## Verify what you run

The npm package is built by GitHub Actions from a tagged commit and published with npm provenance. Run `npm audit signatures`; the npm page links the build to its commit and workflow run. `dist/petasats-mcp.mjs` is not minified. Source under `src/` is exported from the development repository for each release with internal development comments removed and internal names replaced by neutral ones; apart from that it is identical.

## Files, status, and recovery

The kit uses `~/.petasats`. Run `npx petasats-mcp status` for status and `npx petasats-mcp recover` after interruption.

A swap started with version 0.2.0 or 0.2.1 whose USDC lock never landed can stay at "Waiting for BSV lock" and block new swaps and withdrawals. If no other copy of the kit used the same folder while that swap ran, set `PETASATS_RESOLVE_OLD_STUCK_SWAPS=1` in the kit's environment (for example `"env":{"PETASATS_RESOLVE_OLD_STUCK_SWAPS":"1"}` in your client's server entry) and restart the kit. It then sends a zero-value transaction to its own Base address so the old lock can never land, and marks the swap failed once that transaction is final, usually within 30 minutes. Swaps started with 0.2.2 or later resolve without this setting.

## Troubleshooting

`busy`, `limit`, `rate_limited`, `unavailable`, and `declined` mean nothing was locked. If keys-file permissions are wrong, restore owner-only access. For RPC trouble, check your network connection and retry.

## Security, license, and disclaimer

See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). PetaSats uses the Open BSV License v4; third-party notices are in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`. This is experimental software: use small amounts and there is no warranty.

readme.markdown:
# chargehand

> Ask a question about your code from Claude Code or any MCP client and get back claims that each cite a file at a pinned commit, checked before you see them.

**Active**. I work on it this month.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  caller[You or a programCLI · HTTP · MCP] -- request --> intake[Intakepicks an action]
  intake -- answer or split --> workers[Agent sessionsClaude Code or OpenCode]
  intake -- ask · deny · improve --> result
  workers -- claims + citations --> resolver[Evidence resolverchecks each citation]
  resolver --> result[Typed resultclaims · open questions · cost]
  workers -. code preset, driven batches .-> branch[Tested branchor draft pull request]
  resolver --> log[(Run logtokens · cache · prompts)]
```

## Why

Coding agents answer in prose. A program that calls one needs something it can check: claims tied to files at a
commit, diffs, session messages or the caller's own inputs, plus a confidence and the exact prompts behind the answer.
I also wanted the control flow (the task graph, budgets, retries, parallelism) in code rather than in a prompt, so each
agent's context stays small, cached and disposable.

## What it does

**Answers with checked citations.** You ask a question about a repository; chargehand runs a read-only agent session
(Claude Code or OpenCode) on a clone at a pinned commit and returns typed JSON (`result/v1`): claims, open questions, a
confidence, the cost and the prompts behind it. A *citation* is a file and line range, a commit, a diff range, a
session message or an input id. Each one must exist at the pinned commit before a claim leaves its worker; the worker
gets one repair turn, and claims that still fail move to open questions.

You reach it as an MCP server (stdio or HTTP), an HTTP API or a CLI. Presets (`default`, `cheap`, `thorough`,
`strict`, `draft`, `review`) set the tools, the token and dollar budgets and whether a question may be split into 2 to 4
read-only subtasks.

Also in the box, each with its own guide:

- A `code` preset and **driven batches** that write a tested branch or a draft pull request in a sandbox
  ([Writing a branch](docs/guide/writing.md), [Driven sessions](docs/guide/driven.md)).
- `/chargehand:change`, a Claude Code plugin command: one prompt to a reviewed change on a local branch
  ([the change command](docs/guide/change.md)).
- An operator console in the browser ([Web UI](docs/guide/web-ui.md)).
- *Prompt CI*, which gates prompt and preset changes on paired evals; the run log records tokens, cache hits, cost and
  the prompt chain of every call ([Prompt CI](docs/guide/prompt-ci.md)).

Not here: an agent loop of its own, direct calls to model providers, a model gateway, a memory store (it uses yours
over MCP), a hosted service. A citation that resolves points at something that exists; checking that the cited text
supports the claim is planned, not built ([roadmap](ROADMAP.md)).

> [!WARNING]
> Before 1.0. The images have no `latest` tag: pin an exact version and read the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md) before you upgrade.

## Quick start

Ask Claude Code a question about your own repository, with no clone of chargehand.

You need:

- the .NET 10 SDK (`dotnet --version` prints `10.x`), which provides `dnx`;
- Claude Code 2.1.283 on `PATH` (`claude --version`), signed in (run `claude` once);
- a token for the workers: `claude setup-token` prints one for your subscription (an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` works too and
  bills per token).

```bash
claude mcp add chargehand -e CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=<token> -- dnx Chargehand@0.19.4 --yes -- mcp
```

Replace `0.19.4` with the newest version of the [`Chargehand` package](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Chargehand) on
nuget.org and pin it: the package changes before 1.0. In a Claude Code session in the repository you want to ask
about, say: *use chargehand to find where retries are decided, and cite the code.* The answer lists claims, each
with its file and lines. Other editors and agents (Cursor, VS Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and more) are in
[Connect your editor or agent](docs/guide/clients.md).

**From a clone,** to ask one question about chargehand itself without MCP: it needs the .NET 10 SDK, git and the same
Claude Code, signed in. With no profile, the workers use the CLI's own login and default model.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Egoushka/chargehand.git && cd chargehand
cat > request.json <<EOF
{
  "contract_version": "request/v1",
  "text": "Where does a split node decide whether to fork the first node's session? Cite the code.",
  "context": { "interactive": false, "preset": "default",
               "repository": { "path": "$PWD", "commit": "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" } }
}
EOF
dotnet run --project src/Chargehand.Cli -- run < request.json
```

It prints `result/v1` on stdout: claims with citations, open questions, a confidence and the cost. The
[quickstart guide](docs/guide/quickstart.md) explains every field, OpenCode instead of Claude Code, and what to do
when a run fails.

## How it works

1. **Intake** reads the request (`request/v1`) and writes a *Task Spec*: one action, `answer`, `split`, `ask`, `deny`
   or `improve`. The last three stop the run with questions, a reason or a better request. A preset can also stop a
   run for approval above a risk or cost estimate.
2. **Workers** are ordinary Claude Code or OpenCode sessions on a clone of the repository at the pinned commit,
   inside the directories the profile allows. chargehand never calls a model provider itself.
3. **The evidence resolver** checks every citation against git, the session and the request. The invariant: no claim
   reaches the result unless its citations resolved.
4. **The result** (`result/v1`) carries the claims, the open questions, usage and the prompt chain. The same record
   goes to the run log, which `show`, `cache` and `routes` read.

Writing runs follow the same path with a sandboxed worker: the `code` preset verifies a branch with the repository's
tests, and driven batches ad

readme.markdown:
# Crawl Readiness MCP Server

**An MCP server that checks whether a website is set up for AI the way its owner intends: can GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and 50+ other AI crawlers read it, and what does its access policy allow?** Then it generates the files (llms.txt, an AI-crawler robots.txt, JSON-LD structured data), reads your Answer Analysis, and tells you whether a page's published signals permit a use (search, answers, training, agent action), inside Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline, Windsurf and other MCP clients.

Ask Claude "can AI read my site?" and it will actually check, running a live audit against 50+ AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google's and more) and reading the access policy the site states. Then ask it to fix what is blocked, and it can generate a proper `llms.txt`, `robots.txt` or JSON-LD schema and write it straight into your project.

No more copy-paste between your editor and a browser.

---

## What it does

Nine tools your AI assistant can call:

**Audit (no signup):**
- `check_ai_readiness` — Score a site 0–100 against 50+ AI crawlers, with a prioritized fix list; extras that don't affect the score are marked as such
- `validate_schema` — Audit JSON-LD structured data on any URL (20+ types, per-type rules)
- `validate_robots` — Line-by-line robots.txt audit
- `check_content_parity` — Compare what humans see vs what AI crawlers see

**Permission (no signup):**
- `check_permission` — Ask whether a page may be used for search, answers, training or agent action. Reads robots.txt, Content-Signal, Content-Usage, an RSL licence, the TDM reservation, ai.txt and the page's own directives: any reservation wins, and a source that could not be read makes the answer unknown, never allowed. Returns a dated receipt signed with Ed25519, with a hash of every file read. Documented at [machinereadiness.com/permission](https://machinereadiness.com/permission)

**Generate (requires free API key):**
- `generate_llms_txt` — Auto-crawl a site and produce a properly formatted llms.txt
- `generate_robots_txt` — AI-crawler-aware robots.txt with preset policies
- `generate_schema` — Organization / WebSite / Article JSON-LD ready to paste

**Answer Analysis (read-only; needs an API key, and the analyses come with Monitor, Agency or the audit):**
- `get_monitor_trend` — Read your Answer Analysis: for the questions your customers ask, whether live AI search (Perplexity, Google AI Overviews) named your brand or a competitor, and the change run over run (reads existing analyses; doesn't trigger runs)

---

## Install

### Claude Desktop, one click

Download `crawl-readiness-mcp-<version>.mcpb` from the [latest release](https://github.com/Grubbomatic/crawl-readiness-mcp/releases/latest) and double-click it (or drag it into the Claude Desktop window). Claude Desktop shows what the extension does and asks for the optional API key. The bundle carries the server and its dependencies, so nothing else is installed.

### Claude Code, as a plugin

This repository is also a Claude plugin: the `.mcp.json` at its root starts the server (pinned to this version), and the `ai-readiness` skill tells Claude when to use which tool and how to read the results. Add it from the Claude directory once it is listed there. To try it before then, clone the repository and start Claude Code with it loaded:

```bash
claude --plugin-dir ./crawl-readiness-mcp
```

Claude Code asks for the optional API key when the plugin is enabled and keeps it in secure storage; the plugin's own files never contain it.

### For Claude Desktop, by hand

Open your config file:

- **macOS:** `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
- **Windows:** `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`

Add this to the `mcpServers` block:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "crawl-readiness": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "crawl-readiness-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Restart Claude Desktop. You'll see "crawl-readiness" listed in the tools panel.

### For Cursor

Open Cursor Settings → **Features** → **Model Context Protocol** → **Add new global MCP server**.

```json
{
  "crawl-readiness": {
    "command": "npx",
    "args": ["-y", "crawl-readiness-mcp"]
  }
}
```

### For Cline / Windsurf / Continue

Same shape — add `crawl-readiness` to your MCP servers list with `npx -y crawl-readiness-mcp` as the command.

---

## Unlock the generator tools

The five checks (the four audit tools and `check_permission`) work out of the box, no signup. The three generator tools need an API key — free at [crawlreadiness.com/dashboard](https://www.crawlreadiness.com/dashboard) (50 checks/month on the free tier, no credit card). `get_monitor_trend` needs a key too, on a plan that includes Answer Analyses (Monitor, Agency or the audit).

Once you have a key, add it via env in the same config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "crawl-readiness": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "crawl-readiness-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "CRAWL_READINESS_API_KEY": "cr_live_xxxxxxxxxxxx"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Restart the client. All nine tools are now callable.

---

## Example prompts

Once installed, try any of these in your AI client:

- *"Is my portfolio site AI-readable? URL: yourdomain.com"*
- *"Check if ChatGPT can see acme-inc.com"*
- *"Validate the JSON-LD on stripe.com — is anything missing?"*
- *"Compare what humans see vs what AI crawlers see on producthunt.com"*
- *"Generate an llms.txt for my site and save it to `/public/llms.txt`"*
- *"My site scored 68/100 — walk me through the fixes"*
- *"May I train on https://example.com/research? Check what the site publishes."*
- *"Before we build the RAG index, which of these pages reserve AI answers?"*

Your AI can chain tools automatically — audit, identify issues, fix them, and write files to your project without you copy-pasting anything.

# @clipform/mcp-server

MCP server for [Clipform](https://clipform.io) - build and manage video-style forms from any MCP client (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Windsurf, etc.).

## Install

There are two ways to connect: **remote** (recommended, uses your Clipform account) and **local** (anonymous, free-tier limits).

### Remote (recommended)

Use this if you have a Clipform account. Forms are created directly in your workspace and your plan tier applies (no 3-node cap on Pro).

**Claude (claude.ai):** Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector → enter `https://mcp.clipform.io`

**ChatGPT:** Settings → Connectors → Advanced → enable Developer Mode → Create connector → enter `https://mcp.clipform.io` (requires Pro/Team/Enterprise)

**Any MCP client with OAuth:** Point it at `https://mcp.clipform.io` - discovery, registration, and auth are handled automatically via OAuth 2.1 + Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591).

### Local - Claude Code / Claude Desktop / Cursor / etc.

Use this for stdio-based MCP clients. Pass your API key to authenticate with your workspace and plan tier.

**Claude Code:**

```bash
claude mcp add clipform -e CLIPFORM_API_KEY=cf_xxx -- npx -y @clipform/mcp-server
```

**Claude Desktop / Cursor / Windsurf / OpenClaw** - add to your MCP config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "clipform": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@clipform/mcp-server"],
      "env": {
        "CLIPFORM_API_KEY": "cf_xxx",
        "API_URL": "https://api.clipform.io"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Generate an API key in your Clipform dashboard under **Developers > API keys**. The local server always needs one - to try Clipform without an account, connect to `https://mcp.clipform.io` instead (see "How it works").

### Environment variables

| Variable | Required | Purpose |
|----------|----------|---------|
| `CLIPFORM_API_KEY` | For workspace auth | Bearer key - forms land in the key's workspace with its plan limits. Also unlocks the creative tools (search, TTS, video rendering). Required by the local server. |

name: dep-diff-mcp
description: Translates a lockfile diff into a human-readable upgrade plan for npm, PyPI, and GitHub Actions.

readme.markdown:
# dep-diff-mcp

MCP server that translates a lockfile diff into a human-readable upgrade plan.

Point your AI assistant (Cursor, Claude Desktop, Claude Code) at a Dependabot PR, `npm outdated` output, or any pair of package versions, and get back a ranked upgrade plan: semver class, breaking changes pulled from GitHub release notes, CVEs fixed in the range, migration guide links, and a clear recommendation per package.

## What it looks like

Ask your assistant, in plain language:

> Is it safe to bump lodash from 4.17.20 to 4.17.21?

It calls `analyze_package_change` and gets back:

```json
{
  "package": "lodash",
  "ecosystem": "npm",
  "fromVersion": "4.17.20",
  "toVersion": "4.17.21",
  "semverClass": "patch",
  "repoUrl": "https://github.com/lodash/lodash",
  "releaseCount": 0,
  "breakingChanges": [],
  "securityFixes": [
    {
      "id": "GHSA-29mw-wpgm-hmr9",
      "summary": "Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) in lodash",
      "severity": "MODERATE"
    },
    {
      "id": "GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm",
      "summary": "Command Injection in lodash",
      "severity": "HIGH"
    }
  ],
  "migrationLinks": [],
  "recommendation": "RECOMMENDED: 2 security fix(es) (incl. high/critical).",
  "recommendationLevel": "security"
}
```

A patch bump you would normally merge without looking. It closes a **HIGH-severity command injection**. That is the case this server exists for.

### GitHub Actions

Dependabot opens more `actions/*` pull requests than almost anything else, and its
scheduled version updates carry no advisory data. Ask:

> Is it safe to bump tj-actions/changed-files from 45.0.7 to 46.0.1?

```json
{
  "package": "tj-actions/changed-files",
  "ecosystem": "github-actions",
  "semverClass": "major",
  "repoUrl": "https://github.com/tj-actions/changed-files",
  "securityFixes": [
    {
      "id": "GHSA-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3",
      "summary": "tj-actions changed-files through 45.0.7 allows remote attackers to discover secrets",
      "severity": "HIGH"
    }
  ],
  "recommendation": "RECOMMENDED: 1 security fix(es) (incl. high/critical).",
  "recommendationLevel": "security"
}
```

### A whole Dependabot batch

> Here's my Dependabot PR — what's actually risky in it?

`analyze_packages_bulk` takes up to 50 changes at once and ranks them
`security` > `caution` > `review` > `likely-safe` > `safe`:

```json
{
  "totalPackages": 5,
  "bySemverClass": { "major": 1, "minor": 3, "patch": 1 },
  "securityFixesTotal": 7,
  "packagesWithBreakingChanges": 1,
  "packages": [ /* one entry per package, same shape as above */ ]
}
```

Condensing the `recommendation` field of each entry, that batch comes back in this order:

| Package | Change | Class | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lodash` | 4.17.20 → 4.17.21 | patch | **RECOMMENDED** — 2 security fixes (incl. high/critical) |
| `axios` | 1.6.0 → 1.7.9 | minor | **RECOMMENDED** — 1 security fix (incl. high/critical) |
| `express` | 4.18.2 → 5.0.0 | major | **RECOMMENDED** — 2 security fixes; 3 breaking changes, [migration guide](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html) |
| `requests` (PyPI) | 2.31.0 → 2.32.0 | minor | **RECOMMENDED** — 2 security fixes |
| `typescript` | 5.3.3 → 5.4.5 | minor | LIKELY SAFE — minor version, additive changes per semver |

Note the ordering: the `patch` bump outranks the `major` one. Semver tells you how much
changed; it does not tell you what is urgent.

Every response above is real output from the hosted instance, trimmed only where marked.

## Install

### Claude Code

One command, user scope (available in every project):

```bash
claude mcp add -s user dep-diff -- npx -y @digicatalyst/dep-diff-mcp
```

Project scope (writes `.mcp.json` at repo root, team-shared):

```bash
claude mcp add -s project dep-diff -- npx -y @digicatalyst/dep-diff-mcp
```

With an explicit token (skip this if you have the `gh` CLI authenticated — see [GitHub token](#github-token-optional-but-recommended) below):

```bash
claude mcp add -s user --env GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_xxx dep-diff -- npx -y @digicatalyst/dep-diff-mcp
```

Verify:

```bash
claude mcp list
```

Restart the Claude Code session to pick up the server.

### Cursor and Claude Desktop

Add to your MCP client config:

- Cursor: `~/.cursor/mcp.json`
- Claude Desktop: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` (macOS) or `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` (Windows)

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "dep-diff": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@digicatalyst/dep-diff-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Restart your MCP client. Ask something like "what's risky in this Dependabot PR?" and the tools are invoked automatically.

### Hosted remote (no install)

A hosted instance runs at `https://dep-diff.digicatalyst.ca/mcp` over streamable HTTP, so you can skip the npm package entirely:

```bash
claude mcp add -s user -t http dep-diff https://dep-diff.digicatalyst.ca/mcp
```

Or in a client config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "dep-diff": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://dep-diff.digicatalyst.ca/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

The hosted instance authenticates to GitHub with its own token, so release-note lookups work at full rate limits without you configuring anything. Pass `?githubToken=ghp_xxx` on the URL only if you would rather requests counted against your own GitHub quota. It is stateless and keeps no logs of your queries — see [PRIVACY.md](PRIVACY.md). Run the npm package locally instead if you would rather your token never leave your machine.

The same instance is also listed on [Smithery](https://smithery.ai/servers/digicatalyst-systems/dep-diff-mcp), which proxies to it through their gateway.

## GitHub token (optional but recommended)

The server hits the GitHub API to read release notes. Without a token you get 60 requests per hour (GitHub's anonymous limit) — enough for occasional single-package queries, not enough for bulk lockfile analysis.
