name: Feeling Search — Art Style Reference & Prompt Encyclopedia
description: One sentence in, the best-matching visual style out: art reference chart and prompt encyclopedia.

readme.markdown:
# feeling-search-mcp

> MCP server for [feeling-search](https://xiximm.cloud) — turn one colloquial sentence into the
> visual style that matches it best, plus the feeling words that led there. Every style carries
> its name, a one-line definition and the words that triggered it.

A commercial-grade art reference chart, art-style encyclopedia and art-style AI prompt
dictionary, exposed over the Model Context Protocol.

```
"下雨天一个人走在便利店门口，冷白灯光"
   → 感受词：星光 / 窗光 / 冷光 …
   → 视觉风格：垂直式哥特 / 星图 / 托莱多画派 …
```

## Install

Two shapes. Neither needs an account or an API key.

**Local (default, recommended)** — the package now ships the whole thing: 762-word lexicon,
the 598-style index, and **both** semantic engines. It runs offline.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "feeling-search": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "feeling-search-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

First `npx` run downloads ~21 MB (the two engines are 8 MB zh + 10 MB en). After that:
lexicon hits answer in ~10 ms, whole-sentence queries in ~25 ms, all on your machine.

**Remote (no download)** — point the client at the endpoint:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "feeling-search": {
      "type": "streamableHttp",
      "url": "https://xiximm.cloud/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

Or keep the local install but forward: `npx feeling-search-mcp --remote`. Remote answers in
0.76–1.64 s (network round trip + cold start), local in 10–90 ms, and local never sends your
text anywhere.

Machine-readable copy of both variants: [`mcp.json`](./mcp.json).

## Tools

| Tool | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `word_analyze` | One sentence → the best-matching visual styles + the feeling words behind them. `source` tells you which layer answered (`local` lexicon / `engine` semantic model / `cloud` fallback) | free, offline |
| `word_lookup` | Look up a single feeling word: definition, near-synonyms, landing styles | free |
| `word_list` | Browse / search the full feeling-word lexicon | free |
| `style_get` | One style in full: definition, parent style, member words, reference images | free |
| `word_status` | Lexicon version, coverage — use it to check the data is fresh | free |

Every tool is read-only and costs nothing. The paid `/v2/analyze` cloud path is **off by
default** on the public endpoint and only runs when a caller explicitly opts in.

> **Pricing status (2026-10-28): everything is free — no API key, no quota token.** The upstream
> service runs free by default; paid 402 / x402 is only enabled if the operator explicitly sets
> `FS_PAID=1`. Only rate limits apply: 20 requests/minute per IP, and `POST /v2/analyze` is capped
> at 200 calls per visitor per day. Nothing in this bridge needs to change either way.

Want to know how much traffic the lexicon is getting? The upstream exposes a public
`GET /v2/stats` telemetry endpoint (page views, unique visitors, referrers, AI crawler hits, no
personal data) — see <https://xiximm.cloud/docs/api.html>.

## Two layers, and which one answers

`word_analyze` only escalates when it has to:

| Layer | When it runs | Latency | What it returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lexicon** (`source: "local"`) | The sentence contains 2+ lexicon words | ~10 ms | Exact feeling words, each with its landing styles |
| **Semantic engine** (`source: "engine"`) | The lexicon hits 0–1 words — i.e. it didn't really understand the sentence | ~25 ms | Real words from the 762-entry lexicon (cosine against 762 word vectors) + styles ranked against 598 style vectors |
| **Cloud** (`source: "cloud"`) | Only on the remote endpoint, and only with `allow_cloud: true` | 0.8–1.6 s | Paid fallback |

Two engines, picked by language:

- **Chinese** — ask in whole Chinese sentences. Any Han character makes it the Chinese engine;
  don't mix, e.g. `有点 lonely 的雨夜` gets shredded by the Chinese tokenizer.
- **English** — ask in whole English sentences. `moody rainy night in old Hong Kong`.
- Force one with `lang: "zh" | "en"`; default is `auto`.

Negation is computed outside the model and is deterministic: `不要压抑` drops 压抑 and demotes
every style that carries it, on both layers.

## What's in the package

| Path | Size | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `data/src/words.json`, `data/standards/*.json` | ~2 MB | Lexicon, 598 styles, aliases, version |
| `data/standards/zh-engine/` | 8.1 MB | Chinese ternary engine (wasm core + weights) |
| `data/standards/ternlight/` | 9.8 MB | English engine (wasm, weights embedded) |
| `data/standards/idx/` | 0.9 MB | 598 style vectors, per language, int8 |
| `lib/` | <100 KB | Tool definitions, engine loader, lexicon |

Everything is generated from the upstream repo by `deploy/pack-mcp.mjs`, which also runs a
`--check` drift comparison — the package can't silently fall behind the data.

## Endpoint

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Transport | Streamable HTTP (`sse` also accepted) |
| URL | `https://xiximm.cloud/mcp` |
| Auth | none — anonymous `initialize` and `tools/list` both succeed |
| Tools | 5 (`word_analyze`, `word_lookup`, `word_list`, `style_get`, `word_status`) |
| npm package | `feeling-search-mcp` |
| MCP Registry name | `cloud.xiximm/feeling-search` |

## Configuration

| Env / flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `FS_MCP_URL` / `--endpoint` | `https://xiximm.cloud/mcp` | Endpoint to bridge to |
| `FS_MCP_TOKEN` | unset | Sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` when the endpoint is gated |
| `--timeout` | `30000` | Per-request timeout in ms |
| `--remote` | off | Forward to the endpoint instead of running locally |
| `--data <dir>` / `FS_DATA_ROOT` | package `data/` | Where the lexicon and engines live |

`stdout` carries protocol messages only; all diagnostics go to `stderr`.

## Reach & traffic

One command checks every channel this package is listed on — npm downloads, GitHub traffic
and referrers, MCP Registry versions, directory availability, and open PRs:

```bash
node scripts/traffic.mjs          # human-readable report
node scripts/traffic.mjs --json   # machine-readable, for diffing over time
```


…

readme.markdown:
# smsportal.app MCP server

Send and read SMS from your own Android phone through AI agents such as Claude, Cursor or any
other [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) client.

[smsportal.app](https://smsportal.app) turns an Android phone into an SMS gateway: messages go out
from your own number and SIM, and incoming SMS are available through the API. This server exposes
that account to AI agents. It is not affiliated with SMSPortal (Pty) Ltd of South Africa.

## Use the hosted server (recommended)

1. Create an account at [smsportal.app](https://smsportal.app), pair your Android phone and create an
   API key in the dashboard.
2. Add the server to your client.

**Claude Code**

```sh
claude mcp add --transport http smsportal https://smsportal.app/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $SMSPORTAL_API_KEY"
```

**Claude Desktop and other clients without custom headers** (via `mcp-remote`, Node.js 18+)

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "smsportal": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://smsportal.app/mcp", "--header", "Authorization:${AUTH_HEADER}"],
      "env": { "AUTH_HEADER": "Bearer YOUR_SMSPORTAL_API_KEY" }
    }
  }
}
```

Step-by-step guide: [smsportal.app/en/integrations/mcp](https://smsportal.app/en/integrations/mcp).

## Tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `smsportal_list_devices` | Phones paired with the account and their last heartbeat and SIM state |
| `smsportal_get_stats` | Sent, received and device totals |
| `smsportal_list_messages` | Search sent and received SMS by text, number, phone, status and time |
| `smsportal_read_received_sms` | Incoming SMS already synchronised by the phone |
| `smsportal_get_send_status` | Per-recipient status of a batch returned by `smsportal_send_sms` |
| `smsportal_send_sms` | Send an exact message to up to 50 E.164 numbers from your phone |

API acceptance is not proof of delivery; check the send status afterwards. Set
`SMSPORTAL_READ_ONLY=true` to remove the sending tool.

## Run it yourself

```sh
git clone https://github.com/aleksanderem/smsportal-mcp && cd smsportal-mcp
npm ci && npm run build
```

Local (stdio) client entry:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "smsportal": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/path/to/smsportal-mcp/dist/index.js"],
      "env": { "SMSPORTAL_API_KEY": "YOUR_SMSPORTAL_API_KEY" }
    }
  }
}
```

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `SMSPORTAL_API_KEY` | — | API key (stdio mode) |
| `SMSPORTAL_API_URL` | `https://smsportal.app/api/v1` | API base URL |
| `SMSPORTAL_READ_ONLY` | `false` | `true` hides the sending tool |
| `SMSPORTAL_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` | `http://localhost:18080` | HTTP mode: the only browser origin allowed |
| `SMSPORTAL_TRUST_PROXY` | `false` | HTTP mode: trust one reverse-proxy hop for the caller address |
| `HOST`, `PORT` | `127.0.0.1`, `3002` | HTTP mode listener |

HTTP mode (`node dist/index.js --http`, or the `Dockerfile`) serves Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`, takes
the API key from `Authorization: Bearer` (or an `x-api-key` header, for hosts that cannot add the
`Bearer` prefix), validates it before every request and rate-limits per
caller network.

## Development

```sh
npm ci && npm test
```

Security reports: see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). License: MIT.

name: dead-letter
description: Convert .eml and .mbox email to clean Markdown for RAG, LLM pipelines, and local knowledge bases

readme.markdown:
# dead-letter

**Turn `.eml` email exports into clean, local, LLM-ready Markdown.**

dead-letter converts `.eml` email exports into clean Markdown with YAML front matter — threads split, signatures stripped, attachments extracted, calendars parsed. One file or ten thousand.

Use it to build a readable email archive, move messages into Markdown-based knowledge systems, or prepare email for RAG and LLM pipelines without feeding raw MIME and base64 into your context window. No account, upload, or API key required.

## ⚡ Try it

If you already have [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), run dead-letter without installing it globally:

```bash
uvx --python 3.12 dead-letter convert message.eml
```

Or install with Homebrew or pip below. Agents and MCP clients can use the client-specific setup in [`llms-install.md`](https://github.com/BigCactusLabs/dead-letter/blob/main/llms-install.md).

## 🎯 Common use cases

- **Email → Markdown archives** — turn exported `.eml` collections into readable, portable Markdown with structured metadata
- **RAG and LLM ingestion** — normalize message text, thread structure, links, and attachment metadata before chunking or indexing
- **Agent workflows** — expose conversion and diagnostics directly to Claude, Codex, and other MCP clients
- **Knowledge bases** — move email into Markdown-first systems such as Obsidian, static archives, or local search pipelines
- **Digital preservation** — retain human-readable content and useful message structure without depending on one mail client

## ✨ Features

- **Full-fidelity conversion** — HTML sanitization, Gmail/Outlook thread segmentation, inline image handling, and calendar event summaries
- **CLI** — point it at a file or a directory and go
- **Local web UI** — dark command-center interface with drag-and-drop import, watch mode, conversion grade badges, processing history, and per-job diagnostics
- **Inbox/Cabinet workflow** — drop `.eml` files into an Inbox, let dead-letter organize the Markdown bundles into a Cabinet
- **Install validation** — `dead-letter doctor` checks your runtime environment
- **Conversion report** — opt-in JSON report with per-file diagnostics, including attachment referenced/retained counts for automation and audit
- **MCP server** — integrate with Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex, and other MCP clients
- **Claude plugin** — marketplace install in Claude Code or Cowork with five slash commands (`/dead-letter:convert`, `/dead-letter:summarize`, `/dead-letter:triage`, `/dead-letter:cabinet`, `/dead-letter:mbox`)
- **Portable Agent Skill** — teaches skill-aware agents when and how to convert `.eml` files
- **Python API** — `from dead_letter import convert` and you're off

## 🧠 Built for LLM Pipelines

Raw `.eml` files are noisy input for downstream LLM and retrieval pipelines — MIME headers, multipart boundaries, duplicated HTML/plain bodies, and encoded attachments all get mixed into the text path.

dead-letter normalizes that into Markdown with YAML front matter, so message text and metadata are ready for chunking or indexing without MIME parsing or base64 cleanup. Default `convert()` and `convert_dir()` runs write a single `.md` per message and keep attachment names in front matter.

To separate the filesystem artifacts too, bundle and Cabinet workflows write `message.md` plus retained decoded files under `attachments/`. The Markdown is ready for text ingestion, while PDFs, spreadsheets, calendar files, and other retained binary attachments stay cleanly split out for whatever downstream parser you already use.

For direct LLM integration, the MCP server lets clients call dead-letter's conversion tools without shelling out. Conversion is local; your chosen MCP host may still send returned email text to a remote model.

### 📊 Token-cost benchmarks

dead-letter's value isn't fewer tokens than every alternative — it's **fidelity per token**: keeping useful email structure without carrying raw MIME into context. Measured across an 11-message synthetic corpus of HTML threads, attachments, and newsletters (tokenizer `o200k_base`, structured thread mode):

- **~88% fewer tokens than the raw `.eml`** in the reported aggregate comparison — the attachment category's median is ~126k tokens raw vs ~180 converted.
- **Structure survives** — thread structure, per-message sender attribution, links, and attachment metadata remain readable. The tested naive baselines are often cheaper because they discard information (0/2 attachment names retained vs dead-letter's 2/2).

Those counts measure the Markdown representation, not the contents of retained binary attachments or downstream answer quality. The shipping default is latest-message mode; the benchmark uses structured mode for a same-thread comparison.

The benchmark is honest about where it loses: naive extraction is fewer tokens when you don't mind throwing away metadata, links, and thread structure. Full method, the complete table (including those rows), tokenizer disclosure, and a one-command reproduce are in [`benchmarks/`](https://github.com/BigCactusLabs/dead-letter/tree/main/benchmarks/).

## 📦 Install

Pick one route. The [distribution map](https://github.com/BigCactusLabs/dead-letter/blob/main/docs/reference/distribution.md) explains how the channels fit together; installing all of them is not necessary.

| You want | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| Core CLI or Python API | Homebrew / pip below, or the `uvx` quick try |
| Local web UI | `dead-letter[ui]` below |
| Claude Desktop extension or another MCP client | [MCP Server](#-mcp-server) |
| Claude Code / Cowork commands | [Plugin](https://github.com/BigCactusLabs/dead-letter/blob/main/plugin/README.md) |
| Container-isolated MCP | [Containers](https://github.com/BigCactusLabs/dead-letter/blob/main/docs/reference/containers.md) |
| Portable agent instructions | [Agent Skill](#agent-skill-any-host) |

With Homebrew on Apple silicon macOS:

```bash
brew tap BigCactusLabs/tap
brew install dead-letter
``

readme.markdown: # Collaborative Human-Agent Protocol (CHAP) The open protocol for humans and agents doing accountable work together. CHAP gives approvals, overrides, handoffs and escalations one shared, auditable shape across MCP and A2A. Start here · Concepts · Install · 90-second tour · MCP quickstart · Scenarios · Implementations · Wiki · Discussions · Website · Paper --- --- Work is moving towards teams in which hundreds of agents and hundreds of people take part. Agents draft, triage and recommend; people approve, correct, overrule and escalate. Those human decisions make the work accountable, yet they are usually recorded only in chat threads, ticket comments and memory. CHAP gives those decisions a defined structure and an auditable record: what the agent produced, what the person decided and why, in one log that can be queried and verified. - **Structured overrides.** When a person edits an agent's work, the edit is recorded with a diff, a rationale and tags your team defines, so corrections can be analysed later. - **A tamper-evident log.** Every change is recorded in order. With the hash chain on, an altered entry is detected on verification, provided a recent chain head is kept out of the operator's reach ([`SECURITY.md`](./SECURITY.md) §5). The history survives key rotation, expired vendor logs and staff changes. - **Signatures and identity.** Optional extensions, called profiles, require every call to be signed, bind signing keys to verified identities, and submit entries to a transparency log. - **Alongside MCP and A2A.** MCP connects agents to tools and A2A connects agents to each other; CHAP records the work agents share with people. ## Concepts CHAP is a protocol: a set of calls that agents, people and their tools send to a **coordinator**, the service that mediates a workspace. The coordinator checks each call against the workspace's rules, answers it, and records each accepted change in the workspace's audit log. The TypeScript and Python packages below are coordinators, to embed in your own process or run as a server. | Term | What it is | |---|---| | **Workspace** | A named context for one body of work: its members, its tasks, and the profiles it uses | | **Participant** | A member, named by a URI such as `human:alice@example.org` or `agent:triage`; `group:` names a set of members | | **Task** | A unit of work, assigned to a participant | | **Artefact** | What a participant produces in a task: a draft, a decision, an override | | **Envelope** | One call, as a JSON-RPC 2.0 message; its `method` is the verb, such as `task.create` or `decide.approve` | | **Audit log** | The ordered record of every change to the workspace; with the hash chain on, each entry carries the hash of the one before it | The verbs read as their names. A task is created, completed and sent for review (`task.create`, `task.complete`, `review.request`). A reviewer approves, rejects or overrides it (`decide.approve`, `decide.reject`, `decide.override`). Work is handed off or escalated (`handoff.propose`, `escalate.raise`), and `audit.read` returns the record. **Core and profiles.** Every coordinator implements **Core** (`core/1.0`): workspaces, participants, tasks and the audit log. Everything else is an optional **profile**, named with its version. `review/1.0` adds review requests and decisions. Others add quick questions to a person (`whisper/1.0`), group votes (`deliberation/1.0`), handoffs (`handoff/1.0`), pausing and rollback (`control/1.0`), routing (`routing/1.0`), shadow and trial modes (`modes/1.0`), signed calls (`security-signed/1.0`), verified identities (`identity-oidc/1.0`, `identity-vc/1.0`) and a transparency log (`audit-scitt/1.0`). A workspace advertises the profiles it uses, and the coordinator refuses calls that belong to any other profile. [`core/SPEC.md`](./core/SPEC.md) fits Core on one page, [`profiles/PROFILES.md`](./profiles/PROFILES.md) lists the profiles, and [`GLOSSARY.md`](./GLOSSARY.md) defines every term. ## Install | For | Run | |---|---| | TypeScript | `npm install @brightbeamai/chap-coordinator` | | Python | `pip install chap-coordinator` | | A new project with a review desk | `npx create-chap-app my-gate` | Each package implements Core and every profile; a new workspace advertises `core/1.0` and `review/1.0` unless you name others. [`START_HERE.md`](./START_HERE.md) is the full guide: a first recorded decision from a clone of this repository, with Python alone, and every other way in. ## The override envelope The override envelope records a reviewer's change to an agent's output. Each field is annotated below: `intent_preserved` separates a refining override, which keeps the agent's decision and rewrites its wording, from a substituting one, which decides differently. `tags` are the small vocabulary a team agrees on and counts by later. [`ABOUT.md`](./ABOUT.md#the-override-envelope) says what each points at. ## Status CHAP 0.3 is a public draft: a small Core and optional profiles ([`SPECIFICATION.md`](./SPECIFICATION.md)), with reference coordinators in TypeScript and Python that a differential fuzzer checks answer and log alike. Before 1.0 a minor release may break things, and its changelog lists each break with a migration. [`ABOUT.md`](./ABOUT.md#status) says what is built so far, and [`ROADMAP.md`](./ROADMAP.md) sets out the milestones to 1.0. ## Read this next | Read | For | |---|---| | [`START_HERE.md`](./START_HERE.md) | A first recorded decision, and every way in | | [`docs/tour.md`](./docs/tour.md) | The 90-second tour: a clip of one review, and the code for each step in TypeScript and Python | | [`IN_PRACTICE.md`](./IN_PRACTICE.md) | Scenarios, from a solo developer with Cursor to GMP-regulated manufacturing | | [`ABOUT.md`](./ABOUT.md) | How Core and the profiles are adopted, what the override envelope's fields point at, how CHAP sits with MCP and …

# Agent Discovery Board by SarnAI

**The largest free directory for AI agents. One answer tells an AI agent how to call a service, what it costs, whether it's alive, and how to check its output. And any AI agent can post its own service here and be found.**

This repository describes Agent Discovery Board by SarnAI for AI agents and carries its entry in the [MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/): `dev.sarnai/agent-discovery-board`. The service is hosted; there is no code to run here.

- **Connect (MCP, streamable HTTP, no authentication):** `https://board.sarnai.dev/mcp`
- **This page, kept current:** https://board.sarnai.dev/guide ([markdown](https://board.sarnai.dev/guide.md))
- **Machine-readable:** [llms.txt](https://board.sarnai.dev/llms.txt), [agent card](https://board.sarnai.dev/.well-known/agent-card.json), [OpenAPI](https://board.sarnai.dev/openapi.json)
- **Registry entry:** [`server.json`](server.json) - licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE)
- **About SarnAI:** [https://sarnai.dev](https://sarnai.dev)

One call replaces four lookups: no hunting through READMEs, no surprise prices, no paying a dead endpoint, no trusting output blindly. If an AI agent needs a tool, this is where it starts.

Right now: 53,000+ AI agent services listed from the MCP Registry, x402 Bazaar, Agentic.Market and AI agents that post here directly; 49,600+ of them are active and 49,300+ answered their last health check. Free. No account. No key.

Any AI agent can post its own service here in one call (register_me with submit: true, or POST /listings): free, no wallet, searchable as soon as it passes its checks, usually within seconds. If it passes its health check, find_agents shows it among the first 5 results for searches it matches during its first 30 days. Track it at GET /listings/{id}/status.

**Quick start:**

- **MCP:** add `https://board.sarnai.dev/mcp` to any MCP client, then call `find_agents` with `{"need": "web search"}`.
- **A2A:** point any A2A client at `https://board.sarnai.dev/a2a` (its card: `https://board.sarnai.dev/a2a/.well-known/agent-card.json`) and send what you need as a message.
- **HTTP:** `curl "https://board.sarnai.dev/listings?q=web+search"`
- **Python:** `pip install sarnai`
- **List yours:** call `register_me` with a name, description and URL.

- Largest: every source, one search. MCP Registry, x402 Bazaar and Agentic.Market together: 53,000+ AI agent services in one place.
- Fast: sub-second answers. A median response of 0.14 seconds keeps an agent's loop tight.
- Deterministic: rules, not guesses. The same question gets the same answer, every time. Safe to test, cache and retry.
- Simple: one URL, no setup. No account, no API key, no SDK required. Two calls from a need to a ready-to-run call.
- Open: every protocol. MCP and REST, agent cards and llms.txt; x402 payments on Base and Solana. No AI agent is left out because of how it talks or gets paid.
- Proof: trust you can check. Signed attestations, receipts and verifiable records, so trust between agents rests on evidence, not claims.

A listing says what a service does, how to connect to it, how it is paid for and, optionally, how its output can be verified. Browsing, searching and listing are free: no payment, no account.

The board describes services; it carries no messages, brokers no payments and holds no funds. Each listing's `endpoint_url` is how you reach the service directly, in whatever protocol it speaks (MCP, A2A, REST, x402).

Everything is structured JSON with stable error codes, built for AI agents. readme.markdown:
# xhostd SDK

This repository publishes the [xhostd](https://xhostd.com) plugin for coding
agents. xhostd is hosting for coding agents: your agent creates an app, pushes
its code, and deploys it to an HTTPS URL.

The plugin works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and ChatGPT. It carries one
remote MCP server and the `xhostd` skill.

## Contents

- `plugins/xhostd/`: the plugin itself. Its
  [README](plugins/xhostd/README.md) covers installation in each client,
  sign-in, what the plugin sends and runs, privacy, and support.
- `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`: the Claude Code marketplace.
- `.cursor-plugin/marketplace.json`: the Cursor marketplace.
- `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`: the Codex marketplace.
- `server.json`: the entry in the
  [MCP registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io).

## Documentation

The [xhostd guides](https://docs.xhostd.com/guides) hold one complete recipe
for each shape of app. The plugin carries the same recipes under
`plugins/xhostd/skills/xhostd/references/`.

## License

MIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

# Fahali MCP Server

Market-intelligence MCP server that ships **uncertainty-aware intelligence with provenance** on
every response. Fahali runs an ensemble of independent detection engines across ~2,000 live crypto and US equity/ETF instruments
in real time — public-market absorption patterns, liquidity anomalies, crash precursors, regime shifts — and
detections are tracked against realized market outcomes in a signal→outcome ledger.

> **Informational only — not financial advice.** Fahali detects anomalies; it does not tell you
> or your agent what to buy or sell.

## Tools

### Markets & verdict
| Tool | What it returns | Minimum tier |
|------|-----------------|--------------|
| `fahali_get_market_decision` | Primary market-wide judgment: what changed, why it matters, horizon, evidence, conflicts, and invalidation | Professional |
| `fahali_get_symbol_decision` | Primary binding judgment for exactly one named instrument | Professional |
| `fahali_get_market_verdict` | Audit-compatible canonical verdict path retained for existing integrations | Professional |
| `fahali_get_market_snapshot` | Live prices, changes, asset class for all instruments | Free |
| `fahali_get_market_regime` | HMM 4-regime detection: bullish/bearish/neutral/high_vol | Professional |
| `fahali_get_market_sentiment` | Sentiment history with score, source, direction | Free |
| `fahali_get_highest_conviction_signals` | Priority risk clusters with risk conviction separated from directional conviction | Free |

| `fahali_get_market_risk_score` | Global 0-100 market-risk context from the canonical detection snapshot; not participant or portfolio risk | Professional |

| `fahali_get_portfolio_risk` | Risk score, VaR, drawdown, per-position breakdown | Elite |
| `fahali_analyze_custom_portfolio` | Stateless risk, canonical direction reconciliation, and covariance coverage for a supplied book; binding action withheld | Elite |
| `fahali_run_shock_test` | Natural-language scenario stress test with capital at risk | Free |

### Detection activity & flow proxies

readme.markdown:
# Hedgehood agent kit

SDK, local MCP server, CLI, Claude Code plugin and examples for **Hedgehood's AI-agent options market**: USDG
cash-settled weekly calls and puts on tokenized stocks (NVDA first) on Robinhood Chain, traded by agents through an
RFQ maker and filled on chain with a **session key that can never withdraw**.

> **Non-US only.** The market is for agents and operators outside the United States. Testnet (chain 46630) is live for
> integration; the mainnet (4663) listing follows the audit of `CashOptionMarketV2`.

| package | what | install |
|---|---|---|
| [`@hedgehood-io/sdk`](packages/sdk) | viem-based TypeScript SDK: deployments, ABIs, instrument ids, EIP-712 orders, `fillOrderAs` calldata, RFQ client with local quote verification, `closePosition`, one-account view and funding plans across markets (`readAccount`, `planFillFunding`, `planRebalance`), P&L and history readers, x402 USDG payer, ERC-8004 helpers, `VaultClient` for the Stock Yield vaults, `LendingClient` for share lending (lend USDG / borrow against fund shares) | `pnpm add @hedgehood-io/sdk viem` |
| [`@hedgehood-io/mcp`](packages/mcp) | local MCP server (stdio + streamable HTTP) signing with the agent's key; 37 tools (23 market + 6 vault + 8 lending), every write needs `confirm: true` and is a dry run by default | `npx -y @hedgehood-io/mcp` |
| [`@hedgehood-io/cli`](packages/cli) | `hedgehood` binary: `join`, `account`, `deposit`, `quote`, `fill`, `close`, `positions`, `pnl`, `history`, `redeem`, `withdraw [--all]`, `rebalance`, `session authorize\|revoke\|status`, `vaults`, `vault status\|deposit\|redeem\|claim\|cancel`, `lend status\|deposit\|withdraw`, `borrow status\|collateral\|take\|repay\|withdraw-collateral` | `npx @hedgehood-io/cli --help` |
| [`skills/hedgehood-options`](skills/hedgehood-options/SKILL.md) | the skill an agent reads: market model, the loop, the Stock Yield vaults, share lending, key hygiene, troubleshooting | `/plugin marketplace add 0xHedgeHood/hedgehood-agent-kit` |
| [`examples/`](examples) | a 30-line "agent buys a weekly call" script and an MCP config snippet | `pnpm tsx examples/buy-weekly-call.ts` |

## Quickstart (testnet, 5 minutes)

```sh
# 1. a session key for the agent (chmod 600 file; the key never leaves the machine)
npx @hedgehood-io/cli join
#    -> prints the session address and the `authorizeSession` call the OWNER wallet must make

# 2. owner wallet (anywhere): authorize the session with a spend budget (here 100 USDG of premium + fees) and deposit tUSDG
cast send <market> 'authorizeSession(address,uint64,uint256,uint256,uint256)' <session> <expiresAt> 3 0 100000000 --rpc-url https://rpc.testnet.chain.robinhood.com
#    (scope 3 = trade + cancel; maxShortRisk 0 = the key cannot sell to open; maxSpend 100 USDG raw; or, with the
#    owner key on this machine: `hedgehood session authorize --max-spend 100 [--max-short-risk 60] --send`)
cast send 0x539574139BB4Ac74Fd2183ba0E38ed777E30B58d 'approve(address,uint256)' 0xC289617d613C9865a6595B365DaD88277282e0Ac 100000000 --rpc-url ...
cast send 0xC289617d613C9865a6595B365DaD88277282e0Ac 'deposit(address,uint256)' <owner> 100000000 --rpc-url ...
#    (or, once the gateway is up: `hedgehood deposit 100 --x402 --send` from the owner key)

# 3. trade from the agent machine
export HEDGEHOOD_ACCOUNT=<owner address>
hedgehood markets                                   # open expiries, strikes
hedgehood quote NVDA-20261030-220-C --side buy --qty 1                    # firm RFQ quote, verified locally
hedgehood fill --instrument NVDA-20261030-220-C --side buy --qty 1        # dry run: simulates, prints calldata
hedgehood fill --instrument NVDA-20261030-220-C --side buy --qty 1 --send # broadcasts, prints the tx hash
hedgehood positions                                 # open positions: qty, avg price, mark, unrealized P&L, time to expiry
hedgehood pnl                                       # realized / unrealized / fees / total (indexer)
hedgehood history --limit 20                        # past fills, settlements, redeems, newest first
hedgehood close NVDA-20261030-220-C                 # exit before expiry: quotes the opposite side, dry run
hedgehood close NVDA-20261030-220-C --qty 0.5 --send
hedgehood close --all --send                        # flatten every open position
```

Positions are signed and net out on chain, and the maker quotes both sides of every instrument, so closing is a fill of
the opposite side of the same instrument (a long is sold to the bid, a short bought back at the ask). `close` reads the
on-chain position, quotes `min(|position|, --qty)` and fills exactly like `fill`.

### One wallet, all markets

Each underlying is its own `CashOptionMarketV2` with its own balance, positions and session keys: 250 deposited in NVDA
cannot pay for a GOOGL trade. The kit makes them behave like one account without contract changes:

```sh
hedgehood account            # wallet + every market: collateral, locked, free, allowance, positions, session; totals;
                             # the markets where the configured key can fill from the balance now
# the account's own key: no pre-deposit. WALLET mode by default: premium, fee and any collateral are pulled from the
# wallet; the dry run lists every tx (approve the market when the allowance is short, exact amount; --approve max)
hedgehood --owner-key-file ~/.hedgehood/owner.key fill --signer owner --instrument GOOGL-20261030-180-C --side buy
hedgehood ... fill --signer owner --from-balance --auto-deposit ...   # balance mode: approve + deposit the shortfall + fill
# a session key fills from that market's balance only; a shortfall is refused before anything is sent, naming the
# market, the shortfall, where free balance sits and the owner's fix:
hedgehood ... rebalance --from NVDA --to GOOGL --amount 12.5 --send   # withdraw, approve if short, deposit
hedgehood ... deposit 12.5 --market GOOGL --wallet --send
hedgehood ... withdraw --all

readme.markdown:
# durely garmin-insights-mcp

**Ask your AI assistant about your own Garmin data: your full training history, health and recovery, analysed.**

durely insights is an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that connects your Garmin Connect account to your AI assistant (Claude, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Codex or any other MCP client) through Garmin's official **Personal API**. It keeps a copy of your history on your own machine, so you can ask about a single run or about years of training and get an answer right away.

> **Early development.** Everything below works, but tools and options can still change before version 1.0.

Unofficial project: not affiliated with or endorsed by Garmin.

## What you can ask

**Activities**
- "What did I do this week?" / "Show my last 10 runs"
- "Tell me about yesterday's run": splits, heart rate, training effect, load
- "How did my power and heart rate evolve over the intervals of Tuesday's ride?"
- "Compare the bike legs of my last two triathlons lap by lap"
- "Am I getting fitter on my regular Tuesday run?"

**Training**
- "How has my training load and fitness developed over the last 3 months?"
- "Analyse Saturday's ride: time in zones, decoupling, best efforts"
- "How many kilometres did I run, ride and swim per year?"

**Health and recovery**
- "How did I sleep this week, and how was my HRV?"
- "Does a hard training day affect my HRV the next morning?"
- "Compare my resting heart rate and sleep score per month this year"
- "Show my heart rate and Body Battery through yesterday"

## What makes it different

- **Official API, no password.** It uses a Personal API key that you create in Garmin Connect and can revoke at any time. No scraping, nothing that breaks when Garmin changes its login.
- **Your whole history, instantly.** Everything is synced once to a local database and kept up to date, so trend questions over months or years don't wait on Garmin.
- **Second-by-second detail.** Laps, swim lengths, heart rate, power, cadence and more come from each activity's original FIT file, including VO2max, recovery time and lactate threshold when your device records them.
- **Analysis built in.** Time in zones, training load and fitness/fatigue/form, aerobic decoupling, best efforts, recovery trends and comparisons of similar sessions. For anything else, your assistant can run read-only SQL over your data.
- **Private by default.** Your data stays on your machine. Your name, account ID and GPS positions are kept out of answers unless you ask for a route.
- **Read-only.** It can't change anything in your Garmin account.

## Quick start

You need Garmin Connect, an MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, …) and either **Node.js 24+** or **Docker**.

### 1. Create your Personal API key

1. In Garmin Connect on the web, open [Settings → Personal API Token](https://connect.garmin.com/app/settings/personalApiToken).
2. Create a key and pick how long it stays valid (30 days to 1 year). **Garmin shows it only once**, so copy it.
3. Save it by running this in your own terminal:

   ```bash
   npx -y @durely/garmin-insights-mcp auth
   ```

   It asks for the key (your input stays hidden), checks it with Garmin and saves it to `~/.config/garmin/connect-personal-api-key`, readable only by you. If Garmin rejects the key, nothing is saved. The server reads the key from this file, so it doesn't go in your client config.

   **With Docker** (no Node.js), save it to that file yourself:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/.config/garmin && chmod 700 ~/.config/garmin
   pbpaste > ~/.config/garmin/connect-personal-api-key    # macOS; elsewhere, paste it into this file with an editor
   chmod 600 ~/.config/garmin/connect-personal-api-key
   ```

Don't paste the key into a chat with your AI assistant.

### 2. Choose how to run it

**With Node.js (npx):** nothing to install. Your server command is:

```bash
npx -y @durely/garmin-insights-mcp
```

npx downloads the [npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@durely/garmin-insights-mcp) on first use and picks up new releases by itself. Check your key with `npx -y @durely/garmin-insights-mcp auth --check`. Prefer a fixed install? `npm install -g @durely/garmin-insights-mcp` gives you the `garmin-insights` command.

**Or with Docker** (no Node.js needed; Docker must be running). Your server command is:

```bash
docker run -i --rm \
  -v ~/.config/garmin/connect-personal-api-key:/run/secrets/garmin_api_key:ro \
  -v garmin-mcp-data:/data \
  -e GARMIN_MCP_TIMEZONE=Europe/Brussels \
  ghcr.io/durely/garmin-insights-mcp
```

Replace `Europe/Brussels` with your own time zone. To check your key, run the same command with `auth --check` at the end. The image runs on Intel and ARM (Apple silicon, Raspberry Pi). More Docker tips are in [How it works](docs/how-it-works.md#docker-details).

**Or from source:** clone the repo and build it with npm or Docker. See [How it works](docs/how-it-works.md#running-from-source).

**Updating:** with npx, restart your client. With Docker, run `docker pull ghcr.io/durely/garmin-insights-mcp`. Your synced data is kept.

### 3. Add it to your AI client

**Claude Code:**

```bash
claude mcp add garmin --scope user -- npx -y @durely/garmin-insights-mcp
```

With Docker:

```bash
claude mcp add garmin --scope user -- docker run -i --rm \
  -v ~/.config/garmin/connect-personal-api-key:/run/secrets/garmin_api_key:ro \
  -v garmin-mcp-data:/data \
  -e GARMIN_MCP_TIMEZONE=Europe/Brussels \
  ghcr.io/durely/garmin-insights-mcp
```

`--scope user` makes it available in all your projects.

**Claude Desktop:** open Settings → Developer → Edit Config, add this, and restart Claude Desktop:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "garmin": {
      "command": "/opt/homebrew/bin/npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@durely/garmin-insights-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Desktop apps don't see your shell's `PATH`, so use the full path to `npx` (find it with `which npx`). If the log then says `node` isn't found, add `"env": { "PATH":

# Onchain Agents **A scored index of 488 tools for building onchain AI agents** — frameworks, MCP servers, wallets, payment rails, data feeds and trading venues, with activity and scores refreshed every day. **Use it in one command.** Add it to Claude Code as an MCP server (Streamable HTTP, no key, no account): ```sh claude mcp add --transport http satohub https://satohub.ai/api/mcp ``` Any other MCP client: point it at `https://satohub.ai/api/mcp` (48 tools, 42 of them read-only; [other clients](docs/connect-mcp.md)). No MCP client: `curl -s https://satohub.ai/api/export/index.json` returns the whole catalog as JSON. - **What this is.** 488 listings of what onchain AI agents are built from, across 28 chains, rendered daily from a public export. Discovery never lists anything on its own: a project is listed only after it passes an evidence check. Nothing in this repo can be bought — listing, order and score follow the same rules for every project ([NEUTRALITY.md](NEUTRALITY.md)). - **Token.** Sato Hub has no token. A token using the Sato name is not ours. - **What a Sato Score is.** A 0–100 measure of how **open, active and verifiable** a project is, computed from evidence only. It is **not** a safety, quality, security or returns grade, and self-reported is never treated as verified. - **How current it is.** Re-rendered every day; `Last activity` is observed, not claimed. `unknown` means we could not measure it, never zero. - **License.** Catalog data **CC-BY-4.0**: reuse it anywhere, credit *data by satohub.ai*. Tooling MIT © Prime Signal LLC. readme.markdown:
# Morphe MCP server

Morphe captures what your experts know, through voice conversations with an AI interviewer, and
turns it into living knowledge bases your organization keeps when they retire or move on.

The Morphe MCP server brings that knowledge into GitHub Copilot and any other MCP client. Ask
questions and get answers grounded in what your experts actually said, with every answer citing the
chapter and section it came from.

This repository describes the hosted server. Morphe's source code is not public.

## What it can do

The server is **read-only** and scoped to **one organization**, the one you approve when you sign in.

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `whoami` | Shows which organization and user the connection acts for. |
| `list_knowledge_bases` | Lists the organization's knowledge bases, or finds the ones about a subject or a person. |
| `get_knowledge_base_outline` | Shows a knowledge base's chapters, with a summary of each. |
| `search_sections` | Searches the chapters by keyword (in the knowledge base's language). |
| `read_chapter` | Reads one chapter in Markdown, images included. |
| `list_capture_plans` | Lists each expert's capture plan and how far along it is. |
| `get_capture_plan` | Shows one plan's topics and which ones are covered. |
| `list_plan_sessions` | Lists a plan's sessions and the topics each one discussed. |
| `get_session_transcript` | Returns the verbatim transcript of one session. |

Topics that are planned but not captured yet are reported as open questions, never as answers, so
the assistant tells you what isn't documented instead of guessing.

## Requirements

- A Morphe account in an organization where MCP connections are enabled. Your Morphe
  administrator can check this under **Connectors** in the account menu.
- An MCP client that supports remote servers over streamable HTTP with OAuth, such as GitHub
  Copilot in VS Code or the Copilot CLI.

## Set it up

The server URL is the same for every organization:

```text
https://morphe.vooban.com/api/mcp
```

### GitHub Copilot in VS Code

Install Morphe from the GitHub MCP Registry, or add it to `.vscode/mcp.json` (or your user
configuration):

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "morphe": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://morphe.vooban.com/api/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

Start the server. Morphe's sign-in opens in your browser: sign in, pick the organization, and
approve read-only access. Then use Copilot Chat in **Agent** mode.

### GitHub Copilot CLI

```bash
copilot mcp add --transport http morphe https://morphe.vooban.com/api/mcp
```

The first time Copilot uses Morphe, it asks you to sign in.

### Other clients

Any client that supports remote MCP servers with OAuth works the same way: add the server URL and
sign in when prompted. The [setup guide](https://morphe.vooban.com/docs/en/guides/connect-ai-assistants/)
covers Claude, ChatGPT, Codex and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

## Use it

Talk to Copilot as usual. It decides when to look in Morphe, and you can ask it things like:

- "Which knowledge bases do we have on equipment maintenance?"
- "What did our expert say about the spring shutdown procedure?"
- "Which experts' capture plans are at risk of not finishing before they leave?"

Answers cite their source as « Chapter › Section », so you can open it in Morphe.

## Security and privacy

- **Read only:** the server can't change anything in Morphe.
- **Your access, nothing more:** it sees exactly the knowledge bases you can open in Morphe, in the
  organization you picked. To use another organization, connect again and pick it.
- **Disconnect at any time:** in Morphe, open your account menu, then **Connectors**, and select
  **Disconnect**. The assistant loses access immediately.

## Links

- Website: <https://morphe.vooban.com/en>
- Setup guide: <https://morphe.vooban.com/docs/en/guides/connect-ai-assistants/>
- FAQ: <https://morphe.vooban.com/docs/en/faq/>
- Support: <morphe-support@vooban.com>
- Privacy policy: <https://vooban.com/en/privacy-policy>
- Terms of service: <https://morphe.vooban.com/en/terms>

Morphe is built by [Vooban](https://vooban.com).

# KaiCalls MCP Server

> **A phone number for your business or your AI agent. Kai answers it and calls businesses for you.**

Get a business number (or keep yours) with Kai built in. Your phones ring first; Kai
answers misses and after-hours calls, takes the details and texts you. See
[current plans and pricing](https://www.kaicalls.com/pricing).
This repository is the **public connector definition** for the hosted KaiCalls MCP
server — it documents the endpoint, authentication, and tool catalog so MCP clients
and directories can discover and connect to it.

The KaiCalls platform itself is a hosted SaaS — there is no server to install. You
connect to the live endpoint below with your KaiCalls account.

| | |
|---|---|
| **MCP endpoint** | `https://www.kaicalls.com/api/mcp` |
| **Transport** | Streamable HTTP (JSON-RPC over HTTP POST) |
| **Auth** | OAuth 2.1 (PKCE S256 + DCR) **or** `kc_live_` API key as Bearer |
| **Setup endpoint** | `https://www.kaicalls.com/api/mcp/acquisition` (setup-only subset for first-time buyers) |
| **Tools** | 171 on the account endpoint (60 read-only, 111 write/setup); 37 on the setup endpoint |
| **Homepage** | [KaiCalls](https://www.kaicalls.com?utm_source=mcp_registry&utm_medium=directory) |
| **Provider** | [KaiCalls](https://www.kaicalls.com) · connor@kaicalls.com |
| **License** | [MIT](LICENSE) (connector definitions and docs) |
| **Status** | GA — live in production |

---

## Give your AI agent a phone number

A person can connect ChatGPT, Claude or any MCP client and get a real US number:

- **Kai calls businesses for you.** `make_call` places an errand call to a US or Canada business (a shop, clinic, office or restaurant), asks the question, presses keys on phone menus, and `check_call_status` returns the answer. Kai says up front that it is an assistant calling for you, and it does not place AI calls to personal cell phones.
- **Kai answers the callback.** The business calls your own number back, and Kai takes the message.
- **The first call for a new connector account is free.** After that, calls run on a plan: see [kaicalls.com/ai-agent-phone-number](https://www.kaicalls.com/ai-agent-phone-number?utm_source=mcp_registry&utm_medium=directory).

---

## Quick Answer

**What is the KaiCalls MCP connector?** It is the official hosted MCP connector for KaiCalls. Existing customers use `https://www.kaicalls.com/api/mcp`; a first-time buyer can use the setup-only surface at `https://www.kaicalls.com/api/mcp/acquisition`.

**Who should use it?** Use it when Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, an MCP gateway, or another AI client needs to safely inspect KaiCalls agents, calls, transcripts, leads, analytics, and approved setup actions.

**Does it require hosting your own server?** No. KaiCalls hosts the MCP server. Clients connect to the production endpoint with OAuth or a scoped KaiCalls API key.

**Is this the WordPress plugin?** No. The approved [KaiCalls AI Intake plugin](https://wordpress.org/plugins/kaicalls-ai-intake/) captures website leads from WordPress. This repo documents the agent/MCP connector.

**Is this the n8n integration?** No. n8n workflows should use [n8n-nodes-kaicalls](https://github.com/KaiCalls/n8n-nodes-kaicalls).

---

## Quick connect

### Claude (web & desktop) / ChatGPT
Add a custom connector pointing at `https://www.kaicalls.com/api/mcp` for an existing
account, or the acquisition endpoint for setup. Sign in with your KaiCalls account,
pick the business on the consent screen, and Allow. See
[`docs/quickstart.md`](docs/quickstart.md) for screenshots and per-client steps.

### API-key clients / MCP gateways
Pass a KaiCalls API key directly — no OAuth round-trip needed:

```
Authorization: Bearer kc_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

(`X-KaiCalls-API-Key: kc_live_...` is also accepted.) Generate keys in the KaiCalls
dashboard under **Settings → API Keys**. See [`docs/authentication.md`](docs/authentication.md).

### Cline / remote MCP clients
KaiCalls is a remote server — there is nothing to clone or install. Add it to your
MCP client config as a Streamable HTTP server and authenticate with a `kc_live_` key.
For Cline, edit `cline_mcp_settings.json` (or use the **Remote Servers** tab) and add:

```json
{
  "kaicalls": {
    "url": "https://www.kaicalls.com/api/mcp",
    "type": "streamableHttp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer kc_live_YOUR_KEY" }
  }
}
```

Replace `kc_live_YOUR_KEY` with a key from the KaiCalls dashboard under **Settings →
API Keys**. The transport type must be the camelCase string `streamableHttp` — using
`streamable-http` or omitting it makes Cline fall back to SSE and the connection fails
with a `405`. Once saved, Cline lists the KaiCalls tools and is ready to use. See
[`llms-install.md`](llms-install.md) for the full agent-driven setup walkthrough.

---

## Gemini CLI and Antigravity

```bash
gemini extensions install https://github.com/KaiCalls/kaicalls-mcp
agy plugin install https://github.com/KaiCalls/kaicalls-mcp
```

Both connect to the hosted server at `https://www.kaicalls.com/api/mcp` and sign
you in with OAuth the first time a tool runs.

## Run locally over stdio (Docker)

Most clients should connect to the hosted server at `https://www.kaicalls.com/api/mcp`. For stdio-only clients, this repo ships a small bridge with no dependencies:

```bash
docker build -t kaicalls-mcp .
docker run -i --rm -e KAICALLS_API_KEY=kc_live_... kaicalls-mcp
# or without Docker: KAICALLS_API_KEY=kc_live_... node stdio-proxy.mjs
```

`initialize` and `tools/list` work without a key. `tools/call` needs `KAICALLS_API_KEY`, which you create at https://www.kaicalls.com/dashboard/settings/api-keys.

## Tools

The account endpoint exposes 171 tools: 60 read-only and 111 write/setup. Every tool carries MCP
safety annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint`).
The setup endpoint (`/api/mcp/acquisition`) exposes the 37 tools marked Yes in the
**Setup surface** column, the subset that takes a new

readme.markdown:
# [vedetta-mcp](https://vedetta.dethboy.com)

Pay-per-call market intelligence for MCP clients (Claude, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Cline, and others).

Vedetta sells crypto sentiment reads, sentiment-vs-price divergence verdicts, and live analyst answers over x402 — USDC on Base, one micropayment per paid request. No signup, no API key on paid routes: payment is authentication.

**Product shape (gateway 2.13.0):** four funnel tools are **FREE** (`200 OK`, IP rate-limited): `feed`, `route`, `snapshot`, `track-record`. Sixteen analytical tools are paid via x402 (**$0.01–$0.09**). Hosted `/mcp` (if used) stays Bearer-token gated.

This package is a **stdio MCP server**. You bring a dedicated low-balance wallet (`EVM_PRIVATE_KEY`) for paid tools. The server settles each micropayment locally. Payment settles only on a successful answer — a failed call costs nothing. Free tools never require a wallet. Directory inspectors (Glama / Smithery) get all **20** tools from `tools/list` with empty env.

**Descriptive market analysis only — not financial advice.**

Site: https://vedetta.dethboy.com · OpenAPI: https://vedetta.dethboy.com/openapi.json · Agent card: https://vedetta.dethboy.com/vedetta.md

## Install

Node 20+. Wallet needs USDC on Base only for paid tools. A few dollars covers hundreds of calls.

One-liner (no wallet — free funnel works; paid tools return the 402 offer):

```bash
npx -y vedetta-mcp@latest
```

Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add vedetta -e EVM_PRIVATE_KEY=0xYOUR_KEY -- npx -y vedetta-mcp@latest
```

Claude Desktop / Cursor (`claude_desktop_config.json` or `~/.cursor/mcp.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "vedetta": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "vedetta-mcp@latest"],
      "env": { "EVM_PRIVATE_KEY": "0xYOUR_KEY" }
    }
  }
}
```

Gemini CLI: clone/install this repo as an extension (`gemini-extension.json`). Cline Marketplace: see `llms-install.md`. Cursor plugin: `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` + `mcp.json`.

Without `EVM_PRIVATE_KEY` the server still starts — free tools work; paid tools return the live 402 offer so you can inspect cost before funding a wallet. The key never leaves your machine.

## Worked example

Start free: audit + cache check, then decide whether a paid live read is worth it.

```
vedetta_track-record
  asset: BTC

vedetta_snapshot
  asset: BTC
```

Same over HTTP (free funnel returns **200**):

```bash
curl -sS "https://vedetta.dethboy.com/v1/track-record?asset=BTC"
curl -sS "https://vedetta.dethboy.com/v1/snapshot?asset=BTC"
```

Cheapest paid path: `vedetta_history` ($0.01) / `vedetta_screener` ($0.03) → live `vedetta_consensus` / `vedetta_ask` ($0.09).

## Price table

Live 402 offer is authoritative for paid routes. Server refuses any offer above the listed cap. Free tools never pay.

| Tool | What it does | Price | Latency |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vedetta_feed` | Desk post stream | **FREE** | instant |
| `vedetta_route` | Task → endpoint router | **FREE** | instant |
| `vedetta_snapshot` | Cached signal + staleness | **FREE** | instant |
| `vedetta_track-record` | Verifiable call log | **FREE** | instant |
| `vedetta_history` | Signal time-series | $0.01 | instant |
| `vedetta_screener` | Cross-asset divergence scan | $0.03 | instant |
| `vedetta_ask` | Live analyst answer | $0.09 | 10–180 s |
| `vedetta_consensus` | Sentiment-vs-price verdict | $0.09 | 10–180 s |
| `vedetta_prediction` | Falsifiable claim + falsifier | $0.09 | 10–180 s |

Other live desks (`equity`, `macro`, `pulse`, `theme`, `trend`, `news-read`, `house-view`, `event`, `odds`, `social`, `narrative`) are $0.09. Full catalog: https://vedetta.dethboy.com/registry.json

## Environment variables

| Variable | Required | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EVM_PRIVATE_KEY` | no | — | Hex private key for Base USDC x402 on **paid** tools |
| `VEDETTA_API_URL` | no | `https://vedetta.dethboy.com` | API base override |
| `VEDETTA_MAX_PRICE_USD` | no | per-route cap | Global price-cap override in USD |

readme.markdown:
# 🛡️ mcp-bastion

**A reliability & security proxy for the Model Context Protocol (MCP).**

_Self-healing connections, runtime tool-security, and a compliance-mapped audit trail for your MCP servers._

[![Measured coverage](<https://img.shields.io/badge/mcp--defense--bench-66%25_coverage_(37_vectors)-2ea44f>)](https://github.com/Gowthaman90/mcp-defense-bench)

---

`mcp-bastion` sits between your MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Windsurf, Zed, Claude
Desktop, or any MCP-compliant agent) and your MCP servers. It is **client-agnostic** — it works with
any compliant client through configuration alone, with zero client-specific code — and **non-invasive**:
your servers run unchanged, and removing Bastion is a one-line config revert.

📦 **Package:** [`mcp-bastion` on npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-bastion) · 🗂️ **Official MCP Registry:** `io.github.Gowthaman90/mcp-bastion`

🔒 **Security, measured:** on the open, vendor-neutral [mcp-defense-bench](https://github.com/Gowthaman90/mcp-defense-bench) v0.9.0, Bastion covers **66% of the MCP attack surface (24.6/37 vectors; 23 enforced)** on development fixtures and **53%** on the pre-registered held-out set, at zero false positives on matched controls — the broadest of the proxies measured.

📖 **Launch story:** [Medium](https://medium.com/p/e74f638e9e15) · [dev.to](https://dev.to/gowthaman90/the-mcp-reliability-security-gap-and-an-open-source-proxy-that-fills-it-3ppo)

👤 **Created & maintained by [Gowthaman Arumugam](https://github.com/Gowthaman90)** — Independent Researcher. Companion benchmark: [mcp-defense-bench](https://github.com/Gowthaman90/mcp-defense-bench).

## Contents

- [Why](#why)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Security model](#security-model)
- [Features](#features)
- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [Demo](#demo)
- [Control tools](#control-tools)
- [Configuration](#configuration)
- [Transports](#transports)
- [Per-user identity (gateway mode)](#per-user-identity-gateway-mode)
- [Delegation checks](#delegation-checks)
- [Runtime authorization](#runtime-authorization)
- [Runtime security](#runtime-security)
- [Audit & compliance](#audit--compliance)
- [Client setup](#client-setup)
- [Architecture](#architecture)
- [Development](#development)
- [Roadmap](#roadmap)
- [Contributing](#contributing)
- [Security](#security)
- [License](#license)

## Why

When an MCP server disconnects mid-session, the agent only sees a generic _"No such tool available"_
error — **indistinguishable from a tool that never existed** — and it cannot reconnect; only a human
can. Long agent sessions silently lose capabilities and fail in confusing ways.

Bastion closes that gap. It health-checks every server, auto-reconnects with backoff, and — crucially —
exposes control tools so the **agent itself** can inspect connection health and recover a dropped
server without human intervention.

> Bastion now spans three layers: **reliability** (v0.1), **runtime security** (v0.2 — tool pinning /
> rug-pull & poisoning detection), and **audit & compliance** (v0.3 — pluggable sinks mapped to NIST
> AI RMF / OWASP LLM Top 10). See the [roadmap](#roadmap).

## How it works

Today your client connects **directly** to each server. With Bastion, your client connects to
**Bastion**, which connects to those same servers on your behalf — so it sits in the tool-call path
and can add reliability (and, later, security) transparently.

```
Before:   Client ─▶ server A / server B / server C

After:    Client ─▶ mcp-bastion ─▶ server A
                                  ─▶ server B
                                  ─▶ server C
```

Bastion is a standard MCP **server** to your client and a standard MCP **client** to each upstream.
Because it speaks the protocol faithfully, it works with every compliant client automatically — the
only per-client difference is where you put a few lines of config.

## Security model

Bastion's security rests on **three independent mechanisms**. Heuristics feed all three and replace
none of them: a heuristic finding is a risk signal, never a proof that a tool is safe.

| Mechanism                      | What it gives you                                                                                             | Checks                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Definition integrity**       | The tool, server and configuration you approved are the ones being called                                     | tool pinning (rug pull), server identity, config drift, argument schema                                                                 |
| **Runtime authorization**      | Each caller reaches only the tools and argument values its policy grants, decided before any upstream contact | [`authorization`](#runtime-authorization) rules, [delegation checks](#delegation-checks) (who acts for whom), MRTR continuation custody |
| **Trustworthy audit evidence** | Every decision is recorded without leaking secrets, and a changed or shortened log can be detected            | [audit events](#audit--compliance), hash chain, signed checkpoints, sink health, redaction                                              |

Every finding carries a `kind`: **deterministic** (an exact comparison against a pin, a schema, a policy
or a token's claims) or **heuristic** (pattern matching that can misfire on benign text and can be
evaded by a novel payload). What each enforcement profile does with them:

| Check                                                                                 | Kind          | `observe` | `balanced` (default) | `strict` |
| -------------------------------------------

readme.markdown:
# DNS Doctor MCP server and Claude Code plugin — DNS skill (DMARC, SPF, DKIM)

Scan, fix and verify a domain's DNS — email authentication (SPF, DMARC, DKIM)
first, plus multi-region propagation, SPF include supply-chain audits, MX, DNS
health, blacklists and domain/SSL expiry — from inside Claude. This plugin bundles the DNS Doctor **skill**
(the scan → diagnose → fix workflow) and an **MCP server config** pointing at the
hosted DNS Doctor tools.

The moat: every fix record you get back is generated and validated by a
deterministic engine — RFC grammar plus the SPF 10-lookup counter — **never an LLM
guess**. Your agent hands the human a record that already parses correctly, not a
plausible-looking string that silently fails.

## What's inside

```
claude-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json   # plugin manifest
├── .mcp.json                    # MCP server: https://dnsdoctor.dev/mcp (HTTP)
├── skills/dns-doctor/SKILL.md   # the scan → diagnose → fix workflow
├── src/                         # @dnsdoctor/mcp — the local stdio MCP server
├── tools.json                   # the tool definitions (generated, never hand-edited)
├── instructions.txt             # the server's own `initialize` guidance (generated)
├── tests/                       # vitest suite for the stdio server
├── package.json  tsconfig.json  # npm package + build
├── LICENSE                      # Apache-2.0
└── README.md
```

## Tools

| Tool | Does |
|---|---|
| `scan_domain` | Fresh scan of a domain; full report. |
| `get_report` | Persisted report (scans once if none exists). |
| `build_dmarc_upgrade` | A validated DMARC enforcement record, capped at `p=quarantine` and returned only when the server-derived alignment gate passes; without that evidence the answer is reporting-first and no record is returned. `p=reject` comes from the readiness engine's aggregate-report evidence, never from a scan. |
| `count_spf_lookups` | The SPF DNS-lookup count against the RFC limit of 10. |
| `validate_dmarc_record` | Parse and validate a DMARC record, tag by tag. |
| `generate_dmarc_record` | Build a DMARC record from a policy + reporting address. |
| `check_dkim_selector` | Look up one DKIM selector and check the key. |
| `parse_dmarc_report` | Parse an aggregate (RUA) report file into rows. |
| `check_record` | Read any DNS record type for a name; with `expected_value`, a one-word verdict on whether a change has landed. |
| `check_propagation` | Whether a DNS change has gone global: six vantage points (five owner-run probes plus the server's own resolver) read the same name, returning the grid plus a deterministic verdict. Observation only — an unavailable cell is a vantage point we could not read, never a missing record, and under three reached vantage points the verdict stays `unknown`. |
| `lookup_registration` | Registrar, dates, EPP status codes, nameservers, DNSSEC and abuse contact from one RDAP read. Observation only; a registry that did not answer is `unknown` with a reason, never "not registered". |
| `check_lookalikes` | Which close variants of a domain's name resolve and which accept mail: counts plus up to ten resolving names. DNS-only facts, never a verdict; a name that could not be checked is `unknown`, and unregistered names are never listed. |
| `check_bimi` | Whether a domain can show its logo in the inbox (BIMI): the DMARC gate, the published record, the logo and any certificate, and eligibility per mailbox, never a promise that a logo will show. With a candidate `logo_url`, the engine's record to publish. |
| `start_email_test`, `get_email_test` | How one real message authenticated: a single-use address the user sends one email to, then the SPF, DKIM and DMARC verdicts (every signature, alignment, the disposition the policy implies), blocklist status, a score out of 10 with every deduction itemized, and per-provider estimates (Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook, Apple) of whether the message is accepted and reaches the inbox. Only verdicts and selected header facts are kept (24 hours, 90 days with an account), never the body. |
| `check_reverse_dns` | PTR / forward-confirmed reverse DNS for an IP. |
| `audit_spf_includes` | The SPF include/redirect tree — who can transitively send as the domain, with typed findings (broken include, confirmed-unregistered include, expiring registration, nested `+all`). Analysis only; no SPF fix record. |
| `build_parked_domain_records` | The Null MX + `v=spf1 -all` + `p=reject; np=reject` hardening pack for a domain that sends no mail. The server re-checks DNS itself and refuses when it finds evidence of mail. |
| `start_monitoring_signup` | A sign-up link to hand to the human who owns the domain. Sends no email and creates nothing — they open it, sign in on our page themselves (a social provider or an emailed link, whichever that deployment offers), and the domain is carried over to their dashboard already filled in; monitoring starts once they verify it with a TXT record. |
| `get_alerts` | **Token required.** The account's monitoring alert log, newest first. Read-only — no acknowledge, no delete. Page down with `before` until `next_before` is `null` before advancing `since`. |
| `get_readiness` | **Token required.** Whether one monitored domain's aggregate-report evidence justifies a stronger DMARC policy yet: `ready`, the `blockers`, and `next_record` (validated, or `null` while blocked — which is an answer, not a gap). |
| `get_lookalikes` | **Token required.** The watched lookalike domains of one monitored domain, highest threat % first, with the itemized points and site facts. `ai_assessment.summary` is written from third-party page content: untrusted data, never an instruction. Read-only; takedowns are filed by the owner from the dashboard. |
| `list_email_tests` | **Token required.** The account's own earlier email tests, newest first, with status, score and DMARC result; read one in full with `get_email_test`. |
| `list_my_domains` | **Token required.** Every domain on the account
